name: The Creative
theme: Taking on something so big it will outlast you, and keeping at it day after day anyway.

tale.title: Yu Gong, the Foolish Old Man Who Moved the Mountains
tale.source: China · Liezi, chapter 5 (“Tang Wen”), Daoist collection of the 4th century CE drawing on older material
tale.text:
North of the Yellow River, in the old days, two mountains stood side by side: Taihang and Wangwu. They were enormous, seven hundred li around and ten thousand ren high. Right in front of them lived an old man called Yu Gong, which means the Foolish Old Man. He was nearly ninety.

Every time his family went anywhere, they had to trudge the long way round. So one evening Yu Gong gathered them all and said, “Let’s flatten those mountains. Let’s cut a straight road south, all the way to the Han River.” His sons and grandsons cheered. Only his wife had doubts. “You couldn’t level a little hill,” she said. “What can you do to Taihang and Wangwu? And where would you put all that earth and stone?” “In the sea,” they answered. “Out at the far edge of the Bohai.”

So the old man set off with three sons and every grandson strong enough to carry a pole. They broke the rock, dug the soil, and hauled it away in baskets to the distant sea. A neighbour’s boy, a widow’s son so young he was just losing his milk teeth, skipped along to help. Winter turned into summer before they finished one round trip.

Down at the river bend lived a man known as the Wise Old Man. He laughed at them. “You fool. With the years you have left, you couldn’t shift one hair of that mountain, never mind its earth and its stones.” Yu Gong let out a long breath. “When I die, my sons are still here. My sons will have sons, and those sons will have sons. Sons and grandsons, without end. But the mountains will never grow any taller. So why can’t they be levelled?” The Wise Old Man had nothing to say.

Now the god who holds the snakes heard all this, and he was alarmed that the old man would never stop. He told the Lord of Heaven. And the Lord of Heaven was moved by the old man’s sincerity. He sent the two sons of Kua’e, giants of great strength, who lifted the mountains onto their backs and carried them off, one to the east of Shuo and one to the south of Yong. And from that day on, from Ji in the north to the bank of the Han, not one hill stood in the way.
beats: Nearly ninety, two vast mountains blocking his door
He resolves to level them; his wife asks where the stones go
Basket by basket to the far sea; a small boy helps
One round trip takes a whole year
The Wise Old Man mocks; “sons and grandsons, without end”
The mountain god takes fright; Heaven sends giants
Ever after, a clear road south
tale.fits: The Creative is the sky that keeps on turning. The Image says the noble one makes themselves strong and never lets up, and Yu Gong has no magic, only a habit: one basket, then the next, with a sense of time far longer than his own life. That is the last word of the Judgment, constancy, the thing that turns raw strength into creation. The third line is here too: working all day and still steady at nightfall, he takes the mockery calmly and goes on. Heaven answers the effort that does not stop.
when: a friend facing a degree, a renovation or a debt that will take years
someone starting a project they may never see finished
a colleague worn down by people saying it can’t be done
a parent wondering whether small daily efforts add up to anything
tale.open: Have you heard the Chinese story about the old man who decided to move two mountains with a basket?
tale.pause: Slow down after the Wise Old Man’s laughter and let Yu Gong’s long breath come before his answer, because that answer is the heart of the story.
tale.close: End on the empty road: “And from that day on, not one hill stood in the way.” Then say nothing and let it sit.
tale.lesson: Steady effort that outlasts the doubters is a force even heaven gives way to.

also.title: Robert the Bruce and the Spider
also.source: Scotland · legend of King Robert I in hiding (c. 1306), popularised by Walter Scott, Tales of a Grandfather (1828)
also.gist: After a string of defeats by the English, Robert the Bruce, King of Scots, is a hunted man hiding in a poor hut. Lying awake and close to giving up, he watches a spider trying to swing its thread from one roof beam to another. It falls short, and tries again, six times. Bruce has lost six battles himself. He decides that if the spider tries a seventh time and succeeds, he will fight once more. The spider swings, and the thread holds. Bruce goes out again, and in time wins back his kingdom.
also.fits: Where Yu Gong shows the strength that never lets up, Bruce is the first line: the dragon hidden in the deep, beaten and out of sight, gathering itself until it is ready to rise again.

name: The Receptive
theme: When pushing harder won’t work, and strength means bending, carrying, and letting yourself be guided.

tale.title: The Oak and the Reeds
tale.source: Greece · Aesop’s fables (Perry 70), Greek fable tradition, c. 6th century BCE onward
tale.text:
A great oak stood on the bank of a river. It was old and broad, and it was proud of how still it stood. Wind came, and the oak did not move. Rain came, and the oak did not move. For a hundred years that had been enough.

Then one autumn a storm came down the valley like nothing the oak had ever known. The wind leaned on it all night long. The oak set its branches and held, and held, and held. Near dawn there was a sound like a door being torn off its hinges. The roots let go of the bank, and the great tree crashed into the river.

The current took it. It rolled downstream, branches dragging, leaves streaming, until at last it ran aground in a bend where reeds grew thick in the shallows. There it lay, its roots up in the air like an upturned hand. And the reeds were all standing. Thin, pale, hardly anything to them, and every single one still upright, swaying a little in what was left of the wind.

The oak could not understand it. “How is this possible?” it asked them. “I am so big and so strong, and the storm tore me out of the ground. You are so slight and so weak, and it hasn’t harmed one of you.” “That’s exactly why,” said the reeds. “You fought the wind. You stood against it with all your strength, and so it broke you. We don’t fight it. When the storm comes, we bow. We lie flat if we have to. Even when the smallest breeze goes by, we bend with it. And when it has passed, we stand up again.”

The oak lay in the water and said nothing more. All around it the reeds went on moving, this way and that, with every breath of air.
beats: A proud old oak by the river, never moves for wind
The great storm; the oak holds all night
Torn from the bank and swept downstream
Runs aground among thin reeds, all still standing
“How did you survive, when I fell?”
“You fought the wind. We bow, then stand again.”
tale.fits: The Receptive is strength that works by yielding. The Judgment says that whoever leads first loses the way, while whoever follows finds a guide: the reeds let the wind set the moment, and lose nothing. The Image is the earth that carries all things, broad and unbroken because it does not resist. The oak shows what the sixth line warns of: dragons fighting in the open country, a power struggle with a force you cannot match. Both sides bleed, the line says; in this story, only the oak does.
when: a friend locking horns with a new boss they cannot change
someone proud of never bending, now close to breaking
a person in a hard season they can only ride out
a colleague who treats every compromise as a defeat
tale.open: That reminds me of one of Aesop’s fables, about an oak tree and some reeds by a river.
tale.pause: Slow down when the oak runs aground with its roots in the air, and let the listener see the reeds still standing before anyone speaks.
tale.close: End with the reeds moving “this way and that, with every breath of air,” and add nothing.
tale.lesson: Yielding to what you cannot stop is not weakness; it is how you are still standing when it has passed.

also.title: The Annunciation: “Let it be with me”
also.source: Christian scripture · Gospel of Luke 1:26-38 · written late 1st century CE
also.gist: In the town of Nazareth, the angel Gabriel comes to Mary, a young woman engaged to Joseph. He greets her as one favoured by God, and she is troubled, wondering what such a greeting can mean. He tells her she will conceive and bear a son, to be named Jesus. She asks plainly how, since she has no husband. The angel says the power of the Most High will overshadow her, and that her old kinswoman Elizabeth, called barren, is already six months with child: nothing is impossible for God. Mary answers, “See, I am the Lord’s servant. May it happen to me as you have said.”
also.fits: The reed bends because it must; Mary bends because she chooses to. She asks her honest question, then receives what comes, like the earth taking the seed: the Receptive at its most active.

name: Difficult Beginnings
theme: A hard, hungry start where nobody trusts anyone yet, and the only way forward is to get others to join in.

tale.title: Stone Soup
tale.source: European folk tale, told in many versions (stone soup in France and Portugal, nail soup in Scandinavia, axe porridge in Russia); the hero is sometimes a soldier, sometimes a tramp or a monk
tale.text:
A traveller came down the road into a village at the end of a long day. He was tired and hungry, and he had nothing in his pack but an empty pot. It had been a hard year in that village. When people saw a stranger coming, doors closed. Sacks of grain went under the beds. The last carrots and onions were pushed to the back of the shelves. “Sorry,” they said, at one door after another. “We’ve nothing to spare. Nothing at all.”

So the traveller went to the square, filled his pot at the well, and built a small fire under it. Then he took a stone out of his pocket, a smooth grey stone, and dropped it in. Plop.

A child came to look. Then another, then a few grown-ups, arms folded. “What are you making?” “Stone soup,” he said, stirring. “It’s wonderful. I’ve made it all over the country.” He tasted it and smacked his lips. “Mind you, it’s always better with a bit of cabbage.”

A woman glanced at her neighbour, went home, and came back with half a cabbage. In it went. He tasted again. “Lovely. Though a carrot or two would make it fit for a lord.” Somebody found carrots. Somebody found an onion. Someone remembered a handful of barley, someone else a pinch of salt, a bone with a bit of meat on it, a few potatoes they’d been saving. Each time the soup got better, and each time he thanked whoever had brought it.

By dark the whole village was in the square. Someone carried out a table. Someone brought bread. The soup was thick and steaming, and there was enough for everyone, with seconds. “And to think,” said an old man, wiping his bowl, “it’s made from a stone.”

In the morning the traveller fished his stone out of the empty pot, dried it on his sleeve, put it back in his pocket, and walked on down the road.
beats: A hungry traveller; every door says “nothing to spare”
A pot of water on a fire in the square
In goes a smooth stone: “stone soup”
“Better with a bit of cabbage…” and someone fetches it
Carrots, onion, barley, salt: each adds a little
A feast for the whole village
Morning: he pockets the stone and walks on
tale.fits: Difficult Beginnings is the sprout pushing through hard ground, when nothing has form yet and nobody trusts anybody. The Judgment says do not rush ahead, and appoint helpers. The traveller cannot force a single door open; he starts something small and visible and lets others take part, which is the first line’s advice: circle, hold steady, gather the right people. The Image is the noble one sorting tangled threads into a weave. A square of closed doors becomes one shared table, and the stone was only ever the excuse.
when: a friend starting a club, a business or a project from nothing
a new manager inheriting a team that keeps everything to itself
someone who feels they have nothing to bring at the start
a neighbour trying to get a whole street to do something together
tale.open: Do you know the old story of stone soup? It always comes to mind when something has to start from nothing.
tale.pause: Pause right after the stone drops into the pot, and let the listener wonder, with the villagers, what on earth he is doing.
tale.close: Finish with the traveller drying his stone on his sleeve and walking on, and leave the stone in their minds.
tale.lesson: When you have nothing, begin anyway, in plain sight, and let others bring what they have been holding back.

also.title: Issun-bōshi, the One-Inch Boy
also.source: Japan · Otogizōshi (short tales of the Muromachi period, c. 14th to 16th century), with many later folk versions
also.gist: An old couple in Naniwa pray at the Sumiyoshi shrine for a child and are given a son no taller than a fingertip. Years pass and he never grows. So he sets out for the capital with a needle for a sword, a rice bowl for a boat and a chopstick for an oar. He enters service in a great house, and in time leaves it with the lord’s daughter. When an oni attacks them, it swallows him whole; he jabs it from inside with his needle until it flees, dropping a magic mallet. A few shakes of the mallet, and he grows to full height.
also.fits: The smallest possible beginning in the hardest world: Issun-bōshi makes do with a needle, a bowl and a chopstick, and grows only after the struggle, like the sprout that must break the soil before it can stand tall.

name: Youthful Folly
theme: Coming to learn something while already sure you know it, so nothing new can get in.

tale.title: The Full Cup
tale.source: Japan · Zen anecdote told of the master Nan-in (Meiji era, 1868-1912); known mainly from 20th-century collections, earlier written source uncertain
tale.text:
In Japan, in the years when the old ways were giving way to railways and newspapers, there lived a Zen teacher called Nan-in. He lived simply, and people of every kind came to his door. One day it was a professor from the university. A learned man, well dressed, with a reputation, the kind of guest who is used to being listened to. He had read a great deal about Zen, and he had come, he said, to find out what it was really about.

Nan-in welcomed him and sat him down. He set out two cups and put the kettle on. While the water heated, the professor talked. He talked about the books he had read, and the theories he had about them, the schools and the masters and the dates, what Zen most likely meant, and where he suspected the old teachers had gone wrong. Nan-in listened, and nodded, and made the tea.

Then he lifted the pot and began to pour into his guest’s cup. The tea rose to the brim. Nan-in kept pouring. It spilled over the lip, pooled around the foot of the cup, and began to spread across the low table, creeping toward the professor’s knees. Nan-in kept pouring, quite calm, his eyes on the cup, as if nothing at all were happening and there was all the time in the world.

The professor stared. He watched the tea run toward the edge of the table. At last he couldn’t bear it any longer. “Stop! Stop, it’s full. It can’t take any more!” Nan-in set the pot down. “You are like this cup,” he said. “Full to the top with what you already think. What could I possibly pour into you? First you would have to empty your cup.”
beats: Zen teacher Nan-in; a learned professor at the door
He has come to learn what Zen really is
Kettle on; the professor talks and talks
Nan-in pours, and keeps pouring
Tea across the table: “Stop, it’s full!”
“You are like this cup.”
tale.fits: Youthful Folly is about the right way to learn. In the Judgment the teacher says: I do not seek out the young fool, the young fool seeks me. The professor does come, but he brings all his answers with him, the tangled folly of the fourth line, shut inside its own ideas and heading for a humbling. Nan-in does not argue. He lets the overflowing cup make the point, firm without cruelty, as the sixth line asks. What the cup needs is the fifth line: childlike folly, the beginner’s open not-knowing that can actually be filled.
when: a friend who asks for advice and then argues with every answer
a new colleague eager to prove what they already know
anyone about to start lessons, a course or a new job
an expert who has stopped being able to hear beginners
tale.open: There’s a little Zen story about a cup of tea that I think of every time I start something new.
tale.pause: When Nan-in keeps pouring, slow right down and describe the tea creeping across the table, so the listener feels the professor’s discomfort before he cries out.
tale.close: End on Nan-in’s words about emptying the cup. If you happen to be drinking tea together, simply pour and leave it there.
tale.lesson: You can only learn what you leave room for.

also.title: Milarepa and the Towers
also.source: Tibet · The Life of Milarepa, by Tsangnyön Heruka (15th century), about the 11th-century yogi and his teacher Marpa
also.gist: Young Milarepa, who had used sorcery to take revenge on relatives who robbed his family, and caused many deaths, comes to the master Marpa begging to be taught. Marpa gives him no teaching. Instead he orders him to build a stone tower alone, then to tear it down and carry every stone back where it came from. Again and again: a round tower, a half-moon, a triangle, each one demolished on a whim. Milarepa’s back is raw, he despairs, and Marpa’s wife pities him. Only after a great nine-storey tower stands does Marpa reveal that the labour was purifying him, and begin to teach.
also.fits: The other face of the hexagram: the first line’s discipline, firmness meant to free rather than imprison, and a student whose humility finally makes him an empty cup.

name: Waiting
theme: Waiting for a chance you can’t force, and staying calm, ready and true to yourself while it doesn’t come.

tale.title: Jiang Ziya Fishes with a Straight Hook
tale.source: China · legend of Jiang Taigong (Lü Shang) and King Wen: the meeting on the Wei River is in Sima Qian’s Shiji (c. 90 BCE); the straight hook comes from later folk lore · c. 11th century BCE setting
tale.text:
In the last days of the Shang dynasty, when the land groaned under a cruel king, an old man sat on the bank of the Wei River with a fishing rod. His name was Jiang Ziya. He was poor, and he was old, past seventy in most tellings. He had tried his hand at many things, and no court had ever wanted him. And now, every day, he fished.

But he fished strangely. His hook was not a hook at all. It was a straight piece of metal with no bait on it, and he held it above the water, not in it. People walking by would laugh. “Old man, you won’t catch a thing like that!” He would smile and say, “The fish that wants to be caught will come up to the line.” And he went on sitting there, in the sun and the wind, eating his rice, watching the river, in no hurry at all.

To the west ruled a lord of the Zhou people called Ji Chang, later known as King Wen. One day, before he went out hunting, he had the omens read, as was the custom. The answer was strange. “What you catch today will not be a dragon, nor a tiger, nor a bear. It will be the helper of a king.”

So King Wen went out, and on the north bank of the Wei he came upon an old man fishing. He stopped, and they talked. They talked about the land, and the people, and how a country is put right. The more they talked, the more delighted the king became. At last he said, “My grandfather, the Great Duke, used to say a sage would come to Zhou and make it rise. You are the one. My grandfather has been hoping for you a long time.”

He helped the old man into his own carriage and took him home. Jiang Ziya became his teacher and counsellor, and later the general who helped King Wen’s son bring down the cruel Shang and found the Zhou dynasty. To this day, when someone waits calmly for the right one to come to them, people in China say: Jiang Taigong goes fishing, and only the willing bite.
beats: Old, poor Jiang Ziya fishing on the Wei River
Straight hook, no bait, held above the water
Passers-by laugh: “The willing fish will come.”
King Wen’s omen: not a dragon, not a bear, a king’s helper
The king finds the old man; they talk and talk
“My grandfather has waited long for you.” Home in the carriage
He helps found the Zhou dynasty
tale.fits: Waiting is heaven’s strength sitting below water: strong, but the moment has not come. The Judgment says sincerity and inner confidence bring light, and the Image shows the noble one eating and drinking at ease while the clouds gather. That is Jiang Ziya on the riverbank: not fretting, not pushing, not pretending to be busy, simply ready. The fifth line is waiting with food and wine. The sixth line has guests arriving unbidden, to be met with respect, and here the guest is a king who went out hunting for something else.
when: a friend refreshing their inbox for news about a job
an artist or writer waiting for the right person to notice
someone tempted to grab any offer just to end the waiting
an older colleague who feels their moment has passed them by
tale.open: In China there’s a saying about an old man who went fishing with a straight hook. Do you know it?
tale.pause: Pause after the passer-by laughs, so the old man’s quiet answer about the willing fish has room to land.
tale.close: End with the saying itself: “Jiang Taigong goes fishing, and only the willing bite.” Then let them work out who the fish was.
tale.lesson: Make yourself ready and true, then wait without fretting; what is meant for you will come to the line.

also.title: Juan Tamad and the Guava Tree
also.source: Philippines · Tagalog folk tale of Juan Tamad (‘Lazy John’)
also.gist: Juan Tamad, Lazy John, is the Philippines’ favourite good-for-nothing. One day he spots a guava tree heavy with ripe fruit. Climbing it would be work, and shaking it would be work too. So he lies down underneath, right below the ripest guava, opens his mouth wide, and waits for it to drop in. The sun moves across the sky. Flies come and go. People pass by and shake their heads. Juan lies there hour after hour, mouth open, getting hungrier, sure the fruit will come to him if only he waits long enough.
also.fits: The shadow side of Waiting. Jiang Ziya waits ready and purposeful; Juan waits so as not to act at all. The posture is the same, the heart is opposite, and the Judgment’s condition, sincerity and staying true, is what tells them apart.

name: Conflict
theme: Being locked in a fight where neither side will let go, while someone else stands to gain.

tale.title: The Snipe and the Clam
tale.source: China · Zhanguo ce (Strategies of the Warring States), Yan section; the adviser Su Dai to King Hui of Zhao · c. 3rd century BCE
tale.text:
In the time of the Warring States, the kingdom of Zhao was getting ready to march on its neighbour, Yan. Yan sent a clever adviser, Su Dai, to the court of Zhao to try to stop it. Su Dai did not argue about borders, or who had wronged whom. He told King Hui of Zhao about something he had seen on the way.

“As I came here,” he said, “I crossed the Yi River. Out on the mudbank a clam had opened its shell to warm itself in the sun. A snipe came by, one of those long-beaked wading birds, saw the soft meat inside, and stabbed at it. The clam snapped shut, and caught the bird’s beak fast.

“The snipe said, ‘If it doesn’t rain today, and it doesn’t rain tomorrow, there’ll be a dead clam on this bank.’ The clam said, ‘If you can’t get out today, and you can’t get out tomorrow, there’ll be a dead snipe on this bank.’ So there they were. The bird pulling, the shell clamped tight. Neither would give way. Neither would let go first. The sun crossed the sky. And along the bank came a fisherman. He looked at the two of them, and he picked them both up, bird and clam together, and dropped them in his basket.”

Su Dai let that sit for a moment. Then he said, “Now Zhao is about to attack Yan. Yan will hold on. The war will drag on and on, and both our peoples will be worn down to nothing. And I am afraid that mighty Qin will be your fisherman. I beg Your Majesty to think it over carefully.”

The king thought about the snipe and the clam. “Good,” he said. And he called off the attack. The Chinese still say it, whenever two sides wear each other out: when the snipe and the clam grapple, it is the fisherman who profits.
beats: Zhao about to invade Yan; Su Dai sent to talk
A clam sunning itself on the Yi River mudbank
A snipe stabs; the shell snaps shut on its beak
“No rain: dead clam.” “No escape: dead snipe.”
Neither lets go; a fisherman bags them both
“Qin will be your fisherman.” The king calls it off
tale.fits: Conflict is heaven and water pulling apart, each side sure it is right. The Judgment is blunt: stopping carefully halfway brings good fortune, going all the way brings misfortune. The snipe and the clam are both sincere, both blocked, and both go all the way. Su Dai plays the great person the Judgment says to seek out, the fair voice of the fifth line who helps a ruler see past the quarrel. And the king takes the fourth line’s path: he could fight, but he turns back and finds peace by letting go.
when: two siblings fighting over a parent’s house or will
colleagues locked in a turf war while the project sinks
a couple who keep score in every argument
a friend set on going to court on principle
tale.open: There’s an old Chinese story an envoy once told a king to stop a war. It’s about a bird and a clam.
tale.pause: Pause after the clam’s reply, so the stalemate hangs in the air before the fisherman comes along the bank.
tale.close: End with the fisherman dropping them both in his basket, or with the king saying “Good,” and stop there.
tale.lesson: In a fight neither side will drop, the winner is usually someone else.

also.title: The Judgment of Solomon
also.source: Hebrew Bible · 1 Kings 3:16-28 · set in the 10th century BCE
also.gist: Two women who share a house come before King Solomon. Each had a baby, but one baby died in the night, and now both claim the living child. Solomon calls for a sword. “Cut the living child in two, and give each of them half.” One woman cries out, “No, my lord! Give her the child, only don’t kill him!” The other says, “Let him be neither mine nor yours. Cut him.” The king points to the first woman. “Give her the child. She is his mother.” All Israel hears of it, and stands in awe of the king’s wisdom.
also.fits: The fifth line’s just arbiter at work, with a twist from the fourth: the woman willing to lose the dispute is the one who was in the right.

name: The Army
theme: Having to turn a loose group of people into a team that truly follows through, and owning the discipline that takes.

tale.title: Sun Tzu Drills the Palace Ladies
tale.source: China · Sima Qian, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), biography of Sun Wu · c. 90 BCE, about events of the late 6th century BCE
tale.text:
Sun Wu, the man we call Sun Tzu, came from Qi to the kingdom of Wu with a book he had written on war, thirteen chapters long. King Helü of Wu had read every one. “But can you show me?” the king asked. “Could you try it out on a small scale? On women, even?” “I can,” said Sun Tzu.

So the king sent out a hundred and eighty ladies of the palace. Sun Tzu divided them into two companies and put one of the king’s two favourite concubines at the head of each. He gave every woman a halberd. Then he explained, very plainly. “You know your heart, your left hand, your right hand, your back? When I say front, look ahead. Left, turn to your left hand. Right, to your right. Back, turn round.” “Yes,” they said. He had the axes of military law set up, and went over the orders again, and again.

Then the drum sounded for “right.” The ladies burst out laughing. Sun Tzu said, “If orders are unclear and not understood, that is the general’s fault.” He explained everything again, several times over, and had the drum sound for “left.” The ladies laughed again. “If orders are clear,” he said, “and still not carried out, that is the fault of the officers.” And he ordered the two captains put to death.

From his terrace the king saw and sent a messenger running. “I see now that the general can command! But without those two ladies my food will have no taste. Spare them.” Sun Tzu replied, “I have received my commission as general. In the field, there are orders from the ruler a general does not accept.” The two captains were executed, and the next two took their places. The drum sounded again. Left, right, front, back, kneel, rise: every lady moved exactly as ordered, and not one made a sound.

Sun Tzu sent word: “The troops are in order. Your Majesty may come down and inspect them. They would go through fire and water for you now.” The king replied, “Let the general stop and go back to his lodgings. I have no wish to come down.” “The king loves the words,” said Sun Tzu, “but not their practice.” Still, Helü knew now that here was a man who could lead an army, and he made him his general.
beats: The King of Wu has read Sun Tzu’s book: “Show me.”
180 palace ladies, two royal favourites as captains
Orders explained plainly, again and again
The drum sounds; the ladies laugh, twice
Unclear orders: the general’s fault. Clear ones: the officers’
The king begs mercy; the general keeps his command
Now they move in silence; Sun Tzu becomes general
tale.fits: The Army asks for a just cause and a seasoned leader, and the first line warns that an army must set out in good order or fail, whatever its aim. Sun Tzu blames himself first and repeats his orders until nobody can misunderstand, echoing the second line, where the king’s commands come three times. Only then does he hold the officers to account. When the king tries to step in, the fifth line speaks: choose the experienced leader and do not divide the command. It is a hard story about what discipline costs.
when: a new team lead whose people treat deadlines as a joke
a teacher or coach who can’t get a group to take things seriously
a parent whose rules keep getting laughed off
a manager whose own boss keeps undercutting their decisions
tale.open: You know Sun Tzu, The Art of War? There’s a story in the old Chinese histories about how he got his job, and it’s not what you’d expect.
tale.pause: Pause after the ladies laugh the second time, and let Sun Tzu’s calm words about whose fault it is now come slowly.
tale.close: End with the king refusing to come down and Sun Tzu’s dry remark that he loved the words but not their practice, then leave it there.
tale.lesson: Make the rules clear and take the blame for confusion first; once they are clear, hold to them, even when it costs you.

also.title: Gideon’s Three Hundred
also.source: Hebrew Bible · Judges 7 · set in the time of the judges, before the Israelite kings
also.gist: Gideon gathers thirty-two thousand men against the Midianites. God tells him that is too many: Israel would boast it had saved itself. Anyone afraid may go home, and twenty-two thousand leave. Still too many. At the spring the men drink: three hundred lift the water to their mouths with their hands and lap it, while the rest kneel down to drink. Gideon keeps the three hundred. At night he gives each a trumpet and a torch hidden in an empty jar. On his signal they blow the trumpets, smash the jars, hold up the torches and shout. The great Midianite camp panics, turns on itself, and flees.
also.fits: Another side of the Army: its strength lies not in numbers but in a few committed people in good order, all moving on a single signal.

name: Holding Together
theme: A family or group starting to drift apart, and the need to hold together before it is too late.

tale.title: Alan Qo’a and the Five Arrows
tale.source: Mongolia · The Secret History of the Mongols, sections 17 to 22 · 13th century, about the legendary ancestors of Genghis Khan
tale.text:
Long before Genghis Khan, among the forebears of the Mongols, there lived a woman called Alan Qo’a, Alan the Fair. Her husband, Dobun the Marksman, gave her two sons. Then he died. And after his death, Alan Qo’a bore three more sons. The two elder boys began to whisper behind her back. “Our mother has no husband,” they said to each other, “and none of our father’s brothers lives with us. Yet she has had three sons. The only man in the tent is that servant of the Ma’aliq Baya’ut. Those three must be his.”

Alan Qo’a knew what they were saying. One spring day she boiled dried mutton, sat her five sons down in a row, and gave each of them a single arrow shaft. “Break it,” she said. Each of them snapped it easily and threw the pieces aside. Then she tied five arrow shafts tightly together and handed the bundle to each son in turn. “Break this.” The eldest tried. The second tried. The third, the fourth, the fifth. Not one of them could break it.

Then she spoke to her two elder sons. “You wonder whose sons these three are. Night after night, a radiant man, golden as lamplight, came in through the smoke-hole at the top of the tent. He laid his hand on my belly, and his light sank into me. When he left, he slipped away along the rays of the sun or the moon, like a yellow dog. Don’t talk foolishly about this. These boys are sons of Heaven. One day you will see them rule over all.”

Then she said to all five: “You five were born from my one belly. If each of you goes his own way, you are like that single arrow. Anyone at all can snap you. If you stand together, of one mind, you are like the bundle. No one can easily break you.”

Not long after that, Alan Qo’a died. And it was from the youngest of those five, Bodonchar, that the line of Genghis Khan came down.
beats: Widowed Alan Qo’a, five sons, the two eldest suspicious
Whispers about who fathered the younger three
A spring meal; each son snaps a single arrow
Five arrows bound together: none can break them
A man of light through the smoke-hole: sons of Heaven
“Alone, one arrow. Together, the bundle.”
She dies; from the youngest, Genghis Khan’s line
tale.fits: Holding Together is water gathering on the earth into one body, and the Judgment warns that whoever comes late meets misfortune. Alan Qo’a sees the rift while it is still small and acts at once, before she is gone and her sons are left as the sixth line puts it, holding together without a head. She does not order her sons to love each other; she lets them feel it in their own hands. That is the fifth line’s royal hunt with one side left open: no force, only a truth they can test themselves.
when: siblings drifting apart after a parent’s illness or death
a team splitting into camps after a reorganisation
a family where gossip has started to replace talking
old friends from a group who have stopped calling each other
tale.open: There’s a Mongol story, from the old chronicle of Genghis Khan’s ancestors, about a mother and five arrows.
tale.pause: Slow down as each son in turn tries the bundle and fails, and let the count of five do the work.
tale.close: After her words about the single arrow and the bundle, say quietly that she died not long after, and leave the bundle in their hands.
tale.lesson: Together you are hard to break; apart, anyone can snap you.

also.title: The Ten Bridesmaids
also.source: Christian scripture · Gospel of Matthew 25:1-13 · written late 1st century CE
also.gist: Ten young women take their lamps and go out at night to meet a bridegroom and walk him to the wedding feast. Five bring spare oil; five do not. The bridegroom is late, and they all doze off. At midnight a cry goes up: he is coming! The five without oil find their lamps going out and beg the others to share. “There may not be enough for us all. Go and buy some.” While they are gone, the bridegroom arrives, the ready ones go in with him, and the door is shut. When the others come back and knock, he says, “I do not know you.”
also.fits: The Judgment’s warning as a story: whoever comes late meets misfortune. Belonging is not only a feeling; it means being ready and present when the gathering happens.

name: Small Taming
theme: You want to move someone or something that will not budge, and pushing harder only makes them dig in.

tale.title: The North Wind and the Sun
tale.source: Greece · Aesop’s fables, also put into verse by Babrius and Avianus · fable tradition from c. 6th century BCE, written down later
tale.text:
The North Wind and the Sun once fell to arguing about which of them was the stronger. The Wind was loud about it. The Sun mostly smiled.

Far below them, on a long empty road, a traveller was walking along wrapped in a heavy cloak. “There’s our test,” said the Sun. “Whoever can get that cloak off his back is the stronger.” The Wind laughed. It hardly seemed a contest.

The Wind went first. It gathered itself up and blew. It blew so hard the dust lifted off the road and the trees bent over. The traveller’s cloak flapped and tugged at his shoulders, so he grabbed it and pulled it tight. The Wind blew harder. It howled, it shoved, it came at him from every side at once. And the harder it blew, the tighter the man held on, until he was hunched over, both arms wrapped round himself, the cloak clutched shut at his throat. In the end the Wind ran out of breath and gave up.

Then it was the Sun’s turn. The Sun did not do much. It came out from behind a cloud and simply shone. A little warmth on the road, that was all. The traveller straightened up. He loosened his grip. He let the cloak hang open. The Sun shone a little more, steady and patient. The man wiped his forehead. He slowed his pace. Before long he unfastened the cloak, pulled it off and slung it over his arm. In some tellings he grew so warm that he stripped off everything and went down to bathe in a river beside the road.

The Wind watched all of this from the hills, very quiet now.

The Sun had never once raised its voice.
beats: Wind and Sun argue over who is stronger
A traveller walks below in a heavy cloak
Whoever gets the cloak off wins
Wind blows hard; the man clutches the cloak tighter
The harder it blows, the harder he holds
Sun simply shines, gently and steadily
The man takes the cloak off himself
tale.fits: Small Taming is the soft force that restrains the great: wind moving over Heaven, working on surfaces rather than seizing control. The Judgment warns that forcing the release only scatters what is building, and that influence now works through tact and patience. The Wind tries the big move and gets the opposite of what it wants. The Sun acts like the fourth line, the single gentle line among five strong ones, whose sincerity means ‘fear departs’. The cloak comes off because the traveller himself chooses to take it off.
when: a parent locked in a shouting match with a teenager
a colleague trying to bully a reluctant team into a change
a friend nagging their partner to finally see a doctor
anyone convinced that pushing harder will work this time
tale.open: That reminds me of the old bet between the wind and the sun; did you ever hear how it came out?
tale.pause: Slow down after the Wind’s last and biggest gust, with the man hunched over clutching his cloak, so the listener feels the stalemate before the Sun comes out.
tale.close: End on the quiet Wind and the Sun that never raised its voice, then stop. If anything, ask lightly: “Which one have you been lately?”
tale.lesson: People open up to warmth and patience; force only makes them hold on tighter.

also.title: The Lion’s Whisker
also.source: Ethiopia · folk tale
also.gist: A woman marries a widower whose young son will not accept her. Heartsick, she asks a wise old man for a potion to win the boy’s love. He agrees, but says he needs one whisker from a living lion. Each day she carries meat out to a lion, stopping a little closer each time and speaking softly, until after many weeks the lion eats beside her and she plucks a whisker while it dozes. The wise man throws the whisker into the fire. “You approached a lion slowly and patiently,” he says. “Do the same with the boy.”
also.fits: The same gentle influence seen from the inside: no shortcut and no magic, only small daily steps that earn trust, as the fourth line’s sincerity keeps danger from striking.

name: Treading Carefully
theme: You have to live or work close to someone powerful and dangerous, and one careless step could cost you dearly.

tale.title: The Tiger Keeper
tale.source: China · Zhuangzi, ch. 4 “In the World of Men” (Qu Boyu advises Yan He) · Warring States period, c. 4th century BCE
tale.text:
In the state of Wei there was a crown prince, son of Duke Ling, with a cruel streak in him. Nobody could tell him anything. A man named Yan He had just been made his tutor, and he was frightened. He went to the wise old minister Qu Boyu and said: “If I let him do as he likes, he will ruin the state. If I stand in his way, he will ruin me. What do I do?”

“Good,” said Qu Boyu. “You are right to be careful. Keep yourself upright. Seem to go along with him, but do not get swept away. And tell me: have you never watched a keeper of tigers?”

Then he explained. The tiger keeper never throws a live animal into the cage, because the tiger would catch the fury of the kill. He never gives a whole carcass either, because the tiger would catch the fury of tearing it apart. He cuts the meat for them. He knows when they are hungry and when they are full. He watches their moods and works with their nature, never across it. Tigers are not our kind at all, and yet they fawn on the man who feeds them. The ones who get mauled are the ones who rub them the wrong way.

“And think,” said Qu Boyu, “of the man who loved his horse.”

This man adored his horse. He caught its droppings in a fine basket. He caught its water in a great clam shell. Then one day a mosquito landed on the horse, and the man, out of pure love, slapped it hard without warning. The startled horse broke its bit, reared up, and kicked him in the head and chest.

“His love was real,” said the old minister. “His intentions were perfect. But for one moment he forgot what he was dealing with. Can you afford not to be careful?”
beats: A tutor is assigned to a cruel crown prince
He fears both indulging him and opposing him
Old Qu Boyu: have you watched a tiger keeper?
Never live prey, never a whole carcass
He reads the tigers’ moods and goes with their nature
The horse lover slaps a mosquito and gets kicked
Real love, one careless moment
tale.fits: The Judgment of Treading Carefully is stepping on the tiger’s tail without being bitten, because the one who treads is courteous, aware and light of foot. The tiger keeper turns that conduct into a craft: he knows exactly where he stands and never stirs up the fury. The horse lover is the third line, who overrates his footing and is bitten. And Yan He’s whole task is the fourth line: close beside a dangerous power, but wary, and so in the end safe.
when: someone starting work under a famously volatile boss
a carer looking after a sharp-tempered elderly parent
a friend who keeps getting hurt by being ‘just honest’
a new team lead managing a touchy star performer
tale.open: Your situation makes me think of an old Chinese story about a man who kept tigers.
tale.pause: Pause just before the mosquito lands, while the man is still lovingly carrying his basket, so the slap and the kick come as a shock.
tale.close: End with the old minister’s question, “Can you afford not to be careful?”, and let the listener think about whose tiger they are tending.
tale.lesson: Close to power, careful attention to its nature keeps you safe; good intentions alone do not.

also.title: Androcles and the Lion
also.source: Rome · Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 5.14, retelling the Egyptian writer Apion · 2nd century CE, set in the early empire
also.gist: A runaway slave named Androclus hides in a desert cave in Africa. A lion limps in, groaning, and holds out a swollen paw. Androclus draws out a great splinter and cleans the wound. For three years the lion shares its kills with him. Later he is caught, sent to Rome and thrown to the beasts in the Circus. A huge lion bounds toward him, stops, and fawns at his feet: the same lion. Freed and given the lion, Androclus leads it through the streets on a light leash, and people say: here is the lion who was a man’s host, and the man who was a lion’s doctor.
also.fits: The tiger does not bite: care given long ago turns the most dangerous moment into recognition, as the sixth line looks back on a path that comes full circle.

name: Peace
theme: Everything you need is already on the table; whether it feels like plenty depends on whether people reach toward each other.

tale.title: The Long Spoons
tale.source: Folk parable told in many traditions (Jewish, Chinese, Christian and Indian versions); its first teller is unknown, and it was widely recorded from the 19th and 20th centuries
tale.text:
A man who had lived a long life asked to be shown hell and heaven before he died, so he would know what he was choosing between. His guide led him down a corridor to a door and opened it.

Inside was a great hall and a long table heaped with food. Steaming bowls of stew, bread still warm, fruit piled high. Everyone sat at the table. And everyone was starving. Their faces were grey and hollow. Each of them held a spoon, and each spoon was longer than an arm, so long they had to grip it at the very end. They dipped into the stew, lifted, twisted, strained, but no one could bend the spoon back to their own mouth. The food slopped onto the floor. They cursed. They elbowed one another. The hall was full of clatter and groaning, and the food went cold in front of them. “That is hell,” said the guide. “Now come.”

He opened a second door, and the man stopped in the doorway. It was the same hall. The same long table, the same steaming bowls, the same bread and fruit. And the same spoons, every one of them longer than an arm. But here the room was full of talk and laughter, and the faces were round and rosy.

He watched for a while before he understood. A woman dipped her long spoon into the stew, reached across the table, and fed the man sitting opposite. He thanked her, filled his own spoon, and fed the old fellow across from him. All down the table, spoons were crossing in the air. Nobody was feeding themselves. Nobody needed to.

The visitor turned to his guide. “But it is exactly the same,” he said. “The food, the table, the spoons.” “Yes,” said the guide. “Exactly the same.”
beats: A man asks to see hell and heaven
Hell: a feast, and everyone starving
Spoons longer than their arms
They strain, spill and curse
Heaven: same hall, same food, same spoons
There, each feeds the person across the table
“Exactly the same,” says the guide
tale.fits: Peace is Heaven and Earth turning toward each other: the great comes, the small goes, and everything flows because there is open exchange. In this parable heaven and hell have identical conditions; the only difference is whether people reach toward one another. The fourth line pictures those above coming down to mix with their neighbours, unguarded and sincere. The Image asks us to shape good conditions so they actually feed everyone, and the second line asks for generosity across the table, even to the rough and the far away.
when: a team where everyone guards their own targets
siblings squabbling over who cares for an ageing parent
a neighbour sure the street is ‘just unfriendly’
a couple keeping score over the housework
tale.open: There’s an old parable about heaven, hell and some very long spoons; have you heard it?
tale.pause: Pause when the second door opens on the very same spoons, so the listener expects another hell before you describe the laughter.
tale.close: End on the guide’s “Exactly the same” and stop. If the talk goes on, ask who sits across the table from them.
tale.lesson: Plenty becomes peace only when people turn toward one another and feed each other.

also.title: The Peach Blossom Spring
also.source: China · Tao Yuanming, “Record of the Peach Blossom Spring” · c. 421 CE, Eastern Jin to Liu Song
also.gist: In the Taiyuan years of the Jin, a fisherman of Wuling rows up a stream and loses his way. He comes upon a grove of peach trees in blossom, follows it to the stream’s source, and finds a narrow opening in a hill. Beyond lies a quiet valley of fields, ponds and mulberries, where friendly people live whose ancestors fled the turmoil of Qin. They have never heard of the Han, let alone Wei or Jin. They feast him for days and ask him not to speak of them. He marks his way home and tells the prefect, but no one ever finds the place again.
also.fits: Peace as a season that cannot be grasped: the harmony is real, but the moment he tries to secure and report it, it is gone, as the sixth line’s wall falls back into the moat.

name: Standstill
theme: You are offered honour and position by a system you do not trust, and the price may be yourself.

tale.title: The Sacred Tortoise in the Mud
tale.source: China · Zhuangzi, ch. 17 “Autumn Floods” · Warring States period, c. 4th century BCE
tale.text:
It was the time of the Warring States, when kings rose and fell and their ministers often fell with them. Zhuangzi was fishing on the Pu River. He had a line in the water and not much else. The river was slow and brown, and in the reeds along the edge small tortoises were pushing their way through the mud, as they do in every river. It was quiet there. Nobody wanted anything from him.

Then two high officials came picking their way down the bank in their court robes. The King of Chu had sent them. They bowed low and said: “Our king wishes to trouble you with the affairs of his whole realm.” It was the offer most men spent their whole lives hoping for: the running of a great kingdom, with all the wealth and honour that came with it.

Zhuangzi did not turn round. He held his rod and watched the water, where the line lay still. “I have heard,” he said, “that in Chu there is a sacred tortoise. It has been dead for three thousand years. The king keeps it wrapped in cloth, in a fine box, high up in the hall of his ancestors.”

The officials nodded. It was true. Everyone knew of it. “Tell me,” said Zhuangzi. “That tortoise. Would it rather be dead, and have its bones honoured like that? Or would it rather be alive, dragging its tail through the mud?”

The two officials looked at each other. It was not a hard question. “It would rather be alive,” they said, “dragging its tail through the mud.”

“Then off you go,” said Zhuangzi. “I shall drag my tail through the mud.” And he went on fishing.
beats: Zhuangzi fishes on the Pu River
Two officials bring the King of Chu’s offer
He does not even turn round
The sacred tortoise, dead three thousand years, kept in a box
Dead and honoured, or alive in the mud?
“Alive in the mud,” they admit
“Off you go. I’ll drag my tail in the mud.”
tale.fits: Standstill is the time when Heaven and Earth pull apart and the wrong people hold sway. Its Image says the noble one draws their worth inward and ‘does not let themselves be honoured with reward’. That is Zhuangzi on the riverbank: in an age when high office at a warring court could cost a man his life and his integrity, he turns down the prize and keeps his freedom. The second line adds that going along with power profits only the small; for the great, standstill itself brings success.
when: a friend tempted by a big job at a company they distrust
someone courted for a promotion that would change who they are
a colleague invited onto a leadership team they think is rotten
anyone who feels foolish for turning down prestige
tale.open: There’s a story about the Chinese philosopher Zhuangzi and a job offer he got while he was out fishing.
tale.pause: Pause after Zhuangzi asks about the tortoise, and let the listener answer it in their own head before the officials do.
tale.close: End on “I shall drag my tail through the mud” and the picture of him still fishing; no comment needed.
tale.lesson: When a system is unsound, its honours are a gilded box; keeping your life and freedom is worth more.

also.title: Why the Sky Is Far Away
also.source: Philippines · folk myth of the woman pounding rice, told in several regional versions
also.gist: Long ago the sky hung so low that people could reach up and touch it. One day a woman was pounding rice with a long wooden pestle. To work more freely she took off her comb and her beads and hung them on the sky. Every time she lifted the pestle high, it knocked against the sky. In one telling she told the sky to move up out of her way; in others the sky rose by itself, offended. Up it went, higher and higher, carrying her comb and beads, which became the moon and stars. It has stayed far away ever since.
also.fits: The very picture of Standstill: Heaven and Earth drawing apart, where a small daily impatience opens a distance that does not close again.

name: Fellowship
theme: A bond that is chosen rather than inherited, open to the outsider, and strong enough to carry people through loss.

tale.title: Ruth and Naomi
tale.source: Ancient Israel · Hebrew Bible, Book of Ruth · set in the time of the Judges, written down perhaps 6th to 4th century BCE
tale.text:
A famine came to Bethlehem, so a man named Elimelech took his wife Naomi and their two sons across the Jordan into the land of Moab. There the sons married Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. Then, over about ten years, death came for all three men. Naomi was left with nothing but two foreign daughters-in-law.

She heard there was bread again in Judah, and she set out for home. On the road she stopped and turned to the young women. “Go back,” she said. “Go back to your mothers’ houses. You were good to my sons and good to me. May you each find a husband and a home.” She kissed them, and they all wept aloud.

Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye and turned back. Ruth would not let go. She held on to Naomi and said: “Where you go, I will go. Where you stay, I will stay. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried.” Naomi saw she was determined and said no more.

They came into Bethlehem as the barley harvest began. The women of the town said, “Can this be Naomi?” “Don’t call me Naomi,” she said, for the name means pleasant. “Call me Mara, bitter. I went away full, and I have come home empty.”

Ruth went out to glean, gathering the stalks the reapers left behind. As it happened, she came to the field of Boaz, a relative of Elimelech. He noticed the foreign woman working from early morning, and he told his men to let her glean among the sheaves and to drop a little extra for her on purpose.

In time, with Naomi’s careful advice, Ruth asked Boaz for his protection, and before the elders at the town gate he took her as his wife. They had a son, Obed, who would be the grandfather of King David. Naomi held the baby in her lap, and the women said to her: “Your daughter-in-law, who loves you, is better to you than seven sons.”
beats: Famine sends Naomi’s family to Moab
Her husband and both sons die
Naomi tells her daughters-in-law to go home
Orpah goes; Ruth clings: “Your people, my people”
Back in Bethlehem, Naomi calls herself Bitter
Ruth gleans in Boaz’s field, and he looks after her
A grandson in Naomi’s lap: “better than seven sons”
tale.fits: Fellowship is a bond made out in the open country, not a closed circle; the second line even warns of regret when fellowship stops at one’s own clan. Ruth is a foreigner who chooses Naomi’s people as her own, and Boaz widens his circle to take her in, openly, before the elders at the gate. The fifth line could be the plot itself: those who belong together first weep and lament, then they laugh. The story begins with tears on the road and ends with a baby in Naomi’s lap.
when: a daughter-in-law or stepchild unsure whether they truly belong
a friend caring for someone who has lost nearly everything
a newcomer to a town, congregation or team feeling outside
someone tempted to walk away from a bond that has turned hard
tale.open: Do you know the story of Ruth? Not the Sunday school version, just two women on a road.
tale.pause: Slow right down on the road after Orpah walks away, and say Ruth’s words plainly, with a little space between each line.
tale.close: End with Naomi holding the baby and the women saying “better than seven sons”, then let it sit.
tale.lesson: Belonging is something we choose and keep choosing, and it can reach across every border.

also.title: Momotarō, the Peach Boy, and His Companions
also.source: Japan · folk tale, written down in the Edo period (17th to 19th century)
also.gist: An old woman washing clothes in a river sees a giant peach floating by and carries it home. When she and her husband cut it open, a baby boy jumps out. They name him Momotarō, Peach Boy. He grows strong and sets out to fight the ogres of Onigashima, carrying millet dumplings his mother made. On the way a dog, a monkey and a pheasant each ask for a dumpling, and each joins him. At the ogres’ island the pheasant pecks, the monkey climbs in to open the gate, and the dog bites. The ogres surrender their treasure, and Momotarō carries it home.
also.fits: Fellowship as the Image describes it: very different kinds, each given its place, joined by shared food and one open purpose, crossing the great river together.

name: Great Possession
theme: Things are going very well for you, and the real question is how you hold what you have.

tale.title: Croesus and Solon
tale.source: Greece · Herodotus, Histories 1.29 to 33 and 1.86 to 87 · written c. 430 BCE, set in the 6th century BCE
tale.text:
Croesus, King of Lydia, was the richest man in the world. His treasure houses at Sardis were stacked with gold, and wise men from all over Greece came to visit him. Among them came Solon of Athens, who had given his city its laws and then gone off to see the world.

Croesus had his servants show Solon everything, room after room of treasure. Then he asked, as if it were a small question: “Solon, you have travelled far. Who is the happiest man you have ever seen?” He was sure of the answer.

“Tellus of Athens,” said Solon. Tellus had lived while his city prospered. He had fine sons, and he saw grandchildren born to all of them, and all of them lived. Then he died fighting bravely for Athens, and the city buried him with honour where he fell. Croesus frowned. “And second?”

“Two brothers of Argos, Cleobis and Biton.” Their mother had to reach the festival of Hera, and the oxen were late from the fields. So the young men put themselves in the yoke and pulled her cart all the way to the temple, while the crowd cheered. Their mother prayed that the goddess would give her sons the best thing a person can receive. They lay down in the temple that night and never woke.

Now Croesus was angry. “And my happiness is worth nothing to you?” “You are very rich,” said Solon, “and you rule many people. But I cannot call you happy until I know you ended your life well. Look to the end of everything.” Croesus sent him away, thinking him a fool.

Years later Croesus made war on Cyrus of Persia and lost everything. Sardis fell. Croesus was put in chains on a great pyre. And standing there, he groaned the name aloud three times: “Solon! Solon! Solon!” Cyrus asked what he meant, heard the whole story, thought of his own fortune, and ordered the fire put out. But the flames had taken hold. Croesus called out to Apollo, and from a clear, still sky the clouds gathered and rain poured down and put out the fire.
beats: Croesus shows Solon room after room of gold
“Who is the happiest man you have seen?”
Solon names Tellus, then two brothers who pulled a cart
“Look to the end of everything”
Croesus sends him away, later loses his kingdom
On the pyre he cries “Solon!” three times
Cyrus relents, and rain puts out the fire
tale.fits: Great Possession is the sun at noon above Heaven: supreme success, and with it the question of how you hold what you have. The first line advises staying mindful of difficulty while prosperity is still untested; Croesus mistakes his gold for happiness and never asks. The sixth line’s good fortune belongs to the one who, at the very top, still honours what is higher than himself. Croesus learns it only on the pyre, and his humbled cry moves Cyrus, the new owner of everything, to mercy.
when: a friend whose business is booming and who has stopped listening
someone comparing their life to a richer cousin’s
a newly promoted manager who feels untouchable
anyone measuring a whole life by the bank balance
tale.open: Your question reminds me of what an old Greek told the richest king in the world.
tale.pause: Pause on the pyre just before Croesus cries out, so the listener remembers Solon a moment before he does.
tale.close: End with the rain putting out the fire. If you say anything more, just ask: “Who would you have named?”
tale.lesson: Wealth is something we hold for a while, and no fortune is secure until the whole life is seen.

also.title: Heungbu and Nolbu
also.source: Korea · folk tale, best known from the pansori and novel Heungbu-jeon · Joseon period, c. 18th to 19th century
also.gist: Greedy Nolbu takes the whole inheritance and drives his younger brother Heungbu and his family out. Heungbu lives in hard poverty but stays kind. One spring he finds a young swallow with a broken leg and binds it. The next year the swallow brings him a gourd seed. The gourds that grow are full of rice, gold, silks, even carpenters who build him a fine house. Nolbu hears of it, catches a swallow, breaks its leg on purpose and binds it. His gourds release goblins, beggars and creditors who strip him bare. In the end Heungbu takes his ruined brother in.
also.fits: The shadow of Great Possession: wealth chased with a cold heart turns to ruin, while the generous poor brother is ‘blessed by Heaven’, as the sixth line says.

name: Modesty
theme: Someone is trying to get a rise out of you, and real stature means not needing to prove anything.

tale.title: Hillel and the Wager
tale.source: Jewish · Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a · Hillel lived in the 1st century BCE; the Talmud was compiled c. 500 CE
tale.text:
Two men once made a bet: four hundred silver zuz, a small fortune, to whoever could make Hillel lose his temper. Hillel was the head of the sages, the greatest teacher of his day, and famous for his patience. One of the two said, “I will do it.”

It was a Friday afternoon, just before the Sabbath, when every household is rushing. Hillel was at home washing his hair. The man stood outside and shouted: “Who here is Hillel? Who here is Hillel?” No title. No respect.

Hillel wrapped himself in his cloak, hair still wet, and came out. “My son,” he said, “what do you need?” “I have a question.” “Ask, my son. Ask.” “Why are the heads of Babylonians round?” Now Hillel had himself come from Babylon. “You have asked a great question,” he said. “It is because they have no skilled midwives.” The man went away.

He waited a little and came back, shouting again: “Who here is Hillel? Who here is Hillel?” Again Hillel wrapped himself and came out. “My son, what do you need?” This time the man asked why the people of a certain desert town have weak eyes. “A great question,” said Hillel. “Because they live among blowing sand.” The man went away, waited, and came back a third time to ask why the people of a far country have wide feet. “A great question. Because they live in marshy country.”

Then the man said: “I have many more questions. But I am afraid you will get angry.” Hillel wrapped his cloak around him and sat down. “Ask all the questions you like.” “Are you the Hillel they call the prince of Israel?” “I am.” “Then may there not be many like you in Israel.” “Why, my son?” “Because I have lost four hundred zuz on account of you.”

Hillel said: “Mind your temper. Hillel is worth your losing four hundred zuz, and four hundred more, and Hillel will still not lose his temper.”
beats: Two men bet 400 zuz on angering Hillel
Friday, before the Sabbath: Hillel is washing his hair
“Who here is Hillel?” shouted at the door
Hillel comes out: “My son, ask”
Three silly questions, three patient answers
“I lost four hundred zuz because of you”
“Hillel is worth that, and four hundred more”
tale.fits: Modesty is the mountain hidden inside the earth: real stature that does not set itself above others. Hillel is the head of the sages, yet he comes out to a rude stranger again and again and calls each foolish question a great one. The first line speaks of being modest about one’s modesty, with nothing on display; Hillel never mentions his rank until he is asked. And the Judgment says the modest person carries things through to the end: his patience simply outlasts the provocation.
when: a colleague baited every day by a provocative coworker
a parent fielding the hundredth “why?” before bedtime
a senior person who feels disrespected by someone junior
anyone working a service counter at the end of a long week
tale.open: That reminds me of a Talmud story about a man who bet he could make a great rabbi lose his temper.
tale.pause: Pause after the third visit, when the man says he is afraid Hillel will get angry, and let the listener feel the trap closing.
tale.close: End on Hillel’s reply about four hundred zuz and four hundred more, said gently and with a smile, and leave it there.
tale.lesson: True stature shows in what you can bear without needing to prove who you are.

also.title: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom
also.source: Ghana · Ashanti (Akan) folk tale of Kwaku Anansi
also.gist: Anansi the spider gathered all the wisdom of the world into a clay pot, meaning to keep it for himself. To hide it, he decided to put it at the top of a tall tree. He tied the pot to his front and began to climb, but it kept getting in his way and he slipped again and again. His young son Ntikuma watched and said, “Father, why not tie it on your back?” Anansi was furious that a child knew better. He flung the pot down, it shattered, and wisdom scattered on the wind, so everyone got a little of it.
also.fits: Modesty’s opposite: pride and hoarding make Anansi fall, and the world does what the Image describes, taking from excess and evening it out so all receive a share.

name: Enthusiasm
theme: When you feel finished or unwanted, a spark of shared enthusiasm can gather others and get everyone moving again.

tale.title: The Bremen Town Musicians
tale.source: Germany · Brothers Grimm, Children’s and Household Tales no. 27 · 1819 edition, from older oral tradition
tale.text:
A donkey had carried sacks to the mill for his master for many years. Now he was old and tired, and the master was thinking how to be rid of him. The donkey saw which way the wind was blowing and set off down the road to Bremen. There, he thought, I can be a town musician.

Before long he found a hound lying by the road, panting. “I’m old,” said the dog. “I can’t hunt anymore, so my master wanted to kill me.” “Come with me to Bremen,” said the donkey. “I’ll play the lute and you can beat the drum.” Soon they met a cat sitting by the road, looking as gloomy as a week of rain. She was too old to chase mice, and her mistress had meant to drown her. “Come to Bremen,” they said. “You know all about night music.” Then they passed a farmyard where a rooster was crowing with all his might. Guests were coming on Sunday, and the cook meant to put him in the soup. “Come with us, Redcomb,” said the donkey. “Something better than death, you can find anywhere. And you have a fine voice.”

Bremen was too far for one day. In the forest that night, the rooster flew to the top of a tree and saw a light. They followed it to a house where robbers sat at a feast. The four made a plan. The donkey put his front hooves on the windowsill, the dog jumped onto his back, the cat climbed onto the dog, and the rooster flew up onto the cat’s head. Then they all made their music at once: braying, barking, mewing, crowing. They crashed in through the window in a shower of glass, and the robbers ran for their lives.

Later one robber crept back in the dark. The cat scratched his face, the dog bit his leg, the donkey kicked him, and the rooster screamed from the rafters. He ran back gasping: a witch had clawed him, a man had stabbed him, a black monster had clubbed him, and a judge up on the roof had shouted, “Bring the rogue to me!”

The robbers never went back. And the four musicians liked that house so much that they never left it.
beats: An old donkey runs off to be a musician in Bremen
He gathers a hound, a cat and a rooster, all unwanted
“Something better than death, you can find anywhere”
At night they find a robbers’ house with a feast
They stack up and sing all at once
The robbers flee; one creeps back and is routed
They never reach Bremen, and never need to
tale.fits: Enthusiasm is thunder bursting from the earth, a shared mood that carries people along, and its Judgment says it is the time to appoint helpers and set out. The donkey’s plan is barely sensible, but it stirs everyone he meets, and each one joins gladly. The Image honours music as what binds a community, and here one great joint noise is literally what wins the day. The donkey is the fourth line, the source of enthusiasm, with friends gathered round him ‘like hair in a clasp’.
when: a friend just retired or laid off who feels finished
a group of misfits starting a band, club or small business
a parent who thinks it is too late to try something new
someone who needs nerve to start before the plan is perfect
tale.open: You know who you remind me of? The old donkey in the Bremen Town Musicians.
tale.pause: Pause when the four are stacked up at the window, just before the music, and if you dare, make the noise yourself.
tale.close: End with “they never left it.” If someone asks about Bremen, just say: “They never got there.”
tale.lesson: Shared joy and a little nerve can carry the cast-off further than any careful plan.

also.title: David Dances before the Ark
also.source: Ancient Israel · Hebrew Bible, 2 Samuel 6 · set c. 10th century BCE
also.gist: King David brings the Ark of the Covenant up to Jerusalem with shouting and the sound of the horn. When the bearers have gone six paces, he offers a sacrifice. Then David, wearing only a plain linen garment, dances before the Lord with all his might. His wife Michal, Saul’s daughter, watches from a window and despises him in her heart. When he comes home she mocks him for showing himself off like a common fellow in front of the servant girls. David answers that he danced before the Lord, and he will make himself even less dignified than this.
also.fits: The Image itself: music and joy offered up to what is highest. Michal at the window shows the other side, enthusiasm judged from a distance by one who will not join in.

name: Following
theme: Choosing whom to follow, and how a leader earns followers by first being willing to bow to real worth.

tale.title: Three Visits to the Thatched Cottage
tale.source: China · Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang, 207 CE; Chen Shou’s Records of the Three Kingdoms (3rd century) and Zhuge Liang’s own memorial say only that Liu Bei called three times; the details of each visit come from Luo Guanzhong’s Romance of the Three Kingdoms (14th century)
tale.text:
China, near the end of the Han. The empire had cracked into pieces, and every warlord with an army wanted one. Liu Bei was one of them, though a poor one: a distant cousin of the emperor, famous for his kindness, with two loyal sworn brothers and almost no land at all. He was well past forty, and still had no home of his own.

His adviser Xu Shu told him: “There is a young man living on a hill at Longzhong. He farms, he reads, he sings old songs. People call him the Sleeping Dragon. You can go and see him. You cannot send for him.”

So Liu Bei went. He rode out with his brothers, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei, to a little thatched cottage among the bamboo. A boy opened the gate. “The master is out. I don’t know when he’ll be back.” They rode home. Weeks later, in winter, they went again. Snow blew sideways. Zhang Fei grumbled that a country scholar should come to them, not the other way round. At the cottage they found a young man reading by the fire, but it was only the younger brother. The Sleeping Dragon was away. Liu Bei left a letter and rode home through the snow.

In spring he went a third time. He got down from his horse well before the gate and walked the rest of the way. The boy said the master was home, but asleep. Liu Bei told him not to wake him. He stood at the foot of the steps with his hands folded, and waited. Zhang Fei wanted to set fire to the house to rouse the fellow. Guan Yu held him back. The sun moved across the yard. Liu Bei did not move.

At last Zhuge Liang woke, dressed, and came out: a man of twenty-six, twenty years younger than his guest. They talked for hours. Zhuge Liang laid out the whole map of the future: where to take land, whom to ally with, whom to resist. Then he left his cottage and followed Liu Bei, and served him, and after him his son, for the rest of his life. Liu Bei used to say: “Having him is like a fish having water.”
beats: A homeless warlord, past forty, needs a strategist
“You can go and see him. You cannot send for him.”
First visit: the master is out
Second visit, in snow: only the younger brother
Third visit: Liu Bei waits at the steps while he sleeps
Zhuge Liang wakes, maps the future, and follows
“Like a fish having water”
tale.fits: Following says people follow freely only someone who first knows how to follow, and Liu Bei proves it by bowing three times to a man twenty years younger. The first line says to go out of your own gate to meet people, and he does, again and again, through snow. The nine in the fifth place, sincere in following the good, is his trust in real excellence over rank. And the Judgment’s great success comes with a condition, staying true: neither man follows for gain, so the bond holds for life.
when: a manager hoping to hire someone better than themselves
a friend too proud to ask a second time
someone choosing a mentor, a teacher or a cause to join
a leader wondering why nobody really follows them
tale.open: You know, there’s an old Chinese story about a general who knocked on the same cottage door three times…
tale.pause: Slow right down when Liu Bei stands at the foot of the steps while the young man sleeps, and let the waiting fill the room.
tale.close: End on the fish and the water, then let it sit; if you say anything, say: “He went three times. I wonder how many of us would have gone twice.”
tale.lesson: To be followed, first be willing to follow what is better than you; humility toward true worth wins a loyalty no rank can command.

also.title: Elisha Follows Elijah
also.source: Hebrew Bible · 2 Kings 2 · compiled around the 6th century BCE
also.gist: On the day Elijah is to be taken from the earth, he tries three times to leave his disciple behind: stay here, he says, I must go on to Bethel, then to Jericho, then to the Jordan. Each time Elisha swears he will not leave him. Other prophets whisper that the master will be taken today; Elisha hushes them. At the river Elijah strikes the water with his rolled-up cloak and they cross on dry ground. Asked what he wants, Elisha asks for a double share of his master’s spirit. A chariot of fire comes between them, Elijah goes up in a whirlwind, and Elisha picks up the fallen cloak.
also.fits: Here it is the follower who will not be shaken off, the top line’s bond tied tighter still; following to the very end, he inherits the cloak.

name: Repairing the Spoiled
theme: Inheriting a mess that someone before you made, and setting it right without repeating their mistake.

tale.title: Yu the Great Tames the Flood
tale.source: China · legend of Yu, founder of the Xia, in the Book of Documents (Shujing) and Sima Qian’s Shiji (c. 100 BCE), with details from Mencius · legendary setting c. 2000 BCE
tale.text:
In the time of the sage kings, the waters rose and would not go down. Rivers broke their banks and wandered across the plains. Villages stood like islands. People climbed into the trees and onto the hills, and lived up there with the birds.

King Yao asked his ministers who could stop it. They named a man called Gun. Gun was strong and stubborn, and he did what anyone would do: he built walls. He dammed the rivers, raised dykes, blocked the water wherever it came. For nine years he built. And for nine years the water rose behind his walls, broke through, and came down worse than before. In the end Shun, who ruled after Yao, took the work from him and banished him to Feather Mountain, and there Gun died.

Then Shun sent for Gun’s son. His name was Yu. Imagine it: being handed the job that broke your father, by the man who punished him. Yu did not refuse. And he did not rebuild his father’s walls.

First he walked. He crossed the whole land on foot and by boat, climbing the mountains, marking the trees, learning which way the ground fell and where every river wanted to go. Then he dug. Instead of fighting the water, he gave it a road. He cut channels, deepened riverbeds, opened gorges, and led the rivers down to the sea. He worked beside the labourers, a spade in his own hands, until, people said, the hair on his legs had worn away.

Thirteen years he was gone. Three times his road took him past his own front door. Once, the old book says, his baby son was crying inside. He did not go in. He kept walking.

And at last the water went where it belonged. The land came up out of the mud. People came down from the hills and planted millet. When Shun grew old, he passed over his own son and gave the throne to Yu, the son of the man who had failed.
beats: The great flood: people living in the trees
Gun builds walls for nine years; they all burst
Gun is banished; his son Yu is given the job
Yu walks the whole land before he digs
He gives the water a road to the sea
Three times he passes his own front door
The land rises; the throne goes to Yu
tale.fits: Repairing the Spoiled is the hexagram of setting right what the father spoiled, and its first line says that if there is such a son, the late father is free of blame: Yu does exactly that. The Judgment asks for three days of thought before you start, and Yu walks the whole land before he lifts a spade. The Image of wind stirring beneath the mountain is the work itself, shaking stagnant water loose and getting a whole people moving again.
when: someone who has taken over a failing team or family business
a person trying hard not to repeat a parent’s pattern
a friend about to fix a mess the same way it was made
anyone cleaning up after a predecessor and feeling the weight
tale.open: There’s an old Chinese story about a man who was handed his father’s job, the very job his father had failed at…
tale.pause: Pause after “And he did not rebuild his father’s walls”: that is the turn, and the listener should feel it before you tell them how.
tale.close: End with the throne going to the son of the man who failed, and leave it there; or ask lightly, “What would you have built?”
tale.lesson: Repair an inherited failure by understanding it first and changing the method, not by repeating it harder.

also.title: The Augean Stables
also.source: Greece · one of the Labours of Heracles, as told by Apollodorus (Library 2.5, 1st or 2nd century CE) and Diodorus Siculus
