also.gist: King Eurystheus wanted Heracles humiliated, so he set him to clear, in a single day, the stables of King Augeas of Elis, where great herds of cattle had stood for years and the dung had never been taken away. Heracles did not pick up a shovel. He broke open the walls of the yard and turned two rivers, the Alpheus and the Peneus, through it, and the current carried off years of filth. He had bargained with Augeas for a tenth of the herd; Augeas refused to pay, and Eurystheus refused to count the labour, saying it had been done for hire.
also.fits: Like Yu, Heracles cleans by redirecting a river rather than fighting the mess by hand; but a repair done for wages and haggled over leaves a little regret of its own, like the third line’s.

name: Approach
theme: A good season of growth, and the leader who comes close to people to look after them rather than to take from them.

tale.title: Emperor Nintoku and the Kitchen Smoke
tale.source: Japan · Emperor Nintoku, in the Kojiki (712) and the Nihon Shoki (720) · legendary reign, traditionally placed in the 4th or 5th century CE
tale.text:
In old Japan, early in his reign, Emperor Nintoku climbed a high tower and looked out across his land. It was evening, the hour when every house should be cooking. He looked for the thin grey threads of smoke that rise from kitchen fires. There were hardly any.

He understood at once. If no one is cooking, no one has rice. His people were too poor to light their stoves, and the reason, in part, was him: the taxes, the labour owed to the court, the hands taken from the fields. So he stopped it. For three years, no taxes. No forced labour. Nothing taken.

The palace began to fall apart. The fence came down and nobody mended it. The thatch rotted. When it rained, water came through the roof and soaked the bedding, and the emperor moved from corner to corner to keep dry. At night, the old chronicle says, starlight leaked in through the holes onto his bed. His robes wore thin, and he did not replace them. He ate plain food.

Three years later he climbed the tower again. It was evening. And from every village, as far as he could see, smoke was rising, thick as reeds.

He turned to the empress and said, “Now we are rich.” She looked up at the holes in the roof. “The walls are falling down, the rain comes in on our bed, and you call us rich?” He told her that heaven sets up a ruler for the sake of the people. When the people are poor, the ruler is poor. When the people have plenty, so does he.

In the Nihon Shoki’s telling, the people themselves then begged to pay taxes again and to repair the palace, and still he made them wait. When at last he allowed it, they came of their own accord, old and young, carrying timber and baskets of earth, working day and night with no one to drive them. The palace stood again in no time at all. They called him the sage emperor.
beats: An emperor looks out from his tower at evening
Almost no kitchen smoke: his people are hungry
He cancels all taxes and labour for three years
The palace leaks; starlight falls on his bed
Smoke rises everywhere: “Now we are rich”
The empress asks how, with rain on their bed
The people rebuild his palace gladly, unforced
tale.fits: Approach is the hexagram of someone above coming near those below to care for them, and its Image asks for a boundless willingness to tolerate and protect the people. Nintoku draws near by looking: he reads the smoke. The six at the top, the generous approach, is his three years of empty storehouses and a leaking roof. The Judgment’s warning about the eighth month, that every spring turns to autumn, is why he gives before he takes, so the good season lasts.
when: a new manager wondering what to change first
a parent who judges the home by the house, not the people
a small business owner tempted to squeeze the staff
someone who measures success by their own comfort
tale.open: Have you heard how an old emperor of Japan worked out that his people were hungry? He looked at their chimneys.
tale.pause: Pause on the second climb up the tower, before the smoke appears, so the listener leans in to see what he saw.
tale.close: Finish with the people carrying timber up to the palace of their own accord, and say nothing more; let them do the arithmetic.
tale.lesson: Come close enough to see how those in your care really live, and give before you take; loyalty grows back on its own.

also.title: Harun al-Rashid Walks the City at Night
also.source: Arabic · One Thousand and One Nights, in frame tales such as “The Porter and the Three Ladies of Baghdad” · medieval collection; the caliph reigned 786 to 809
also.gist: In many tales of the Nights, the caliph Harun al-Rashid grows restless in his palace, puts on a merchant’s clothes, and slips out into Baghdad after dark with his vizier Ja’far and his swordsman Masrur. In one, they talk their way into a strange house kept by three sisters, promise not to ask about anything they see, and cannot help asking. The next morning the caliph summons everyone he met, hears each of their stories in full, and puts right the wrongs behind them. The ruler learns the truth only by coming down, unknown, into the street.
also.fits: This is the fourth line’s complete approach, a ruler genuinely reaching those below; but he does it in disguise, a reminder that people show their real lives most readily to someone they do not fear.

name: Contemplation
theme: Seeing only part of the picture and mistaking it for the whole, and the need to look wider before you judge.

tale.title: The Blind Men and the Elephant
tale.source: India · Udāna 6.4 in the Pali Buddhist canon, a teaching the Buddha gives at Sāvatthī · early Buddhist, written down in Sri Lanka around the 1st century BCE
tale.text:
In the Buddha’s time, the city of Sāvatthī was full of wandering teachers, and they could not stop arguing. The world is eternal, said one. The world is not eternal, said another. The soul and the body are the same; no, they are different. They quarrelled in the squares and wounded each other with words, each one shouting: this is the truth, and everything else is nonsense.

The monks told the Buddha about it, and he told them a story. Long ago, a king of this same city said to one of his men: “Go and gather together all the people in Sāvatthī who were born blind.” When they were assembled, he had an elephant led in, and he let each of them touch one part of it. Then he asked them: “Tell me. What is an elephant like?”

The ones who had touched the head said, “An elephant is like a water jar.” The ones who had felt the ear said, “No, it’s like a winnowing basket.” Those at the tusk said, “A ploughshare.” Those at the trunk said, “The pole of a plough.” Those who had felt its body said it was a storehouse for grain; its leg, a post; its rump, a mortar; its tail, a pestle; the tuft at the end of the tail, a broom.

“It’s like this!” “It is not, it’s like that!” The argument grew louder, until they were hitting each other with their fists. The king watched it all, and he was delighted.

The Buddha said the wandering teachers were like those men. Each had hold of one piece and called it the whole, and so they fought. Then he spoke a short verse: some people cling to their views, and quarrel, because they see only one side of a thing.
beats: Teachers in a city quarrel over what is true
A king gathers everyone in the city born blind
Each touches a different part of an elephant
Water jar, basket, ploughshare, post, broom
They argue, then come to blows
The king watches, delighted
Each held one piece and called it the whole
tale.fits: Contemplation is about seeing clearly and seeing whole. The blind men are its first two lines: the child’s way of looking, and peeping through the crack of a door, a narrow slice taken for everything. The king stands where the two strong lines stand at the top, high enough to see the whole animal and the whole quarrel. And the Image of the ancient kings going out to observe before they taught is the Buddha’s own method here: he listens to the arguments, then tells a story.
when: two colleagues each sure the other has misread the data
a family arguing about what is wrong with a relative
someone who has read one article and is now certain
a friend stuck in an online fight they cannot win
tale.open: This argument reminds me of something the Buddha is supposed to have told his monks, about an elephant…
tale.pause: Slow down through the list of objects and give each group its own confident voice, so the listener feels how reasonable every one of them sounds.
tale.close: End on the king watching, delighted, and stop; or wonder aloud, “I wonder which part we’re holding.”
tale.lesson: Each of us touches only part of the truth; hold your view lightly and look for the whole before you fight for it.

also.title: The Frog in the Well
also.source: China · Zhuangzi, chapter 17 (“Autumn Floods”) · 4th to 3rd century BCE
also.gist: A frog lives in a broken-down old well. To a great turtle from the Eastern Sea he boasts of his happy life: hopping along the rim, resting in the gaps of the crumbling brickwork, swimming with water up to his armpits, sinking his feet in soft mud. What could be better? Come in and see! The turtle tries, but before his left foot is in, his right knee is already stuck. He backs out and tells the frog about the sea: in the great floods of Yu’s time it never rose, and in the droughts of Tang’s time it never sank. The frog is stunned and quite at a loss.
also.fits: The frog is the first line’s child’s way of looking, perfectly content with a narrow view; it shows the shadow of Contemplation, not knowing there is more to see.

name: Biting Through
theme: A lie or a wrong stuck in the middle of things that has to be bitten through with a clear, firm judgment.

tale.title: Judge Bao and the Ox’s Tongue
tale.source: China · Bao Zheng (999 to 1062) as magistrate of Tianchang county; recorded in his biography in the History of Song (Song shi, 14th century) and retold in later Judge Bao lore
tale.text:
Long before the operas painted him with a black face and a crescent moon on his brow, Bao Zheng was the magistrate of a farming county called Tianchang, in Song dynasty China. Rice paddies, mud, and oxen. In those days the ox was everything: it pulled the plough, and without it a family went hungry. So the law was strict. No one was allowed to slaughter a farm ox.

One morning a farmer came into the court, shaking with anger. Someone had crept into his stable in the night and cut out his ox’s tongue. The animal was still alive, but it could not eat. It would die slowly. Who would do such a thing? He had no idea. He had no witness. He wanted justice, and there was nothing to go on.

Bao Zheng listened. Then he said something the farmer did not expect. “Go home. Kill the ox. Sell the meat.”

The farmer stared at him. Kill it? That was against the law. But the magistrate himself had said it, so he went home, slaughtered the ox, and sold the meat. The neighbours watched him do it.

Not long after, another man came into the court. He had a crime to report. “That farmer,” he said, “has slaughtered his ox without permission. Everyone saw him selling the meat.” He stood there, looking pleased with himself.

Bao Zheng looked at him for a long moment. Then he asked: “Why did you cut out his ox’s tongue, and then come here to accuse him?” The man went white. He had no answer. He confessed on the spot. Bao had only needed to wait for the one person who wanted the farmer ruined more than he wanted to stay hidden.
beats: A Song dynasty county where the ox is everything
Someone cuts out a farmer’s ox’s tongue at night
No witness, no suspect, nothing to go on
Bao says: go home, kill it, sell the meat
Killing an ox is illegal; a man comes to report it
“Why did you cut out his tongue, then accuse him?”
tale.fits: Biting Through is the open mouth with something stuck between the teeth, and its Judgment says it is favorable to administer justice. Here the obstacle is a hidden spite with no witness, and Bao bites through it with one question. The Image of thunder and lightning is that sudden flash in which the culprit stands exposed. And the six in the fifth place, biting dried lean meat and finding yellow gold, is the judge in the center: firm, fair and clear-headed, never cruel.
when: a manager facing a quiet saboteur on the team
a friend caught in a dispute where nobody has proof
a parent trying to work out which child started it
someone hoping a lie will simply go away by itself
tale.open: There’s a story about Judge Bao, the famous Chinese magistrate, and a farmer whose ox had its tongue cut out…
tale.pause: Pause after “Go home. Kill the ox. Sell the meat,” and let your listener be as puzzled as the farmer was.
tale.close: Stop on the judge’s question and the man going white; if they ask how he knew, say only, “He let the man’s own spite walk him through the door.”
tale.lesson: A clear mind can cut through a knot of lies by giving the wrongdoer room to reveal himself.

also.title: Ali Cogia, Merchant of Baghdad
also.source: Arabian Nights · one of the tales added by Antoine Galland to his French translation (1704 to 1717)
also.gist: Before a long journey, Ali Cogia leaves a jar of olives with a neighbour; beneath the olives lie a thousand gold pieces. Seven years pass. One evening the neighbour opens the jar for olives, finds the gold, keeps it, and refills the jar with fresh olives. Ali finds his gold gone, and the judge clears the neighbour for lack of proof. Then Harun al-Rashid, walking at night, hears children playing at the trial. The boy playing judge asks olive sellers whether seven-year-old olives could still be fresh. Next day the caliph lets that boy judge the real case, and the fresh olives give the thief away.
also.fits: Another lie bitten through by one clear, simple question; and a reminder that the clearest judgment can come from an unexpected mouth.

name: Grace
theme: Being so taken with the packaging that you overlook what it was meant to hold.

tale.title: Buying the Box and Returning the Pearl
tale.source: China · Han Feizi, chapter 32 (“Outer Collection of Sayings, Upper Left”), told by the scholar Tian Jiu to the King of Chu · 3rd century BCE
tale.text:
The King of Chu once put a question to a scholar named Tian Jiu. “The philosopher Mozi is a great man. His ideas are good. So why are his speeches so plain? Why doesn’t he speak beautifully?”

Tian Jiu answered with stories. First he told of a lord of Qin who married his daughter to a prince of Jin. He sent her off with seventy maids, every one of them dressed in embroidered silk. When they arrived, the people of Jin fell in love with the maids, and hardly looked at the bride. “That,” said Tian Jiu, “was a man good at marrying off maids. Not at marrying off his daughter.” Then he told another.

A man from Chu had a pearl to sell, a really fine one, and he took it to the market in the state of Zheng. He wanted it to look its best. So he had a box made for it out of magnolia wood. He perfumed the box with cinnamon and pepper. He studded it with jade and pearls, set it with red gemstones, and trimmed it with kingfisher feathers, blue as deep water.

It was a wonderful box. People crowded round. A man from Zheng held it in his hands, breathed in the scent, turned it in the light, and bought it on the spot. Then he opened it, took out the pearl, and handed it back to the seller. He didn’t need that. He walked home with his box.

“You could call that man very good at selling boxes,” said Tian Jiu. “You could not call him good at selling pearls.” The clever talkers of our day, he went on, decorate their words so finely that people admire the words and forget what they were for. Mozi speaks plainly because he does not want his listeners to keep the box and hand back the pearl.
beats: A king asks why a wise man speaks so plainly
Seventy finely dressed maids outshine a bride
A Chu merchant takes a pearl to Zheng
He builds a perfumed box of magnolia, jade and feathers
The buyer keeps the box and hands back the pearl
“Good at selling boxes, not at selling pearls”
tale.fits: Grace is the beauty of form, and the Judgment gives it only small success: ornament, not substance. The box is grace overgrown, like the six in the second place, giving grace to the beard, fussing over what only follows the chin. The Image warns that a lovely surface serves for small matters but not for grave ones. And the nine at the top, simple white grace, is Mozi’s plain speech: form so honest it no longer needs decoration.
when: a colleague polishing the slides before the idea is ready
a friend planning the wedding more than the marriage
someone choosing a job for the office and the logo
a writer whose style is starting to hide the point
tale.open: That makes me think of an old Chinese story about the most beautiful box in the market…
tale.pause: Linger over the making of the box, one ornament at a time, so the listener falls for it too before the pearl is handed back.
tale.close: End with the buyer walking home with his empty box, pleased with himself, and let a moment pass before anyone speaks.
tale.lesson: When the wrapping is too fine, people keep the wrapping and miss the gift; let form serve substance.

also.title: “Eat, My Coat!”
also.source: Turkey · Nasreddin Hodja folk anecdote · Hodja is traditionally placed in 13th-century Anatolia; the tales are told from the Balkans to Central Asia
also.gist: Nasreddin Hodja hears of a feast and goes along in his everyday clothes. No one greets him, no one offers him a seat, and the dishes pass him by. So he slips home, puts on his finest fur coat and comes back. Now the host bows, leads him to the place of honour and sets the best food in front of him. Hodja dips the sleeve of his coat into the soup. “Eat, my coat, eat!” he says. The guests stare. “Well,” says Hodja, “it seems it was the coat you invited, not me.”
also.fits: The other side of the box and the pearl: here the world itself honours the wrapping over the person, and Hodja turns that into a joke that shows it up.

name: Splitting Apart
theme: A slow decline that starts small and quietly, and the cost of refusing to see it while it can still be stopped.

tale.title: Bian Que and Duke Huan of Cai
tale.source: China · Han Feizi, chapter 21 (“Illustrating Laozi”) · 3rd century BCE; Sima Qian’s Shiji tells a similar story with Duke Huan of Qi
tale.text:
Bian Que was the most famous doctor of ancient China. People said he could look at a man and see straight through him, as if the body were made of clear water.

One day he came before Duke Huan, the lord of Cai. He stood and looked at the duke for a while, and then he said, “My lord, you have an illness. It is in the skin. If you do not treat it, it will go deeper.” The duke said, “I have no illness.” When the doctor had gone, the duke said to his courtiers, “Doctors love to cure people who are not sick. Then they can take the credit.”

Ten days later Bian Que came again. “My lord, the illness is in your flesh now. If you do not treat it, it will go deeper.” The duke did not answer. He was not pleased. Ten days after that: “My lord, it has reached your stomach and bowels. If you do not treat it, it will go deeper still.” Again no answer. Again the duke was not pleased.

Ten more days passed. This time, when Bian Que caught sight of the duke from a distance, he simply turned round and hurried away. The duke was curious and sent someone after him to ask why. Bian Que said: “When an illness is in the skin, warm compresses can reach it. In the flesh, needles can reach it. In the stomach, strong hot draughts can reach it. But once it is in the marrow, it belongs to the god who rules over life and death, and there is nothing anyone can do. It is in the marrow now. So I had nothing more to say.”

Five days later, the duke’s body began to ache all over. He sent people running to find Bian Que. But the doctor had already gone, over the border to the state of Qin. And soon after that, the duke died.
beats: The doctor who could see through a body
“Your illness is in the skin.” “I’m not ill.”
Ten days: in the flesh. No answer.
Ten days: in the stomach. No answer.
Ten days: the doctor turns and hurries away
“In the marrow, nothing can reach it”
Five days later the duke aches; the doctor is gone
tale.fits: Splitting Apart shows decay climbing from below: the legs of the bed, then the frame, then, in the six in the fourth place, the skin of the one lying in it, when the blow can no longer be dodged. The duke’s illness climbs in just such steady stages, ten days at a time. The Judgment says it does not pay to go anywhere, and Bian Que’s quiet exit is that wisdom: once decline has run too far, do not fight it. The time to act was at the legs of the bed.
when: a friend shrugging off a small but nagging health worry
a business owner waving away the early bad numbers
a couple who keep saying the problem isn’t serious
someone annoyed at the colleague who keeps raising the alarm
tale.open: There’s an old Chinese story about a doctor who kept visiting a duke who swore he wasn’t ill…
tale.pause: Pause just before Bian Que turns and hurries away without a word; that silence is the diagnosis.
tale.close: End plainly with the doctor already gone to Qin; if you add anything, add only: “He did come four times.”
tale.lesson: Decline creeps in by small stages; heed the warnings while the trouble is still only skin deep.

also.title: Pandora’s Jar: Hope Remains
also.source: Greece · Hesiod, Works and Days, lines 42 to 105 · c. 700 BCE (the ‘box’ is a much later mistranslation of the Greek pithos, a storage jar)
also.gist: Because Prometheus stole fire for humankind, Zeus planned a gift with a sting in it. He had Hephaestus shape a woman from earth and water, and the gods dressed her in every grace; she was named Pandora, ‘all gifts’. Prometheus had warned his brother Epimetheus never to accept a gift from Zeus, but Epimetheus took her in. Pandora lifted the lid of a great storage jar, and out flew the troubles and sicknesses that now wander the world in silence. Only Hope stayed inside, under the rim, for by Zeus’s will she put the lid back before it could fly out.
also.fits: When everything has flown apart, one thing is left inside: the nine at the top, the great fruit still uneaten, whose seed will grow again.

name: Return
theme: Turning back after you have gone astray, and being welcomed home sooner than you dared to hope.

tale.title: The Prodigal Son
tale.source: Gospel of Luke 15:11 to 32 · a parable of Jesus, written down c. 80 to 90 CE
tale.text:
A man had two sons. One day the younger one came to him and said, “Give me my share of what I’ll inherit.” The father divided up what he had. A few days later the boy turned his share into money and set off for a country far away.

There he threw it all around, living as he pleased, until nothing was left. Then a hard famine came over that land. He hired himself out to a local man, who sent him into the fields to mind the pigs, and he was so hungry he longed to eat the bean pods the pigs were eating. Nobody gave him anything.

There, among the pigs, he saw himself clearly. “At home my father’s hired workers have more bread than they can eat, and here I am starving. I’ll go back. I’ll say: Father, I have done wrong, against heaven and against you. I’m not fit to be called your son any more. Take me on as one of your hired men.” He got up and set off.

He was still a long way from the house when his father saw him. The father’s heart went out to him, and he ran down the road and threw his arms around his son and kissed him. The son began his speech: “Father, I have done wrong. I’m not fit to be called your son…” He never got to the part about the hired men. The father was already calling to the servants: “Quick! The best robe, put it on him. A ring for his hand, sandals for his feet. Kill the fattened calf. We’ll eat and celebrate. This son of mine was dead and has come back to life. He was lost, and he has been found.”

The elder son was out in the fields. Coming home, he heard music and dancing, and when he learned why, he was furious and would not go in. So the father came out to him. “All these years I’ve slaved for you,” said the son, “and never once disobeyed you. You never gave me so much as a young goat to feast with my friends. But this son of yours comes back after wasting your money, and you kill the fattened calf for him!”

“My child,” said the father, “you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate. This brother of yours was dead, and is alive. He was lost, and is found.”
beats: The younger son takes his inheritance and leaves
He wastes it all in a far country
Famine: minding pigs, envying their food
He rehearses a speech and heads home
The father sees him far off and runs
Robe, ring, sandals, a feast
The elder brother stands outside, angry
tale.fits: Return is the light coming back after the darkest point, and its Judgment promises going out and coming in without harm, and friends arriving. The son’s turning among the pigs is the six in the fourth place, walking among others and returning alone. His honest speech, with no excuses, is the great-hearted return of the six in the fifth place. And the elder brother, standing outside the music, is the shadow at the top: the moment of return is there, and he may miss it.
when: a friend ashamed to call home after a long silence
a parent wondering how to receive a child who strayed
a sibling who always did right and feels unseen
someone who broke a promise to themselves and wants to restart
tale.open: There’s a story Jesus told, about a father and his two sons, and I always think of it at times like this.
tale.pause: Slow down when the father sees him from far off and starts to run; let the listener picture the long road between them.
tale.close: End on the father’s words to the elder son and stop there; if anyone asks, say, “The story never tells us whether he went in.”
tale.lesson: It is never too late to turn back, and the welcome is often warmer than the shame that kept us away.

also.title: Urashima Tarō
also.source: Japan · folk tale; early forms in the Nihon Shoki, the Man’yōshū and the Tango fudoki (8th century), the familiar version shaped by the Otogizōshi (14th to 16th century) and later retellings
also.gist: A young fisherman, Urashima Tarō, saves a turtle from some children who are tormenting it. In thanks the turtle carries him to the Dragon Palace beneath the sea, where the princess Otohime welcomes him. After what feels like three years he grows homesick and asks to go back. The princess gives him a lacquered box and begs him never to open it. On the shore nothing is as it was: his house is gone and no one knows his name, for hundreds of years have passed. In his grief he opens the box. White smoke drifts out, and he is suddenly an old man.
also.fits: The shadow of Return: he comes home too late, to a home that no longer exists, like the top line’s missed return, and does the one thing he was told not to do.

name: Innocence
theme: Things happen to us that we did not plan or deserve, and we are quick to call them good or bad before the story is over.

tale.title: The Old Man at the Frontier Loses His Horse
tale.source: China · Huainanzi, ch. 18 (“Among Men”), compiled at the court of Liu An · c. 139 BCE
tale.text:
Out on the northern frontier of China, where the fields give way to the open steppe, there lived an old man who was good at reading the signs of things. One morning his horse slipped its rope and galloped off across the border, into the land of the nomad horsemen. A horse was a small fortune. The neighbours came round, shaking their heads, to say how sorry they were. What bad luck, they said. What a loss.

The old man only shrugged. He said it quietly, the way you might mention the weather. “How do you know this isn’t a blessing?” And he went back to his work.

Some months later the horse came trotting home, and running beside it were horses from the steppe, fine strong animals, better than anything in the village. Now the neighbours came to congratulate him, and to admire the horses. The old man said, “How do you know this isn’t a disaster?”

The house was rich in good horses now, and the old man’s son loved to ride. He rode the wild new ones, and one day he was thrown, and his thigh bone broke. It healed crooked. He would limp for the rest of his life. The neighbours came again, with long faces. And the old man said, “How do you know this isn’t a blessing?”

A year went by. Then the horsemen from beyond the border came over in force. Every able-bodied young man on the frontier was called up, took his bow and went to fight. Of the families along the border, nine sons in ten never came home. The old man’s son, because he was lame, was never sent.

So father and son stayed on together in their house at the edge of the steppe, with their horses, and watched the seasons turn.
beats: Old man on the northern frontier, horse runs off
Neighbours sorry; he asks, how do you know?
Horse returns with fine steppe horses
Neighbours glad; he asks again
Son rides, falls, breaks his thigh, limps
War comes; nine in ten sons die
The lame son stays home with his father
tale.fits: Innocence is about meeting the unexpected without scheming. The old man never tries to fix fate or bend it; he simply refuses to rush to a verdict. The third line speaks of undeserved misfortune, a cow taken by a passing traveller, and the son’s fall is exactly that kind of blow. The fifth line says an illness you did nothing to cause needs no frantic medicine, and it will pass. The old man does nothing clever at all, and his calm turns out to be the wisest response in the story.
when: a friend who just lost a job and is sure life is ruined
a colleague celebrating a promotion a little too hard
a parent panicking over a child’s rejection letter
anyone who keeps rereading one piece of news, good or bad
tale.open: “You know, there’s an old Chinese story about a man whose horse ran away, and it’s not finished being clever yet…”
tale.pause: Pause after each “How do you know?” and let your listener guess what comes next, because the rhythm of the turns is the whole story.
tale.close: End on the father and son at home with their horses, then just say, “And the story doesn’t say what happened next.”
tale.lesson: We rarely know, at the moment it happens, whether a thing is good or bad, so hold your verdicts loosely and stay steady.

also.title: The Death of Hundun
also.source: China · Zhuangzi, ch. 7 (“Fit for Emperors and Kings”) · c. 4th to 3rd century BCE
also.gist: Shu, the emperor of the southern sea, and Hu, the emperor of the northern sea, often met in the land of Hundun, emperor of the centre, and Hundun always treated them very kindly. They wanted to repay him. “Everyone has seven openings, to see, hear, eat and breathe,” they said, “but he has none. Let’s make some for him.” Each day they bored one hole. On the seventh day, Hundun died.
also.fits: This is the shadow of Innocence: a kindness built on a plan, forced on a nature that was whole, which the Judgment warns turns to misfortune.

name: Great Taming
theme: A season of plenty or strength is the time to store it up and train it, so that it is there when it is truly needed.

tale.title: Joseph and the Seven Years of Plenty
tale.source: Hebrew Bible · Genesis 41 · text set down in the 1st millennium BCE
tale.text:
Pharaoh, king of Egypt, had two dreams in one night. In the first he stood by the Nile, and seven cows came up out of the river, sleek and fat, and grazed in the reeds. Then seven more came up after them, thin and ugly, and the thin cows ate the fat ones, and were still as thin as before. In the second dream, seven ears of grain grew on one stalk, full and good. Then seven more sprouted, withered and scorched by the east wind, and the thin ears swallowed the full ones.

Pharaoh woke troubled. He called every magician and wise man in Egypt, and none of them could tell him what it meant. Then his chief cupbearer went pale and remembered something. Years before, in prison, a young Hebrew slave had explained his dream, and it had come true. The cupbearer had promised to speak for him, and then forgotten.

So they brought Joseph up from the dungeon. He shaved, he changed his clothes, and he stood before the king. “It is not in me,” he said. “God will give Pharaoh his answer.” The two dreams were one, he said. Seven years of great plenty were coming to Egypt. After them would come seven years of famine so hard that the plenty would be forgotten. Let Pharaoh find a wise man and set him over the land. In the good years, take a fifth of the harvest and store it in the cities, under guard, against the years to come.

Pharaoh looked at him and said, “Where would we find anyone like this man?” He took the ring from his own hand and put it on Joseph’s, and dressed him in fine linen, and put a gold chain round his neck. Joseph was thirty years old.

The seven good years came. Joseph went through the land gathering grain, city by city, until it was heaped up like the sand of the sea, and they stopped counting, because it could not be counted.

Then the seven bad years came. And people came from every country on earth to Egypt, to buy grain.
beats: Pharaoh dreams: fat cows eaten by thin cows
Full ears swallowed by withered ears
No wise man can explain; cupbearer remembers Joseph
Joseph from prison: seven fat years, seven lean
Store a fifth of each harvest in the cities
Joseph gets the ring; grain piles up uncounted
Famine comes; the whole world comes to Egypt
tale.fits: In Great Taming the strength of Heaven is held inside the Mountain: great power stored rather than spent. Joseph’s granaries are exactly that, a sky’s worth of harvest kept in walls. The Judgment says “not eating at home” brings good fortune, meaning the capable person should serve in public life, and Joseph goes straight from a dungeon to the second chariot of Egypt. It also says it is favourable to cross the great river. The stored grain is what carries a whole world across the famine.
when: a friend in a great job year who is spending every penny
a young colleague with real talent who wants to quit and coast
someone who feels stuck waiting, like Joseph in prison
a family deciding what to do with an unexpected windfall
tale.open: “That makes me think of Pharaoh’s dream, the one with the fat cows and the thin cows. Do you remember how it goes?”
tale.pause: Slow down when the thin cows eat the fat ones and stay just as thin, because that strange image is what makes the warning stick.
tale.close: Finish with “people came from every country on earth to Egypt, to buy grain,” and let the silence do the rest.
tale.lesson: Good years are for gathering and training strength, so it is there when the lean years come.

also.title: Kuang Heng Borrows the Light
also.source: China · Xijing zaji (Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital), about the Han scholar Kuang Heng · compiled c. 4th to 6th century CE
also.gist: Kuang Heng was a poor boy who loved to study, but his family could not afford candles. His neighbour had candles, but their light did not reach him. So he made a hole through the wall, let the neighbour’s light shine through, and read his books by it. A rich man in the town owned many books. Kuang Heng worked for him as a labourer and asked for no wages, only to read them all. The man lent him his books, and Kuang Heng became a great scholar, and in time chancellor of the empire.
also.fits: It is the Image of Great Taming in small: a poor boy storing up the words and deeds of the ancients, one borrowed beam of light at a time.

name: Nourishment
theme: What we feed on, and what we envy in other people’s plates, quietly shapes the life we end up living.

tale.title: The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse
tale.source: Greece and Rome · Aesop’s fables (c. 6th century BCE tradition) and Horace, Satires 2.6 (c. 30 BCE); this telling follows Horace
tale.text:
A country mouse once had a visitor: an old friend from his younger days, who now lived in the city. The country mouse lived in a small hole in the hillside, and he was careful with what he had, but for a guest he brought out everything. Chickpeas he had saved. Oats. A dried raisin. A few scraps of bacon fat, nibbled at the edges. He himself chewed on a bit of straw so that his friend could have the best.

The town mouse picked at it all with the tip of his nose. “My dear fellow,” he said, “how can you live like this, out here in the woods? Life is short. Come with me to the city and see how a mouse should live.”

The words worked on the country mouse, and that very night they set off. Around midnight they slipped under the door of a great house. Inside, the couches were covered in purple cloth, and on the table were the leftovers of a grand dinner, baskets heaped with things the country mouse had no names for. The town mouse played host. He settled his friend on a soft cushion and ran back and forth, bringing him one dish after another, tasting each first like a proper servant. The country mouse lay back and thought, this is the life.

Then the great doors banged open. Servants came in, and with them two huge hunting dogs, barking until the whole house rang. The mice ran wildly round the room, half dead with fright, looking for any crack to hide in.

When it was quiet at last, the country mouse came out, his heart still pounding. “Thank you,” he said. “This life is not for me. Give me my wood and my hole, where I can eat my plain seeds in peace.”

And he went home.
beats: Country mouse serves his best simple food
Town mouse sneers: life is short, come to the city
Midnight feast on purple couches
Town mouse waits on him dish after dish
Doors bang, dogs bark, mice run for their lives
Country mouse goes home to his seeds
tale.fits: The Judgment of Nourishment says: watch what a person seeks to fill their own mouth with. The first line is the country mouse in the city, letting go of his own magic tortoise, his self-sufficiency, to stare open-jawed at someone else’s table. The Image asks for moderation in eating and drinking. The feast is real, but it comes with dogs. The country mouse’s plain seeds are true nourishment because they come with peace, and in the end he is wise enough to choose them.
when: a friend tempted by a richer job they would hate
someone scrolling through other people’s holidays and feeling poor
a colleague who keeps saying their life is too small
a teenager dazzled by a glamorous crowd
tale.open: “Have you heard Horace’s version of the town mouse and the country mouse? It’s better than the one we learned as kids.”
tale.pause: Pause on the country mouse lying back on the purple cushion, thinking this is the life, just before the doors bang.
tale.close: Say simply, “And he went home,” and let your listener decide which mouse they are.
tale.lesson: A rich table eaten in fear is worse than plain food eaten in peace; choose what truly nourishes you.

also.title: Daniel and the Vegetables
also.source: Hebrew Bible · Daniel 1 · text c. 2nd century BCE, set in Babylon in the 6th century BCE
also.gist: In Babylon, young captives from Judah were chosen to be trained for King Nebuchadnezzar’s court and fed from the king’s own table. Daniel resolved not to defile himself with the king’s food and wine. The official in charge was afraid the young men would look sickly and he would pay with his head. So Daniel proposed a test: ten days of vegetables and water for him and his three friends. After ten days they looked healthier than all the others, and they went on to surpass every wise man in the kingdom.
also.fits: The other side of the mouse’s choice: Daniel chooses his nourishment on purpose, from inside the palace itself, and his plain diet feeds both body and integrity.

name: Great Exceeding
theme: When a whole situation is about to give way, someone has to take extraordinary measures, even if it means standing alone.

tale.title: Noah Builds the Ark
tale.source: Hebrew Bible · Genesis 6 to 8 · text set down in the 1st millennium BCE
tale.text:
In the days of Noah, the earth had gone bad. The book says it was filled with violence, and that God looked at it and was grieved to the heart. But there was one man who walked with God, a good and blameless man in his generation, and his name was Noah.

God told Noah what was coming: a flood that would cover the earth. And He told him what to do. Build an ark of gopher wood. Seal it with pitch inside and out. Make it three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, thirty high, with three decks, a door in the side, and a window near the roof. Bring your wife, your sons and their wives. Bring every kind of living creature, two by two, male and female, and food for all of them.

And Noah did all of it, just as he was told. Think of him out there, a man nearly six hundred years old, hammering a ship on dry land, with no sea in sight, while the world around him went on as it always had.

Then the rain began. It rained forty days and forty nights. The springs of the deep burst open, the windows of heaven opened, and the water rose. It lifted the ark off the ground. It covered the hills, then the highest mountains. Everything that breathed on land was gone. Only the ark floated, alone, on a world of water.

At last God remembered Noah. A wind blew over the earth, the waters went down, and the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. Noah opened the window and sent out a raven, which flew back and forth. Then he sent out a dove, but she found nowhere to land and came back to his hand. He waited seven days and sent her again. That evening she came back with a fresh olive leaf in her beak.

He waited seven days more and sent her out once more. This time she did not come back.
beats: The earth full of violence; one good man
God gives Noah exact plans for the ark
Noah builds a ship on dry land
Forty days of rain; mountains covered
The ark alone on a world of water
Raven, then dove; an olive leaf in the evening
The dove does not come back
tale.fits: The Image of Great Exceeding is the lake rising over the trees: a flood. Its teaching is that the noble one, standing alone, is not afraid. That is Noah, hammering a ship on dry ground while his world goes on as usual. The Judgment sees a ridgepole about to break, a time when ordinary measures will not do, yet says it is favourable to have somewhere to go. Noah’s careful, exact building is like the first line, laying white rushes beneath a heavy load: great care in a great crisis.
when: a friend making a big change everyone else calls overcautious
a manager quietly preparing for a crisis nobody believes in
someone holding a family together through a disaster
anyone waiting for the first sign that the worst is over
tale.open: “Everyone knows Noah’s ark from picture books, but the actual story has a quieter moment I love, with the dove…”
tale.pause: Pause on the image of an old man building a ship on dry land, because that loneliness is the heart of it.
tale.close: End with the dove that does not come back, and say nothing after it.
tale.lesson: In an extraordinary time, do the extraordinary thing carefully and without needing anyone’s approval.

also.title: The Boy and the Dike
also.source: Netherlands setting · a story told within Mary Mapes Dodge’s American novel Hans Brinker, or the Silver Skates (1865); not a genuine Dutch folk legend, though later embraced in the Netherlands
also.gist: A boy of Haarlem, the son of a sluice-keeper, was walking home along the dike at dusk when he heard a trickle and saw water seeping through a small hole. He knew a small leak becomes a great breach and drowns a country. He pushed his finger into the hole and stopped it. No one passed. All night he stayed there, cold, calling for help, holding back the sea. In the morning someone came by, found him, and the dike was mended.
also.fits: Where Noah prepares for the flood, the boy shows the other answer of Great Exceeding: one small person bracing the ridgepole alone, before the break.

name: The Abyss
theme: When we are in danger again and again, fighting the current only drowns us; staying true and moving with it carries us through.

tale.title: The Swimmer at Lüliang Falls
tale.source: China · Zhuangzi, ch. 19 (“Mastering Life”) · c. 4th to 3rd century BCE
tale.text:
Confucius was travelling with his students, and they came to Lüliang, where a river falls from a great height. The book says the waterfall hung thirty fathoms high, and the white water below it foamed for forty li. It was so fierce that no fish, no turtle, no water creature of any kind could swim in it. And there, in the middle of the churning water, Confucius saw a man.

He thought the man must be in some great trouble, and had thrown himself in to die. So he sent his students running along the bank to pull him out. But a few hundred paces downstream, the man came up out of the water on his own. His hair was loose down his back. He strolled along under the bank, singing to himself.

Confucius hurried after him. “I took you for a ghost,” he said, “but now I see you are a man. Tell me, do you have a way, a method, for swimming like that?”

“No,” said the man. “I have no method. I began with what I was given, I grew up with my nature, and I came to my fate. I go down with the swirl, and I come up with the surge. I follow the way of the water, and I don’t put any of myself in its way. That is how I swim.”

Confucius asked him what he meant. “I was born in these hills, and I am at home in the hills: that is what I was given. I grew up by this water, and I am at home in the water: that is my nature. I don’t know why I do what I do, and yet I do it: that is my fate.”

And he went on along the bank, with his wet hair, singing.
beats: Confucius at a waterfall no fish can swim
A man in the white water
Students run to rescue him
He climbs out downstream, singing
“Do you have a method?” “No.”
Down with the swirl, up with the surge
He walks on, wet hair, singing
tale.fits: The Abyss is water within water, danger after danger, and its teaching comes from water itself: it fills each hollow and flows on without losing its nature. The swimmer does exactly that. He does not fight the falls; he goes down with the swirl and up with the surge. The Judgment says that if you are sincere, your heart finds its way through. The swimmer has no technique to show off, only a nature formed by long, plain practice in the water, as the Image says, by constancy.
when: a friend going through one hard thing after another
a nurse or carer worn out by constant emergencies
someone who keeps asking for the trick that will fix everything
a colleague thrashing against a situation they cannot change
tale.open: “There’s a story in Zhuangzi about Confucius trying to rescue a man from a waterfall, and it goes completely the other way…”
tale.pause: Pause after the students run along the bank, so your listener expects a rescue, before the man climbs out singing.
tale.close: End on him walking away with his wet hair, singing, and leave it there.
tale.lesson: You get through danger by being true to yourself and moving with it, not by fighting it or looking for a trick.

also.title: Ariadne’s Thread
also.source: Greece · myth of Theseus, as told by Plutarch (Life of Theseus) and others, from older tradition
also.gist: Every few years Athens had to send young men and women to Crete, to be fed to the Minotaur in the Labyrinth, a maze no one ever left. The hero Theseus went among them. King Minos’s daughter Ariadne fell in love with him and gave him a ball of thread. He tied one end at the entrance and unwound it as he went deeper, through turn after turn. He found the Minotaur and killed it, then followed the thread back to the light.
also.fits: The Labyrinth is pit within pit, the doubled abyss. Ariadne’s thread is the one sincere line that holds through all of it and leads back out.

name: The Clinging
theme: Brightness and talent burn out when they forget what holds them up, and last when they keep to the middle way.

tale.title: Icarus
tale.source: Rome · Ovid, Metamorphoses 8 · c. 8 CE, retelling an older Greek myth
tale.text:
Daedalus, the great craftsman, was a prisoner on the island of Crete. King Minos held the land and held the sea, and the old man was homesick. One day he looked up. “He may block the land and the waves,” he thought, “but the sky is open. We will go that way.”

So he began to make something new. He laid out feathers in a row, the small ones first, then longer and longer, the way a shepherd’s pipe rises in steps. He tied them in the middle with thread and fixed them at the base with wax, and bent them gently into the curve of a bird’s wing. His young son Icarus played beside him, laughing, catching feathers as they blew about, pressing the yellow wax with his thumb, getting in his father’s way.

When the wings were done, Daedalus tried them himself and hung in the air. Then he fitted the boy’s wings and gave him his warning. “Fly the middle course, Icarus. Too low, and the spray will make your feathers heavy. Too high, and the sun will burn them. Stay between. Follow me.” And as he spoke, his cheeks were wet, and his hands shook, and he kissed his son.

They flew. Below them a fisherman, a shepherd leaning on his staff and a ploughman at his plough looked up in wonder, and thought they must be gods. They passed islands on the left and on the right.

And the boy began to love it. The rush of it, the height. He left his father’s path and climbed, higher, toward the sky. Near the sun, the sweet-smelling wax went soft. The feathers slid away. He beat his bare arms, but there was nothing left to hold the air. He called his father’s name, and the blue sea closed over him.

Daedalus, no longer a father, called out, “Icarus! Icarus, where are you?” Then he saw the feathers on the water.
beats: Daedalus trapped on Crete: “the sky is open”
Feathers, thread and wax; the boy plays with wax
Warning: fly the middle course
Fishermen and shepherds think they are gods
Icarus climbs for joy; the wax melts
Feathers on the water
tale.fits: Fire, in The Clinging, has no shape of its own; it lives only by clinging to something. Icarus’s wings cling by wax, and he forgets it. The second line, yellow light, is the gentle middle way, the course his father begs him to fly. The fourth line is Icarus himself: it comes suddenly, flares up, dies down, is thrown away. The Judgment praises the patient cow over brilliance that is proud and grasping. Daedalus’s tears as he fits the wings carry the whole weight of the warning.
when: a gifted young person rising very fast
a friend thrilled by a new venture and ignoring every limit
a parent watching a child outgrow their advice
a colleague burning out on their own success
tale.open: “Do you know how Ovid tells the Icarus story? There’s a detail with the boy playing with the wax that gets me every time.”
tale.pause: Slow right down at the father’s warning and the kiss, because that is the moment everything is still safe.
tale.close: End with Daedalus calling his son’s name and then seeing the feathers on the water. Say nothing more.
tale.lesson: Brilliance lasts only when it remembers what holds it up and keeps to the middle way.

also.title: The Water Spider Brings Fire
also.source: Cherokee · ‘The First Fire’, recorded by James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (1900)
also.gist: Long ago the world was cold. The Thunders sent lightning into a hollow sycamore on an island, and it burned, but the animals could not reach it. Raven flew over and came back scorched black. Screech Owl looked in and got red eyes; Hooting Owl and Horned Owl came back with rings of ash round theirs. The black racer and the climber snake both went and were burned black. Then little Water Spider ran across the water, wove a tusti bowl from her own thread, carried a single coal home in it on her back, and the people have had fire ever since.
also.fits: Every animal who grabs at the fire is scorched; only Water Spider gives it a vessel. The Clinging says fire lives by what it clings to, and here it is held safely because it clings to the right vessel, a humble bowl made by the smallest creature.

name: Influence
theme: The deepest bond is not won by pressing or pleasing, but by two people who truly hear each other.

tale.title: Bo Ya and Zhong Ziqi, the Friend Who Knew the Sound
tale.source: China · Liezi, ch. 5 (“Questions of Tang”) and Lüshi chunqiu (“Ben wei”) · c. 3rd century BCE to 4th century CE; the broken qin is from the Lüshi chunqiu
tale.text:
In old China there was a musician called Bo Ya, a master of the qin, the long zither with silk strings that is played lying flat on a table. People came from far away to hear him. And there was a man called Zhong Ziqi, who was a master of something rarer. He was a master of listening. When Bo Ya played with high mountains in his mind, Zhong Ziqi would say, “How fine! Towering, like Mount Tai.” When Bo Ya played with flowing water in his mind, Zhong Ziqi would say, “How fine! Broad and rolling, like the great rivers.” Whatever Bo Ya was thinking as he played, Zhong Ziqi heard it.

Once Bo Ya was wandering on the north side of Mount Tai when a sudden storm broke over him. The rain came down in sheets. He took shelter under an overhanging rock, and as he sat there, cold and alone with the noise of the water, he felt sad, so he took up his qin and played. First he played the sound of long, steady rain. Then he played the sound of a mountain crumbling. And every time he played a tune, Zhong Ziqi caught exactly what it meant.

Bo Ya put down his instrument and sighed. “Ah, your listening! What you imagine is just what is in my heart. Where can I hide my sound from you?”

The years went by, and Zhong Ziqi died.

Bo Ya went to the qin. He broke it, and he cut its strings. For the rest of his life he never played again, not one note. There was no one left in the world, he felt, worth playing for. The Chinese still call a true friend zhiyin: someone who knows the sound.
beats: Bo Ya plays the qin; Ziqi listens
Mountains: “Like Mount Tai!” Water: “Like the rivers!”
Storm under a rock: rain, then a falling mountain
“Where can I hide my sound from you?”
Ziqi dies
Bo Ya breaks the qin, never plays again
Zhiyin: one who knows the sound
tale.fits: Influence is two forces responding to each other, one heart moving another. Its Image is a lake resting on a mountain, and it says the noble one receives others with an open, empty mind. That is Zhong Ziqi: he does not judge or advise, he simply has room inside to receive what Bo Ya plays. The fourth line is the heart itself, the source of real influence. Bo Ya’s music never needed to persuade anyone. It needed one listener, and when that listener was gone, it had nothing left to move.
when: someone grieving a friend who really understood them
a person who feels nobody hears what they make
a couple who have stopped listening to each other
a friend wondering what real friendship is
tale.open: “There’s a Chinese word for a true friend, zhiyin, and it comes from a story about a musician and the one man who could hear him.”
tale.pause: Pause after “Zhong Ziqi died,” and let it sit before you touch the broken qin.
tale.close: End with the word zhiyin and what it means, then ask quietly, “Who knows your sound?”
tale.lesson: We are truly moved, and truly move others, only through open, attentive listening.

also.title: Malakas and Maganda, from the Split Bamboo
also.source: Philippines · Tagalog creation myth, recorded in several versions from the Spanish colonial period onward
also.gist: In the beginning there was only sky and sea, and a great bird flew between them with nowhere to rest. At last it came upon a stalk of bamboo. From inside the bamboo, a voice called out to be set free. The bird pecked and pecked at the stalk until it split open. Out of the two halves stepped the first man and the first woman: Malakas, the strong, and Maganda, the beautiful. From them, the story says, came all the peoples of the islands.
also.fits: Influence is the mutual attraction of two halves, the strong and the gentle, Mountain and Lake. Here they literally come from one stem.

name: Duration
theme: What lasts, in a marriage or a life, is not something grand but a steady faithfulness renewed every ordinary day.

tale.title: Philemon and Baucis
tale.source: Rome · Ovid, Metamorphoses 8 · c. 8 CE, set in Phrygia (Asia Minor)
tale.text:
In the hills of Phrygia there is an oak and a linden tree growing side by side, with a low wall around them. This is how they came to be there. Jupiter and Mercury once came down to earth dressed as poor travellers. They knocked at a thousand doors asking for a place to rest, and a thousand doors were bolted against them. Only one opened. It belonged to a tiny cottage roofed with straw and reeds, where an old woman, Baucis, and her husband, Philemon, had lived since they married young. They had grown old there together. They were poor, and they did not hide it, and they bore it lightly. There were no masters and no servants in that house. The two of them were the whole household.

Baucis blew the old embers back into flame with her own tired breath. Philemon took down a piece of smoked pork that had hung from the rafters a long time. They warmed water for the guests to wash, and spread their one good cover on the couch. The table had one short leg, so Baucis propped it with a broken piece of pot and wiped it with fresh mint. Olives, pickled cherries, radishes, cheese, eggs roasted in the ashes, then nuts, figs, apples, grapes, a honeycomb. And above all, kind faces.

Then the old couple saw that the wine bowl kept filling itself, however much was poured. They were afraid, and begged pardon for the poor meal. They tried to catch their only goose to cook for their guests, but the goose ran, flapping, straight to the gods, who said, “Let it be.”

The gods led them up the hill. Below, the whole valley sank into a marsh. Only their cottage stood, and it was turning into a temple, with a golden roof.

“Ask for anything,” said Jupiter. Philemon spoke with his wife, then answered. “Let us be the keepers of your temple. And since we have lived our whole lives together, let us die in the same hour, so I never see her grave, and she never has to bury me.”

Years later, standing on the temple steps, they saw leaves begin to grow from each other. As the bark rose over their faces, they said, together, “Goodbye, my dear.”
beats: An oak and a linden, side by side
Two gods disguised; a thousand doors shut
One poor cottage, an old couple, no servants
A propped table, mint, kind faces
Wine bowl refills; the goose runs to the gods
Their wish: to die in the same hour
Turning into trees: “Goodbye, my dear”
tale.fits: Duration takes its picture from marriage: Thunder and Wind always moving, always together, so that their bond stays the same. The Image says the noble one stands firm and does not change direction. Philemon and Baucis live this. Nothing about them is grand. Their faithfulness is renewed in small acts, the breath on the embers, the table propped with a shard. The Judgment speaks of success and no mistake for those who keep their course, and the gods give the couple the only reward they want: to go on together.
when: an old couple’s anniversary, or a toast at a golden wedding
a friend who thinks their marriage is too ordinary
someone with little money who still feeds every guest
a young couple worried whether love can last
tale.open: “Have you ever heard why there’s a story about an oak and a linden tree growing side by side? It’s from Ovid.”
tale.pause: Slow down at the table with the short leg and the mint, because those small acts of care are the story.
tale.close: End with the two of them saying, together, “Goodbye, my dear,” and the oak and the linden still standing.
tale.lesson: Love lasts through small faithful acts renewed every day, not through grand gestures.

also.title: Savitri and Satyavan
also.source: India · Mahabharata, Book 3 (Aranyaka Parva) · composed c. 4th century BCE to 4th century CE
also.gist: Princess Savitri chose Satyavan, son of a blind, exiled king living in the forest. The sage Narada warned that Satyavan would die in a year; she would not change her choice. On the fated day she went with him into the woods. He grew faint and lay with his head in her lap, and Yama, lord of death, came and drew out his soul. Savitri followed Yama, step after step, speaking with such wisdom that he granted her boons, until she asked for sons by Satyavan, and Yama had to give him back.
also.fits: The other face of Duration: constancy not as gentle routine but as a will that will not turn aside, even when following means walking after Death.

name: Retreat
theme: Walking away at the height of success, before a powerful situation turns against you.

tale.title: Fan Li Sails Away
tale.source: China · Sima Qian, Shiji (ch. 41, the House of Goujian of Yue, and ch. 129) · c. 100 BCE, events of the 5th century BCE
tale.text:
Two and a half thousand years ago, in the south of China, the small kingdom of Yue was crushed by its neighbour Wu. Its king, Goujian, had to beg for peace and bow as a servant to the king of Wu. Two ministers stood by him through all of it: Fan Li, the strategist, and Wen Zhong, who knew how to run a country.

For twenty years they worked. Goujian kept a bitter gall beside his seat and tasted it, so he would never forget. Fan Li trained the army; Wen Zhong filled the granaries and won the people. And at last Yue rose up and destroyed Wu completely. Goujian was master of the south. Fan Li was made supreme general. Everything they had suffered for had come true.

That was the moment Fan Li chose to leave.

He packed his pearls and his lightest treasures, gathered his own people, boarded a boat and put out to sea. He never came back. From far away he sent a letter to his old friend Wen Zhong. “When the high birds are all shot down, the good bow is put away. When the clever hare is dead, the hunting dog is cooked. Our king has a long neck and a mouth like a bird’s beak. You can share hardship with a man like that, but not good fortune. Why haven’t you gone?”

Wen Zhong read it. He stopped going to court and said he was ill. But he stayed. Soon someone whispered that he was plotting, and the king sent him a sword with a message: “You taught me seven ways to defeat Wu. I used three, and Wu fell. The other four are still with you. Take them and go try them out on my late father.” Wen Zhong understood, and used the sword on himself.

And Fan Li? He went to the state of Qi, changed his name, and farmed by the sea with his sons. He grew rich. Qi begged him to be its chief minister. He sighed, sent back the seal of office, gave his fortune away to friends and neighbours, and moved on again, to a town called Tao. There he grew rich once more, and there he lived to a ripe old age.
beats: Yue is crushed; King Goujian bows to Wu
Fan Li and Wen Zhong serve him twenty years
Yue destroys Wu; Fan Li made supreme general
At the summit, Fan Li packs and sails away
His letter: when the hare is dead, the hound is cooked
Wen Zhong stays, pleads illness, receives the sword
Fan Li farms by the sea, gives fortunes away
tale.fits: Retreat is a mountain under Heaven: you step back while you still can, not when you are forced. Fan Li leaves at the very peak, the ‘admirable retreat, well timed’ of the nine in the fifth place, and goes on to the top line’s carefree retreat, far and free. Wen Zhong is the third line: a retreat that is held back, with sickness and danger. He pretended to be ill but could not let go. The Judgment says retreat itself brings success, and Fan Li’s long, easy later life proves it.
when: a colleague who has just won the big project and feels untouchable
a friend wondering whether to leave a job while things are going well
someone who keeps staying in a group that no longer wants them
a founder wondering when to hand over the company
tale.open: “Have you heard about the Chinese minister who quit on the day he won?”
tale.pause: Pause after “That was the moment Fan Li chose to leave,” so the listener feels how strange it is before anything is explained.
tale.close: End with Fan Li in Tao, old and comfortable, then add quietly: “And Wen Zhong had the same letter.”
tale.lesson: Leave while leaving is still your choice; strength kept intact is worth more than glory held too long.

also.title: Laozi at the Pass
also.source: China · Sima Qian, Shiji (ch. 63, biography of Laozi) · c. 100 BCE
also.gist: Laozi kept the archives of the Zhou court for many years. When he saw the dynasty sliding into decline, he simply left, heading west. At the border pass the gatekeeper, Yin Xi, recognised him and said: ‘You are about to disappear from the world. Please, write something down for me first.’ So Laozi wrote a short book in two parts, some five thousand words, on the Way and its power. Then he went through the pass, and Sima Qian says no one knows where he ended his days.
also.fits: A quieter retreat: no enemy to escape, only a time gone sour. Laozi keeps his distance without anger, as the Image asks, and leaves behind the one thing worth keeping.

name: Great Power
theme: Having plenty of strength and wanting to push, when the real test is whether to hold back.

tale.title: The Two Goats on the Bridge
tale.source: Greece · Aesopic fable, best known from later European fable collections and La Fontaine’s Fables (book XII, 1694)
tale.text:
High in the hills there was a stream that ran deep and fast between two steep banks. Across it lay a single narrow plank, just wide enough for one animal at a time. One morning a white goat came down from the meadow on one side, wanting the fresh grass on the other. At the same moment a black goat came down from the far side, wanting exactly the same thing the other way round. They both stepped onto the plank. They both kept walking. And right in the middle, above the roaring water, they met nose to nose.

“Back up,” said the white goat. “I was here first.” “You were not,” said the black goat. “And I have never backed up for anyone in my life.” Now, either one of them could have turned around. It would have taken a dozen careful steps. Or one could have lain down flat on the plank and let the other pick its way over its back. There was room for that, just. But each goat looked at the other one’s horns, and thought about what the other goats would say.

So they lowered their heads. They pawed at the wood. They each stepped back half a pace, not to give way, but to get a run at it. And then they charged. The crack of their horns echoed off the rocks. The plank shook. They pulled apart and butted again, and again, horns locked, legs braced, neither giving an inch, while the plank bucked and groaned under them. And then, with one last shove, both of them lost their footing at once.

They went into the torrent together. The water rolled them over and over and carried them far away downstream, and neither of them ever got the grass on either side.

The plank settled back into place. It was still there the next morning, exactly as wide as it had always been.
beats: Narrow plank over a deep, fast stream
Two goats from opposite sides step on at once
They meet in the middle, nose to nose
Either could turn back or lie down; neither will
Heads down, they charge, horns locked
Both fall into the torrent and are swept away
The plank stays, just as wide as before
tale.fits: Great Power is thunder high above Heaven: plenty of force, and the whole question is how it is used. The nine in the third place says it plainly: the small-minded use force, the noble one does not, and the ram that butts the hedge gets its horns caught. The top line goes further: the ram can go neither back nor forward. The two goats are strong enough to cross, strong enough to yield, and they spend it all on the one move that drops them both into the water.
when: two siblings locked in a standoff over who apologises first
a colleague about to escalate an email war to the boss
a driver who will not let anyone merge
a couple arguing about whose turn it is to give in
tale.open: “Did you ever hear the one about the two goats and the bridge? It’s short.”
tale.pause: Slow down at the moment either goat could still turn back, and let the listener picture the easy way out.
tale.close: Finish on the plank still lying there, exactly as wide as always, and say nothing more.
tale.lesson: Real strength includes the strength to give way; force spent proving a point leaves everyone in the river.

also.title: Thor in the Hall of Utgard-Loki
also.source: Norse · Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda (Gylfaginning) · c. 1220 CE
also.gist: Thor, with Loki and the swift boy Thjalfi, comes to the giant king Utgard-Loki’s hall and is mocked as small. Loki loses an eating match to Logi; Thjalfi loses a race to Hugi. Thor cannot drain a drinking horn, lifts only one paw of a grey cat, and is forced onto one knee wrestling an old nurse, Elli. Next morning the king confesses: Logi was wildfire, Hugi was thought, the horn’s end lay in the sea, the cat was the World Serpent, Elli was old age. Thor raises his hammer, and king and hall vanish.
also.fits: The other face of Great Power: the strongest god finds his strength is real and still not enough, because he could not see what he was pushing against. Seeing the difficulty, says the top line, is where good fortune begins.

name: Progress
theme: Rising in the world, when your chance comes through generosity and a little help from others.

tale.title: Dick Whittington and His Cat
tale.source: England · folk tale, ballads and chapbooks from the early 17th century, loosely based on Richard Whittington, Mayor of London (died 1423)
tale.text:
There was once a poor orphan boy called Dick Whittington, and in his village everyone said the streets of London were paved with gold. So Dick walked to London. The streets were mud and stone. He slept in doorways, hungry, until a rich merchant, Mr Fitzwarren, found him on his step and gave him work in the kitchen.

The kitchen was ruled by a cook with a hard hand and a sharp tongue. Dick slept in an attic so full of rats and mice he could hardly close his eyes. With the first penny he earned, he bought a cat. She cleared the attic in a week, and Dick loved her.

Then Mr Fitzwarren sent a ship to trade in faraway lands, and as was his custom, every servant in the house could send something along, for a share of the luck. The others gave coins and trinkets. Dick had nothing but the cat. So, with tears in his eyes, he sent her.

The cook mocked him worse than ever, and at last, early one morning, Dick ran away. He got as far as Highgate Hill and sat down on a stone. And across the fields came the sound of the Bow Bells of London, and they seemed to be ringing words: “Turn again, Whittington, thrice Lord Mayor of London.” Lord Mayor? Him? Well, if that was what was coming, he could put up with the cook. He turned round and was back in the kitchen before anyone missed him.

Meanwhile the ship had reached the coast of Barbary. The king there gave the captain a feast, and the moment the dishes came out, rats and mice swarmed over the table and ate everything. The captain fetched Dick’s cat. She went through them like a storm. The king was so delighted that he paid more for that one cat than for all the rest of the cargo.

The treasure came home, and Mr Fitzwarren gave every bit of it to Dick. Dick gave gifts to the whole household, even the cook. He married Fitzwarren’s daughter, Alice, and in time, just as the bells had said, he was Lord Mayor of London three times over.
beats: Poor boy walks to London for golden streets
Kitchen boy, cruel cook, attic full of rats
Buys a cat with his first penny
Sends the cat on his master’s trading ship
Runs away; Bow Bells call him back from Highgate
Barbary king’s feast overrun; the cat clears it
Treasure, marriage, thrice Lord Mayor
tale.fits: The Judgment of Progress speaks of a prince honoured with many horses and received three times in a single day, and the bells promise Dick ‘thrice Lord Mayor’. The first line fits his kitchen years: progressing but held back, not trusted, so be generous and calm. He gives the only thing he owns. The third line, ‘everyone is in agreement’, is the whole household sending their share. And the Image, the sun rising over the earth, is a boy who turns round on the hill and walks back toward the city.
when: a young person in a first job that feels like a dead end
a friend about to quit just before things might turn
someone wondering whether a small generous act is worth it
a newcomer to a city who hasn’t found their footing yet
tale.open: “Do you know why there’s a stone with a cat on it at the bottom of Highgate Hill?”
tale.pause: Pause when the bells begin to ring on the hill, and let them ‘speak’ slowly, as if you were hearing them yourself.
tale.close: Say “and the bells were right,” and leave it there.
tale.lesson: Progress often comes from giving the little you have and turning back just before you give up.

also.title: The Carp That Leapt the Dragon Gate
also.source: China · folk legend of Longmen on the Yellow River, known since Han times and later tied to the imperial exams
also.gist: Where the Yellow River crashes through the narrow gorge at Longmen, the Dragon Gate, the falls are so high and fierce that fish cannot climb them. Every spring the carp gather in the pool below and try. They leap and fall back, leap and fall back, battered on the rocks. Most give up and drift away downstream. But it is said that the carp who clears the top is changed in that instant into a dragon and rises into the sky. In China, a student who passed the great exams was said to have leapt the Dragon Gate.
also.fits: Progress earned the hard way: no patron and no lucky cat, only effort climbing toward the light. It has the fifth line’s spirit, leaping again without taking each fall to heart.

name: Darkening of the Light
theme: Enduring humiliation in a dark time without giving away who you really are.

tale.title: Han Xin Crawls Between the Butcher’s Legs
tale.source: China · Sima Qian, Shiji (ch. 92, biography of Han Xin, Marquis of Huaiyin) · c. 100 BCE, events of the late 3rd century BCE
tale.text:
In the town of Huaiyin, a little more than two thousand years ago, there lived a tall young man called Han Xin who had nothing. No money, no trade, no post. He wore a sword everywhere as if he were somebody, and he ate wherever someone would feed him. People grew tired of him. For weeks an old woman washing silk by the river shared her rice with him. When he promised to repay her one day, she snapped at him: she fed him out of pity, not for any reward.

One day in the market a young butcher stepped into his path. “Look at you,” he said, loud enough for everyone. “Big man, big sword. Inside, a coward. If you’re not afraid to die, stab me. If you are, crawl between my legs.”

The market went quiet. Han Xin looked at him for a long time. He was strong. He had the sword. Then he bent down, got on his hands and knees in the dirt, and crawled between the butcher’s legs.

The whole market roared with laughter. For years, Huaiyin knew him as the coward.

Then the empire fell apart in war. Han Xin joined the rebels, was ignored, was nearly executed, and was finally noticed by Liu Bang, the man who would found the Han dynasty. Han Xin became his greatest general. He won battle after battle, and in the end he came home to his own country as a king.

He sent for the old washerwoman and gave her a thousand pieces of gold. And he sent for the butcher. The man came shaking, sure he was about to die. Han Xin made him an officer. Then he turned to his generals and said: “This is a brave man. When he shamed me, could I not have killed him? But killing him would have won me no name. So I bore it, and came to this.”
beats: Han Xin, poor and idle, wears a sword
A washerwoman feeds him out of pity
Butcher’s challenge: stab me, or crawl
He looks long, then crawls; the market laughs
War comes; he becomes the Han’s great general
Home as a king: gold for the washerwoman
The butcher made an officer: ‘This is a brave man’
tale.fits: Darkening of the Light is the sun gone into the earth: a time to veil your light and endure. The Image says the noble one lives among the people with the light hidden, and Han Xin lets a whole market think him a coward rather than throw his life away on a butcher. The six in the fifth place names Prince Ji, who hid his worth under a tyrant and stayed true. And the third line’s warning, do not expect to set everything right at once, is in his final words.
when: someone humiliated at work who is tempted to blow everything up
a teenager being taunted and itching to hit back
a friend stuck under a bad boss until the right move comes
anyone who must swallow pride to keep a bigger plan alive
tale.open: “There’s a famous Chinese general who started out as the town coward. Do you know how?”
tale.pause: Pause on “Han Xin looked at him for a long time,” and let the silence of the market hang.
tale.close: End on his words to the generals, “So I bore it, and came to this,” and stop.
tale.lesson: In a dark time, bearing shame and hiding your strength can be the bravest way to keep your light alive.

also.title: David Feigns Madness Before Achish
also.source: Hebrew Bible · 1 Samuel 21 (compare Prince Ji, named in this hexagram’s fifth line)
also.gist: Fleeing King Saul, who wanted him dead, young David ran to Gath, a Philistine city. But the servants of Achish, its king, recognised him: this was the hero the women sang about, the one who had slain his tens of thousands. David was afraid. So he pretended to be mad. He scratched marks on the doors of the city gate and let spit run down into his beard. Achish looked at him in disgust: ‘Do I lack madmen, that you bring me this one?’ They let him go, and David escaped to the cave of Adullam.
also.fits: Like Prince Ji, who feigned madness under a tyrant, David hides his light behind folly. It is the more cunning side of this hexagram: to be underestimated is to be left alive.

name: The Family
theme: Shaping the people you love by what you do and where you put them, not by lectures.

tale.title: Mencius’s Mother Moves Three Times
tale.source: China · Liu Xiang, Lienü zhuan (Biographies of Exemplary Women), ‘The Mother of Meng Ke of Zou’ · 1st century BCE, about the 4th century BCE
tale.text:
When the philosopher Mencius was a small boy, his mother watched everything he did. At first they lived near a graveyard. Soon little Mencius was playing at funerals: digging, heaping up mounds, burying things, wailing the way the mourners did. His mother watched and said, “This is no place to raise my son.” So they moved.

Next they lived beside the market. Before long the boy was playing at buying and selling, crying his wares like the traders. His mother watched and said, “This is no place to raise my son.” So they moved again.

This time they lived beside a school. And now the boy played at setting out the ritual vessels, at bowing to his elders and letting them go first, at entering and leaving a room with proper manners. His mother watched and said, “This is truly a place to raise my son.” And there they stayed.
