Years later, Mencius was a young man away at his studies. One day he came home. His mother was at her loom, weaving, and she did not stop. She asked, “How far have your studies come?” He shrugged. “About where they were.” She picked up a knife and cut straight through the cloth on her loom.

Mencius was frightened. That was weeks of work, and their living. He asked her why. “You giving up your studies,” she said, “is like me cutting this cloth. A woman weaves to keep her family fed and clothed. A man learns to make his name and keep himself from harm. Drop it halfway, and you will end up a servant, never free of trouble.”

After that Mencius studied morning and night without a break. He became a disciple in the line of Confucius’s own grandson, and in time he was counted the greatest sage of China after Confucius himself.
beats: Near a graveyard, the boy plays funerals; they move
Near the market, he plays at hawking; they move
Beside a school, he plays at courtesy; they stay
Years later, the young man drifts home
‘About where they were,’ he shrugs
She cuts the cloth on her loom
He studies day and night, becomes a great sage
tale.fits: The Judgment of The Family praises the steadfastness of the woman of the house, and the six in the second place has her seeing to what is within, not following whims. Mencius’s mother runs her home as the place where a person is formed. The Image asks for words with substance and conduct with constancy: she gives no long lecture, she changes the surroundings, and when words are needed she backs them with a knife through her own work. The first line’s firm boundaries are there too.
when: parents debating whether to move house for a better school
a friend whose teenager is drifting toward bad company
a manager wondering why the team copies the wrong habits
a student thinking of dropping a course halfway through
tale.open: “There’s an old Chinese saying about Mencius’s mother moving house three times. Do you know the story?”
tale.pause: Pause just before the knife, while she is still quietly weaving and waiting for his answer.
tale.close: Finish with “And that boy became Mencius,” and let them think about the mother.
tale.lesson: We become what surrounds us, so a home is shaped more by its setting and example than by speeches.

also.title: The Old Grandfather and the Grandson
also.source: Germany · Brothers Grimm, Children’s and Household Tales, no. 78 · 19th century
also.gist: An old man’s eyes had dimmed and his hands shook, so at table he spilled his soup on the cloth. His son and daughter-in-law, disgusted, sat him in the corner behind the stove and fed him from a clay bowl, never quite enough. When his trembling hands dropped and broke the bowl, they scolded him and bought him a wooden one for a few pennies. One day their four-year-old was fitting little boards together on the floor. ‘What are you making?’ ‘A little trough, for you and Mother to eat from when I’m big.’ They looked at each other and wept, and brought Grandfather back to the table.
also.fits: The shadow side of The Family: a household teaches whether it means to or not, and the child copies what he sees. In the fifth line the king ‘draws near to his family’, and here the parents finally do.

name: Opposition
theme: Two people at odds, when one chooses not to fight because something larger is at stake.

tale.title: Lian Po Carries the Thorns
tale.source: China · Sima Qian, Shiji (ch. 81, biographies of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru) · c. 100 BCE, events of the 3rd century BCE
tale.text:
In the time of the Warring States, the kingdom of Zhao had two great men. One was Lian Po, an old general who had won battle after battle. The other was Lin Xiangru, who had started out as a mere household retainer and risen by his wits. Twice he had faced the mighty king of Qin, and twice he had come away with Zhao’s honour whole. So the king of Zhao raised him to the highest rank at court, above Lian Po.

Lian Po was furious. “I took cities and fought in the field. He did it all with his tongue, and he was born a nobody. I will not stand below him. The day I meet him, I’ll shame him.”

Lin Xiangru heard. From then on, whenever there was a court gathering, he said he was ill, so the two would never have to quarrel over who stood first. One day, out in the city, he saw Lian Po’s carriage coming down the road. He had his driver turn aside and hide until it passed.

His own followers were ashamed. “We left our families to serve you because we admired you. Now you hide from him like a frightened child. Let us go home.” Lin Xiangru asked them, “Who is more terrible, General Lian or the king of Qin?” “The king of Qin, of course.”

“I shouted at the king of Qin in his own hall and shamed his ministers. Would I be afraid of General Lian? But think. Why does Qin not dare attack Zhao? Because the two of us are here. If two tigers fight, they cannot both live. I put the danger to our country first, and my own quarrel second.”

The words reached Lian Po. He stripped to the waist, tied a bundle of thorny branches across his bare back, and went to Lin Xiangru’s gate to beg his pardon. “I am a coarse, small man,” he said. “I did not know how big your heart was.” From that day they were friends, the kind who would die for each other.
beats: Zhao’s old general and its clever new minister
The newcomer is ranked higher; the general vows revenge
Lin Xiangru stays home, turns his carriage aside
His followers are ashamed and want to leave
‘If two tigers fight, they cannot both live’
Lian Po, bare-backed, carries thorns to his gate
Friends ever after, ready to die for each other
tale.fits: Opposition is fire over the lake: two forces moving apart. The nine in the second place says he meets his lord in a narrow lane, and it is no mistake: Lin Xiangru’s whole art is the side street where he lets the general pass. The Image says the noble one stays their own person amid what is shared, and he never stops being proud, only quiet. The top line is Lian Po: he sees an enemy, draws his bow, then puts it down, and what comes instead is friendship.
when: two colleagues competing for the same promotion
a newcomer resented by an old hand on the team
siblings who have to share a parent’s care
someone who has just realised they were unfair to a rival
tale.open: “The Chinese have a phrase, ‘carrying thorns to ask forgiveness’. It comes from a great story.”
tale.pause: Pause after Lin Xiangru’s question, “Who is more terrible?”, and let the listener answer it in their own head.
tale.close: End on the old general at the gate with thorns on his back, then simply: “They were friends for life.”
tale.lesson: Stepping aside from a rival for something larger is strength, and it leaves the other room to come round.

also.title: Jacob and Esau Meet Again
also.source: Hebrew Bible · Genesis 32 and 33
also.gist: Twenty years after cheating his brother Esau out of their father’s blessing, Jacob must go home, and hears that Esau is coming to meet him with four hundred men. Terrified, Jacob sends herds ahead as gifts, drove after drove. That night he wrestles with a mysterious stranger until dawn. In the morning he goes ahead of his family, bowing to the ground seven times. But Esau runs to him, throws his arms round him, kisses him, and they both weep. Then, gently, they go separate ways: Esau to Seir, Jacob to Succoth.
also.fits: Reconciliation without merging: the brothers make peace and still go their separate ways. That is Opposition’s Judgment exactly, good fortune in small matters.

name: Obstruction
theme: Running from the thing you must face, and finding every road blocked until you turn back.

tale.title: Jonah
tale.source: Hebrew Bible · Book of Jonah, one of the twelve minor prophets · probably written after the Babylonian exile, 5th or 4th century BCE
tale.text:
God told Jonah to go to Nineveh, the great city of Israel’s enemies, and cry out against its wickedness. Jonah got up and went the other way. He went down to the port of Joppa, paid his fare, and boarded a ship for Tarshish, as far west as the world went.

At sea a great wind came up, and the ship began to break apart. The sailors cried to their gods and threw the cargo overboard. Jonah was fast asleep down in the hold. The captain shook him awake: “Get up and call on your god!” The sailors cast lots to see who had brought this on them, and the lot fell on Jonah. He told them the truth: he was running from the God who made the sea. “Throw me in, and it will go calm.” They rowed hard for land instead, but the sea only grew wilder. At last they threw him over, and the sea lay still.

A great fish swallowed Jonah. For three days and three nights he sat in its belly, in the dark, and there he prayed. Then the fish spat him out on dry land.

The word came a second time: “Go to Nineveh.” This time he went. He walked a day into the city and called, “Forty days, and Nineveh will be overturned!” And the whole city believed him. The king came down from his throne and sat in ashes. Everyone, even the cattle, went without food and wore sackcloth. And God spared them.

Jonah was furious. This was exactly why he had run. He sat outside the city to sulk, and God made a plant grow up over him for shade, and Jonah was glad of it. At the next dawn a worm chewed it, and it withered, and the sun beat on his head until he wanted to die.

Then God said: “You pity a plant you did not tend, that came up in a night and died in a night. Should I not pity Nineveh, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and all those animals?” And the book ends there, on the question.
beats: Told to go to Nineveh, Jonah sails the other way
Storm at sea; Jonah asleep in the hold
The lot falls on him: ‘Throw me in’
Three days in the fish; he prays
Second call; he goes; the city repents
Jonah sulks; the shade plant withers
God’s question about the city, left unanswered
tale.fits: Obstruction is water on the mountain: danger ahead, steepness behind. Its lines keep saying the same thing: going leads into obstruction, coming back brings praise, union, great good fortune. Jonah flees and meets the storm, the sea and the belly of the fish; only when he turns back does the way open. The Image says the noble one turns inward, and Jonah’s turning starts in the dark, in prayer. Yet the story is honest: he goes back, and still has not finished turning.
when: a friend avoiding a hard conversation that keeps finding them anyway
someone who keeps changing jobs to escape the same problem
a colleague who did the right thing but resents how it turned out
anyone sulking because a person they dislike got forgiven
tale.open: “You know Jonah and the whale? Most people forget how it ends.”
tale.pause: Slow right down when the worm eats the plant; the listener should feel Jonah’s heat before God speaks.
tale.close: Ask God’s last question just as the book does, and do not answer it.
tale.lesson: The block in the road is often the very thing we are fleeing, and turning to face it is the way through.

also.title: The Monkey and the Crocodile
also.source: India · Panchatantra, book 4 (‘Loss of Gains’) · Sanskrit, early centuries CE
also.gist: A monkey living in a rose-apple tree by the water made friends with a crocodile and fed him sweet fruit every day. The crocodile took some home to his wife, who decided that a monkey who ate such fruit must have a sweet heart, and demanded it. So the crocodile invited his friend home on his back. Halfway across the water he confessed the plan. The monkey said calmly: ‘Why didn’t you say so? I left my heart up in the tree. Take me back and I’ll fetch it.’ Back on shore, he climbed high and never came down to that crocodile again.
also.fits: Obstruction met with a clear head: in the middle of the water, with no way forward, the monkey’s only move is to go back, and going back saves him.

name: Deliverance
theme: Letting someone off, or being freed yourself, and finding that release runs both ways.

tale.title: The Lion and the Mouse
tale.source: Greece · Aesop’s fables, ancient Greek collections (also in Babrius) · tradition from the 6th century BCE
tale.text:
On a hot afternoon a lion lay asleep in the shade, his great head on his paws. A little mouse came scurrying along, not looking where it was going, and ran straight up over the lion’s nose. The lion woke with a snort. One paw came down, and there was the mouse, pinned by the tail, its heart going like a drum.

“Please,” squeaked the mouse. “Please let me go. I didn’t mean it. And if you spare me, I promise, one day I’ll repay you.” The lion stared at it. Then he began to laugh, a deep rumbling laugh that shook the grass. A mouse? Repay a lion? What could a mouse ever do for him? But the joke had put him in a good mood, and the mouse was hardly a mouthful anyway. He lifted his paw. “Go on.” The mouse was gone in a flash.

Some time later, hunters came into that country. They wanted the lion alive, so they strung a great net of rope between the trees, and one evening the lion walked into it. The ropes dropped over him. He roared and twisted and clawed, and every time he struggled the knots pulled tighter, until he could barely move. His roars rolled out across the whole plain.

The mouse heard them. It knew that voice. It ran as fast as its legs would carry it, and found the lion bound up in the net, worn out and helpless. “Hold still,” said the mouse. And it began to gnaw.

It chewed through one rope, then another, then another. It took a long time. The lion lay quiet and let it work. Then a strand gave, and another, and suddenly there was a hole big enough. The lion shook himself and stepped out free.

The mouse sat up on a root and looked at him. “You laughed at me,” it said. “Now you know. Even a mouse can repay a lion.”
beats: A mouse runs over a sleeping lion’s nose
Pinned, it begs and promises to repay
The lion laughs and lets it go
Hunters’ net; struggling only pulls the knots tighter
The mouse hears the roar and comes running
‘Hold still’: it gnaws rope after rope
The lion steps out free; the mouse sits on a root
tale.fits: Deliverance is thunder and rain: the tension breaks. The Image says the noble one pardons mistakes and forgives wrongs, and that is all the lion does, a careless act of mercy. The fourth line says free yourself, and a companion comes whom you can trust. The fifth line says only the noble one can free himself, and the lion learns that thrashing just tightens the knots. Release comes when he holds still and lets a small friend do the work.
when: someone deciding whether to let a small offence go
a manager who has just caught a junior’s mistake
a friend tangled in a mess, thrashing and making it worse
anyone too proud to accept help from someone ‘beneath’ them
tale.open: “I keep thinking of that old fable, the lion and the mouse. Do you remember how it goes?”
tale.pause: Pause on “Hold still,” and slow the gnawing right down, one rope at a time.
tale.close: End with the little mouse on the root, looking up at the lion, and give it the last word.
tale.lesson: Mercy given lightly comes back, and some knots loosen only when we stop struggling and accept help.

also.title: The Gordian Knot
also.source: Greece · Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 2.3, and Plutarch, Life of Alexander 18 · 2nd century CE, events of 333 BCE
also.gist: In the city of Gordium stood an ancient wagon, tied to its yoke with a knot of cornel bark so tangled that no one could see where it began or ended. An oracle said whoever loosened it would rule Asia. Alexander came, studied it, and could find no end to pull. So, in the best-known telling, he drew his sword and cut straight through it. Another account, from his officer Aristobulus, says he pulled out the peg that held the yoke to the pole and slid the knot free. Either way, that night there was thunder and lightning.
also.fits: Deliverance at its most decisive: the top line’s prince who brings down the hawk on the high wall. If something still needs doing, says the Judgment, act quickly, and Alexander does not wait.

name: Decrease
theme: Having less, by necessity or by choice, and finding that what remains is enough.

tale.title: Diogenes Throws Away His Cup
tale.source: Greece · anecdote of Diogenes of Sinope in Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers, book 6 · text c. 3rd century CE, 4th century BCE setting
tale.text:
Diogenes lived in Athens, more than two thousand years ago, and he had decided to own almost nothing. He slept in a big clay storage jar near a temple. He had one rough cloak, which he folded double at night so it could be his blanket as well. He had a walking stick, a small bag for his bread, and a drinking cup. That was all.

People thought he was mad, or showing off, and sometimes he was a bit of both. He liked to say that the gods need nothing, and that the less a person needs, the closer they come to the gods. He had pared his life down, piece by piece, year after year, and if we are honest, he was rather proud of how little was left.

One hot day he went to a public fountain to drink. A boy got there first. The boy had no cup at all. He just bent over, put his two hands together under the water, and drank out of them, slurping, perfectly happy.

Diogenes stood and watched him. Then he reached into his bag, took out his cup, looked at it for a moment, and threw it away. “A child has beaten me,” he said, “at living plainly.”

Not long after, he saw another boy who had broken his dish. The boy did not fuss. He pressed a hollow into his piece of bread and scooped up his lentils with that. And Diogenes, so the story goes, threw away his bowl as well.

After that, when the old philosopher was thirsty, he did what the boy had done. He went down to the fountain, bent over, and made a cup of his own two hands.
beats: Diogenes in Athens owns a cloak, a stick, a bag, a cup
He is proud of how little he has left
A boy at a fountain drinks from cupped hands
Diogenes throws away his cup: “A child has beaten me”
Another boy eats lentils from a hollow of bread
Diogenes throws away his bowl too
Ever after, he drinks from his own two hands
tale.fits: Decrease is about stripping things back to what is real, and the Judgment says two simple bowls are enough for the offering. Diogenes finds that even fewer will do. Notice who teaches him: a child, someone below him, with less than he has. The hexagram shows the lower giving to build up the higher, and here the gift flows up from the small boy to the proud philosopher. The Image asks the noble one to rein in desire; Diogenes discovers that even his plainness had a little vanity in it, and he lets that go too.
when: a friend overwhelmed by possessions in the middle of a house move
someone cutting back after losing a job and feeling ashamed of it
a colleague convinced the project needs more tools before it can start
anyone a little too proud of their own minimalism
tale.open: “That makes me think of Diogenes, the Greek who lived in a jar, and what a little boy taught him.”
tale.pause: Pause after the boy drinks from his hands, so your listener can picture Diogenes looking down at the cup in his own bag.
tale.close: End on the picture: “After that, when he was thirsty, he just made a cup of his hands.” Then let it sit.
tale.lesson: Less, chosen honestly, can be more than enough, and the lesson often comes from someone who has even less.

also.title: The Widow’s Two Coins
also.source: Judea · Gospel of Mark 12:41-44 (also Luke 21:1-4) · 1st century CE
also.gist: In the Temple at Jerusalem, Jesus sat facing the treasury chests and watched people bring their gifts. Rich people put in large sums, and the coins rang. Then a poor widow came and dropped in two tiny copper coins, the smallest money there was, together worth almost nothing. Jesus called his disciples over. She has put in more than all of them, he told them. They gave out of what they had to spare. She, out of her need, gave everything she had, all she had to live on.
also.fits: This is the Judgment’s two simple bowls in their purest form: a tiny offering that outweighs lavish ones because it is sincere. Where Diogenes lets go for his own freedom, the widow lets go for something beyond herself.

name: Increase
theme: A season of growth, when those who have more give of themselves and everyone ends up richer.

tale.title: The Monkey King Who Became a Bridge
tale.source: India · Mahakapi Jataka (Jataka no. 407), Pali Buddhist birth stories · commentary in its present form c. 5th century CE, from older oral tradition
tale.text:
High in the Himalaya, on the bank of the Ganges, there grew a mango tree whose fruit was sweeter than any other. Eighty thousand monkeys lived in it, and their king was a great monkey, strong and wise. He had one rule. “Never let a single mango hang over the water. If one floats downstream, men will taste it, and men will come.” So the monkeys picked every fruit that grew above the river, even the little green ones.

But one mango hid behind an ants’ nest, and they missed it. It ripened, it fell, and the river carried it all the way down to Benares, where the king was bathing inside a net stretched across the water. The mango caught in the net. The king tasted it, and he wanted more. He took boats, foresters and archers upriver until they found the tree.

At night his men surrounded it. “At dawn,” said the king, “shoot them all.” The monkeys trembled and came to their own king.

The monkey king did not hesitate. He ran out along a branch over the river and leapt, a huge leap, to the far bank. There he cut a long bamboo cane, tied one end to a tree, tied the other round his own waist, and leapt back. But the cane was too short, short by the length of his own body. So he gripped a branch of the mango tree with his hands, stretched himself out, and made his body the last stretch of the bridge. “Go,” he said. “Quickly, and gently.” And eighty thousand monkeys ran across his back to safety.

The last to cross was a monkey who hated him. That one jumped down hard on his back, and something broke inside the monkey king. He hung there alone.

The human king had watched it all. He had the monkey king lowered gently, bathed and laid on a soft bed. “You made yourself a bridge for them,” he said. “Why?” “I am their king,” said the monkey. “They were afraid. I do not grieve for my body.” He taught the king how a true ruler cares for his people, and then he died. And from that day, the king of Benares ruled differently.
beats: Monkey king rules a sweet mango tree on the Ganges
One hidden mango floats down to the king of Benares
Archers surround the tree, ready to shoot at dawn
Monkey king leaps the river and ties a cane
Cane too short: he stretches his body to finish it
Eighty thousand cross; a rival breaks his back
The human king tends him, and learns how to rule
tale.fits: Increase is the hexagram in which the one above decreases himself to enrich those below, and so everything grows. The monkey king lays his own body down so his people can cross, and the Judgment’s ‘favorable to cross the great river’ becomes a living picture. The six in the fourth place speaks of being relied upon in moving the capital: a whole people moved to safety on one trusted back. And the nine in the fifth place says a truly kind heart does not ask; his kindness changes even the king who came to kill him.
when: a new manager wondering what leadership actually asks of them
a parent quietly carrying the whole family through a hard move
someone who gives a great deal and wonders if anyone notices
a team lead deciding who should get the credit this time
tale.open: “There’s an old Buddhist story about a monkey who turned himself into a bridge. Have you heard it?”
tale.pause: Slow right down when the cane turns out too short; let your listener feel the gap before he fills it with himself.
tale.close: Finish with the human king: “And from that day, the king of Benares ruled differently.” Leave it there.
tale.lesson: Real growth comes when those who have more give of themselves so that others can cross.

also.title: Honi and the Carob Tree
also.source: Jewish · Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 23a · compiled c. 5th to 6th century CE, about a sage of the 1st century BCE
also.gist: Honi the Circle Maker was walking along a road when he saw a man planting a carob tree. How long until it bears fruit, he asked. Seventy years, said the man. And you expect to live seventy more years? The man said: I found the world full of carob trees; my ancestors planted them for me, and I am planting for my children. Honi sat down to eat, fell asleep, and rocks rose up around him and hid him. He slept seventy years. When he woke, a man was gathering carobs from that tree: the planter’s grandson.
also.fits: The long side of Increase: the gain may come long after you, to people you will never meet. The Image says to move toward the good when you see it, whether or not you will taste the fruit.

name: Breakthrough
theme: The moment when something everyone half knows has to be said out loud.

tale.title: The Emperor’s New Clothes
tale.source: Denmark · Hans Christian Andersen, “The Emperor’s New Clothes” (1837), based on tale 32 of Juan Manuel’s El Conde Lucanor (Spain, 1335)
tale.text:
There was once an emperor who loved new clothes more than anything in the world. He did not care about his soldiers, or the theater, or riding in the park, except as chances to show off a new coat. He had a different outfit for every hour of the day.

One day two swindlers came to town. They said they were weavers, and that they could weave the finest cloth there had ever been. It had one marvelous quality: it was invisible to anyone who was unfit for his position, or simply too stupid. “Perfect,” thought the emperor. “With clothes like that, I could find out who in my empire is no good.” He gave them gold and the finest silk thread, which they stuffed into their own bags. Then they sat at two empty looms and pretended to weave, late into the night.

The emperor sent his honest old minister to look. The old man stared at the empty looms, and his heart sank. Am I stupid? Am I unfit? So he praised the colors and the pattern, and went back and said it was magnificent. A second official went, and did the same. At last the emperor went himself, with his whole court, and saw nothing at all. But everyone around him was saying, “Gorgeous!” So he said, “Gorgeous!” too.

On the day of the great procession, the swindlers dressed him, fussing over the long train and smoothing the sleeves of nothing. He walked out under a canopy, and the whole city cheered. No one would admit to seeing nothing.

Then a little child said, “But he hasn’t got anything on!”

“Listen to the innocent,” said the child’s father. And people whispered it to each other, one to the next, until the whole crowd was calling out, “He hasn’t got anything on!”

The emperor shivered, because he knew they were right. But he thought, I must see this procession through. So he held himself prouder than ever, and his chamberlains walked behind him, holding up the train that was not there.
beats: An emperor who loves clothes above all else
Swindlers sell cloth invisible to the stupid and unfit
Minister, official, emperor: all see nothing, all praise it
The grand procession; the whole city cheers
A child: “But he hasn’t got anything on!”
The whisper spreads until the whole crowd says it
He marches on prouder; chamberlains carry the empty train
tale.fits: Breakthrough asks that the matter be made known at the king’s court and declared truthfully, though there is danger, and that no one take up arms. The child does exactly that: no force, just one plain sentence in public, and the spell breaks. The Image warns the noble one against resting on their own virtue, which is the emperor’s whole trouble. And the nine in the third place, the one who walks alone and gets soaked in the rain: whoever speaks first stands alone for a moment, until the crowd finds its voice.
when: a colleague afraid to say the project plan obviously will not work
a friend in a group that keeps pretending everything is fine
a leader surrounded by people who only bring good news
a young person wondering whether their honest question sounds stupid
tale.open: “It’s a bit like the emperor’s new clothes, isn’t it? Do you remember how that one actually ends?”
tale.pause: Pause just before the child speaks, then say the line simply, in a small clear voice.
tale.close: End on the empty train: “and his chamberlains walked behind him, holding up the train that wasn’t there.” Let your listener decide what that means.
tale.lesson: One plain, true sentence, said openly and without force, can break a spell everyone else is too afraid to break.

also.title: Nathan and David: “You Are the Man”
also.source: Israel · Hebrew Bible, 2 Samuel 12:1-13 · set c. 10th century BCE, written down centuries later
also.gist: King David had taken Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and arranged for Uriah to die in battle. The prophet Nathan came to him with a case to judge. A rich man with great flocks had a guest to feed, but instead of taking an animal of his own, he took his poor neighbor’s only possession: one little ewe lamb the poor man had raised like a daughter, letting it eat from his plate and sleep in his arms. David blazed with anger. That man deserves to die! Nathan said: You are the man. And David said: I have sinned.
also.fits: Breakthrough done with skill: Nathan declares the truth at the king’s court, in real danger, but lets a story carry it, so the king passes judgment on himself.

name: Coming to Meet
theme: The small first step of something you should not let in, which looks harmless when it arrives.

tale.title: The Camel’s Nose in the Tent
tale.source: Arab world · traditional fable behind the proverb of the camel’s nose · widely told in English since the 19th century; its exact origin is uncertain
tale.text:
Out in the desert, on a bitter night, a traveler had pitched his small tent. Outside, his camel knelt in the sand. The wind came hard off the dunes, but the man wrapped himself in his blanket and was just warm enough to sleep.

Then the tent flap moved. “Master,” said the camel, “it is so cold out here. Let me put just my nose inside the tent. Only my nose.” The man thought: a nose takes up no room at all. “Very well,” he said.

A little while later, the camel spoke again. “Master, my nose is warm now, but my head is freezing. Let me bring in my head.” The man shifted over. “All right. Just your head.”

Later still: “Master, the wind is cutting my neck. If I could only bring in my neck and my front legs, I could rest.” The man pulled his knees up to his chest. “Fine. But that is all.”

Each thing the camel asked was so small. Each thing the man had already given had cost him so little. And the camel was always so very polite.

By the middle of the night, the camel’s whole great body was inside the tent, folded up and steaming, and the man was squashed against the canvas with the cold coming through it. The camel looked at him kindly. “This tent,” it said, “is really too small for the two of us. And I am the larger. Perhaps it would be best if you slept outside.”

And so the traveler, who owned the tent, who had carried it across the desert and set it up with his own hands, spent the rest of that night outside in the sand, with his blanket round his shoulders, listening to his camel snore.
beats: Cold desert night: a man in his tent, his camel outside
The camel asks to put just its nose in
Then its head
Then its neck and front legs, ever so politely
By midnight the whole camel is inside
“The tent is too small for two. You go out.”
The owner sleeps outside, listening to his camel snore
tale.fits: Coming to Meet shows a single yielding line slipping in beneath five strong ones: the first small sign of something that will grow. The six at the beginning says it plainly: tie it to a brake of bronze, for if you let it go forward you will see misfortune, and the lean pig is already pacing. The camel’s nose is that first line. Each yes looks reasonable on its own. The Judgment warns against binding yourself to such a power, and by the time the whole animal is inside, the warning has come too late.
when: a friend whose ‘just this once’ favor has become a weekly habit
a colleague whose job keeps growing by one small request at a time
someone letting a new habit in, one drink or one scroll at a time
a parent negotiating bedtime with a very persuasive child
tale.open: “That sounds like the camel’s nose. Do you know the old Arab story behind that saying?”
tale.pause: Pause after each request and give the man’s little shrug; the rhythm of small yeses is the whole tale.
tale.close: End with the snore: “and he spent the night outside, listening to his camel snore.” Nothing more.
tale.lesson: What you let in at the start decides what you will have to live with, so the time to say no is at the nose.

also.title: The Farmer and the Snake
also.source: Greece · Aesop’s Fables (Perry 176) · tradition from c. 6th century BCE
also.gist: One winter day a farmer found a snake lying stiff with cold. He felt sorry for it, picked it up, and tucked it inside his coat, against his chest, to warm it. Slowly the snake came back to life. As soon as its strength returned, it did what snakes do: it bit the man who had saved it. As he was dying, the farmer said: I have earned this, for taking pity on a creature I knew to be wicked.
also.fits: The same warning seen from the side of kindness: what you take into your bosom without seeing it clearly can be the thing that harms you, as the Judgment warns about binding yourself to a power you cannot control.

name: Gathering Together
theme: People coming together around something greater than any one of them, and what it costs to arrive.

tale.title: The Conference of the Birds
tale.source: Persia · Farid ud-Din Attar, Mantiq al-Tayr (The Conference of the Birds) · 1177 CE
tale.text:
In the old Persian poem, all the birds of the world gathered together one day: the nightingale and the parrot, the peacock and the hawk, the duck, the owl, the little finch, thousands upon thousands of them. They had a problem. Every land has a king, they said. We have none.

The hoopoe stepped forward, with a crest on its head like a crown. It had traveled far. “We do have a king,” it said. “His name is the Simorgh. He lives beyond Mount Qaf, at the edge of the world. He is close to us, but we are far from him. The road is long and hard, and few come back.”

At once the birds began to make excuses. The nightingale could not leave his rose. The parrot wanted only the water of eternal life. The peacock dreamed of the garden of paradise. The duck would not leave her pond, the hawk was content on the king’s wrist, the owl loved its treasure in the ruins, and the finch said it was far too small and weak. To each of them the hoopoe answered, with a story. And in the end they set out together.

The road ran through seven valleys: the Valley of the Quest, of Love, of Understanding, of Detachment, of Unity, of Bewilderment, and last, the Valley of Poverty and Nothingness. Birds turned back. Birds were lost in deserts and drowned in seas, burned by the sun, worn out by the road. Of all the thousands who set out, only thirty arrived, ragged, featherless, with nothing left.

At the court of the Simorgh, they were turned away at first. Go home, they were told. They stayed. At last the door was opened, and they looked up to see their king.

What they saw was thirty birds.

In Persian, “thirty birds” is si morgh. They had come all that way to find the Simorgh, and the Simorgh was them, all thirty, together.
beats: All the birds gather: every land has a king but us
The hoopoe: our king is the Simorgh, beyond Mount Qaf
Every bird has an excuse; the hoopoe answers each
Seven valleys, from Quest to Nothingness
Thousands set out; only thirty arrive
Turned away at the door, they stay
They see their king: thirty birds, si morgh
tale.fits: Gathering Together is about a crowd becoming a people around a center. The Judgment says to go to the ancestral temple and see the great person, and the birds’ whole journey is that seeking. The six at the beginning, sincere but not to the end, now confusion and now gathering, is the flock with its excuses. The six at the top, sighing with tears and running nose, is the thirty who arrive with nothing left. And what they gather around turns out to be what they became by gathering.
when: a team that keeps waiting for the perfect leader to arrive
a community group losing members to one small excuse after another
a friend about to begin a long, hard project with others
someone who feels a group is less than the people in it
tale.open: “There’s a Persian poem about birds searching for their king, and the whole ending hangs on a pun. Want to hear it?”
tale.pause: Pause before you reveal what they saw, and let your listener wonder what the Simorgh looks like.
tale.close: Say the pun slowly: “In Persian, thirty birds is si morgh.” Then stop, and let them work it out.
tale.lesson: What a group searches for outside itself is often what it becomes by searching together.

also.title: The Giant Turnip
also.source: Russia · folk tale “Repka”, collected by Alexander Afanasyev (1860s); best known in the telling that ends with the mouse
also.gist: An old man planted a turnip, and it grew enormous. He pulled and pulled, but it would not come up. He called his wife; she held on to him, and they pulled together. Nothing. Their granddaughter held on to the old woman. Still nothing. The dog held on to the granddaughter, and the cat held on to the dog. Still the turnip would not move. At last a little mouse held on to the cat, they all pulled together, and up came the turnip.
also.fits: The homely side of Gathering Together: success needs everyone, and, as the six in the second place says, even a small sincere offering counts. Here it is the mouse.

name: Pushing Upward
theme: Growing strong or great slowly, by adding a little every single day.

tale.title: Milo and the Calf
tale.source: Greece · legend of Milo of Croton, Olympic wrestler of the late 6th century BCE · the calf in Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria book 1; the bull at Olympia in Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae book 10
tale.text:
In the Greek city of Croton, in the south of Italy, there lived a boy named Milo, and what he wanted, more than anything, was to be strong.

One spring a cow on the farm gave birth to a calf. It was small and wobbly on its legs. Milo bent down, put his arms under it, and lifted it up onto his shoulders. It was not heavy. He walked around the yard with it, and set it down again.

The next day he did the same. And the day after that. Every day, without missing one, he lifted the calf onto his shoulders and carried it.

Now, a calf grows a little every day. Not so you would notice. One day’s growth is nothing, a mouthful of grass. So each day the calf was only a tiny bit heavier than the day before. And each day Milo was only a tiny bit stronger than the day before. There was never a morning when the calf was suddenly too heavy for him. There was never a morning when he woke up and felt suddenly strong.

The seasons turned. The calf grew into a young bull, broad and solid. Milo grew into a young man. Neighbors stopped on the road to stare, because there was Milo still, walking round the farm with a bull across his shoulders, as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world. For him, it was.

Milo became the most famous wrestler in all of Greece. He won at the Olympic Games again and again, over more than twenty years. And people told how once, at Olympia, in front of the whole crowd, he lifted a full-grown bull onto his shoulders and carried it the whole length of the stadium.
beats: Milo, a boy in Croton, wants to be strong
A calf is born; he lifts it onto his shoulders
He carries it every single day
Each day the calf grows a little, and so does Milo
Never a day when it is suddenly too heavy
The calf becomes a bull; the boy becomes a champion
At Olympia he carries a grown bull down the stadium
tale.fits: The Image of Pushing Upward is wood growing up from within the earth, and the noble one piles up small things until they become high and great. Milo’s calf is that line made flesh. The six in the fifth place, climbing the steps, is the whole method: no leap, just the next step, every day. The six at the top asks you to be ceaselessly steady even when you cannot see the progress, and Milo never once feels himself getting stronger. Growth here is never dramatic. It is simply the sum of days.
when: a friend starting at the gym who wants results by Friday
a student facing a whole language or instrument to learn
someone saving a small amount each month and losing heart
a colleague growing into a role that still feels too big
tale.open: “Have you heard about the Greek wrestler who trained by carrying a calf?”
tale.pause: Slow down at “one day’s growth is nothing”, so your listener feels how invisible the change is.
tale.close: End on the stadium, the grown bull across his shoulders, and let your listener connect it to the wobbly calf on its first day.
tale.lesson: Great strength is built from small daily loads that grow just as fast as you do.

also.title: Ninomiya Sontoku Plants the Cast-off Seedlings
also.source: Japan · from the life of Ninomiya Sontoku (Kinjirō, 1787 to 1856), as told in the Hōtokuki and later biographies
also.gist: Ninomiya Kinjirō grew up poor in a Japanese farming village, orphaned young and living with his uncle. At rice-planting time the farmers threw away the seedlings left over once their paddies were full. Kinjirō gathered up the cast-off seedlings and planted them in a neglected patch of land nobody bothered with, tending them in his spare hours. In the autumn they gave him a whole bale of rice. From this he drew the idea he taught all his life: pile up the small, and it becomes the large.
also.fits: Pushing Upward from the soil itself: the Image’s small things piled high, and the nine in the second place, a small sincere offering that is favorable. Where Milo grows his own strength, Kinjirō grows a harvest out of what others threw away.

name: Exhaustion
theme: Being at the end of your strength, when no one seems to hear you and the only way out is through.

tale.title: Kisa Gotami and the Mustard Seed
tale.source: India · story of Kisa Gotami in Dhammapala’s commentary on the Therigatha, also in the Dhammapada commentary · c. 5th to 6th century CE, set in the Buddha’s lifetime
tale.text:
In the city of Savatthi, in the Buddha’s time, there lived a young woman so thin that people called her Kisa Gotami, Gotami the Lean. She came from a poor family and married into a rich one, and in her husband’s house they looked down on her. Then she gave birth to a son, and everything changed. Now she was the mother of the heir. Now she was respected.

The boy grew until he could just run about. And then, suddenly, he fell ill and died.

Gotami could not take it in. She lifted him onto her hip, the way she always carried him, and went from house to house through the city. “Medicine,” she begged. “Give me medicine for my son.” People stared. Medicine, for a dead child? Some laughed at her. She did not hear them.

At last a wise man said, “I have no medicine. But I know someone who might. Go to the Buddha.”

She found the Buddha and asked him. He said, “Yes. Bring me a few mustard seeds. But they must come from a house where no one has ever died.”

Mustard seed! Every house had mustard seed. She hurried back into the city and knocked at the first door. Of course they had mustard seed; they brought it out. “And has anyone ever died in this house?” “What are you asking? Here the living are few, and the dead are many.” She went to the next house, and the next, door after door, all day. Everyone would give her mustard seed. No one could give her a house without death.

By evening she understood. It was not only her. It was everyone.

She carried her son to the charnel ground, laid him down, and said goodbye. Then she went back to the Buddha. “Did you bring the mustard seed?” he asked. “I am done with mustard seed,” she said. “Teach me.” She became a nun, and in time, the tradition says, one of the wisest women of the Buddha’s order.
beats: Kisa Gotami, scorned, finally respected when her son is born
The little boy dies
She carries him door to door, begging for medicine
The Buddha: mustard seed from a house without death
Every house has seed; no house is without death
By evening she understands, and lays her son down
Returning: “I am done with mustard seed”
tale.fits: Exhaustion is a lake with no water, a person drained to the bottom. The Judgment says that when you speak you are not believed, and Gotami, begging medicine for a dead child, is laughed at in every street. The six in the third place could be her story: you enter your house and the one you love is not there. Yet the Judgment also promises success through steadiness, and the six at the top says that going forward brings good fortune. She does go forward, door after door, and the going itself teaches her.
when: a friend some months into grief, ready to talk about it
someone who feels they are the only one this has happened to
a worn-out caregiver still searching for a cure that is not there
anyone quietly asking “why me?” after a loss
tale.open: “There’s an old Buddhist story about a mother and some mustard seed. It’s sad, but it helped me once.”
tale.pause: Pause after the first neighbor says the living are few and the dead are many, and let it land before the next door.
tale.close: End with her words, “I am done with mustard seed,” and then say nothing for a moment.
tale.lesson: No one is spared loss, and seeing that we share it is what lets us lay down what we carry.

also.title: Su Wu Herds the Sheep
also.source: China · Han shu (Book of Han), biography of Su Wu, compiled by Ban Gu · 1st century CE; events c. 100 to 81 BCE
also.gist: Around 100 BCE, Su Wu went as the Han emperor’s envoy to the Xiongnu. He was seized there and pressed to change sides. He refused. They shut him in a pit without food, and he lived by eating snow and chewing the wool of his felt rug. So they sent him to the frozen shore of the North Sea to herd rams, and told him he could go home when the rams gave milk. He dug up wild rats’ stores of grain to eat, and held the emperor’s staff every day until its tassels had all fallen off. After nineteen years he came home.
also.fits: Exhaustion as endurance: the Image says the noble one stakes their life on carrying out their purpose. Hemmed in for nineteen years, Su Wu keeps his staff in his hand and does not let hardship change who he is.

name: The Well
theme: The deep source people draw on, and why keeping it clear matters more than a cleverer bucket.

tale.title: The Gardener and the Well-Sweep
tale.source: China · Zhuangzi, chapter 12 (“Heaven and Earth”) · c. 4th to 3rd century BCE
tale.text:
Zigong, the clever disciple of Confucius, was traveling home through the country south of the Han river when he saw an old man working in his vegetable garden.

The old man had dug a sloping tunnel down into a well. He would walk down it, fill a big clay jar, hug it to his chest, carry it back up, and pour it over his rows of vegetables. Then down he went again. Puffing and panting, he was working terribly hard and getting very little done.

Zigong could not bear to watch. “Sir,” he said, “there is a machine for this. In one day it can water a hundred plots, with hardly any effort. Wouldn’t you like one?”

The old man looked up. “How does it work?”

“You take a wooden beam,” said Zigong, “heavy at the back and light at the front. It lifts the water as easily as pulling up a rope, so fast it seems to bubble over. It is called a well-sweep.”

The gardener’s face flushed with anger, and then he laughed. “I have heard my teacher say this. Where there are clever machines, there will be clever schemes. Where there are clever schemes, there will be a scheming heart. With a scheming heart in your chest, you lose your simplicity, your spirit grows restless, and the Way has nowhere to settle. It is not that I don’t know about your machine. I would be ashamed to use it.”

Zigong blushed, looked at the ground, and found nothing to say.

After a while, the old man asked who he was. “A disciple of Confucius.” “Ah,” said the gardener. “One of those who learn a great deal in order to look like a sage. Off you go, and don’t hold up my work.”

Zigong walked away pale and shaken. He went thirty li down the road before he began to feel like himself again.
beats: Zigong passes an old man watering his garden
He walks down into the well, carries up one jar
Zigong describes the well-sweep: a hundred plots a day
The gardener laughs: clever machines make a scheming heart
“I know of it. I’d be ashamed to use it.”
Zigong has no answer and is sent on his way
He walks thirty li before he feels himself again
tale.fits: The Well says the town can be moved, but not the well: the source stays the same while everything around it changes. Zigong offers a better rope and jug, and the Judgment agrees these matter, since a short rope or a broken jug brings misfortune. But the gardener is guarding the spring itself, the clear cold water of the nine in the fifth place, and fears the muddied well of the six at the beginning, where no one drinks. The tale leaves the same tension the hexagram holds: how to draw well without spoiling the source.
when: a colleague excited to automate the one task they actually love
a friend wondering why the new app hasn’t made them calmer
someone burned out from optimizing every hour of the day
a craftsperson told that their slow way is inefficient
tale.open: “There’s a Chinese story, over two thousand years old, about a man who refuses a labor-saving gadget.”
tale.pause: Pause after Zigong’s sales pitch, before the gardener laughs, so your listener sides with Zigong first.
tale.close: End with Zigong walking thirty li before he felt like himself again, and perhaps add, “I still can’t decide which of them was right.”
tale.lesson: How you draw from the source shapes the one who draws, so tend the spring before you improve the bucket.

also.title: The Woman at the Well
also.source: Samaria · Gospel of John 4:1-42 · late 1st century CE
also.gist: Tired from walking, Jesus sat down at Jacob’s well in Samaria around noon. A Samaritan woman came to draw water, and he asked her for a drink. She was startled, since Jews and Samaritans kept apart. He told her that if she knew who was asking, she would have asked him, and he would have given her living water. Whoever drinks this water will be thirsty again, he said, but the water I give becomes a spring inside, welling up to eternal life. He told her about her own life. She left her jar and ran to tell the town.
also.fits: The Well turned inward: the deepest source is in a person, and the six at the top, do not cover the well, is a woman who leaves her jar behind and calls everyone to come and drink.

name: Revolution
theme: Becoming who you really are takes a long, hard season, and the change shows only when its time has come.

tale.title: The Ugly Duckling
tale.source: Denmark · literary fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen, “Den grimme Ælling”, in New Fairy Tales (1843)
tale.text:
On a farm beside an old manor house, a duck sat on her nest among the tall burdock leaves. One by one the eggs cracked, and out tumbled little yellow ducklings. But the biggest egg took its time. When it finally split, out came a large, grey, clumsy chick. “That’s a turkey,” said an old duck. “Put it in the water and you’ll see.” But it swam beautifully. So it was hers after all, said the mother, and not so ugly if you looked at it properly.

The rest of the farmyard did not look properly. The ducks bit him. The hens pecked him. The girl who fed the poultry kicked at him. Even his own brothers and sisters turned on him. So one day he ran, flapped over the hedge, and was gone.

The wide world was not much kinder. In the marsh, the wild ducks laughed at him. Then the hunters came, guns cracking over the reeds, and a huge dog pushed its nose right up to him, then splashed away. “I’m so ugly even the dog won’t bite me,” he thought. He sheltered in an old woman’s cottage, where the cat asked if he could purr and the hen asked if he could lay eggs. He could do neither. When he said he longed to float on open water, they told him he was mad. So he left.

One autumn evening, a flock of great white birds rose out of the bushes, with long, curving necks, and flew away south. He gave a strange cry, a sound he had never made before, and he could not forget them. Then came winter. One night the pond froze around him, until a farmer broke the ice. It was a long, cold, miserable season, and I won’t tell you all of it.

But the sun came back. The larks sang. He lifted his wings and found they were strong, and they carried him to a garden where three white swans were gliding on the water. “I’ll go to them,” he thought. “Let them kill me for daring. It’s better than the farmyard.” He landed, bowed his head, and waited.

And there, in the water, he saw himself. Not a grey, awkward bird. A swan.

Children ran to the bank. “There’s a new one! He’s the most beautiful of all!” The old swans bowed to him. And he tucked his head under his wing, not proud at all, because a good heart never is.
beats: Big grey chick hatches last from the biggest egg
Farmyard bites, pecks and kicks him, so he runs
Marsh, hunters, a dog too disgusted to bite him
Cat and hen: can you purr? Can you lay eggs?
Autumn: white birds fly south, he cries out strangely
Frozen into the pond through a miserable winter
Spring: flies to the swans, bows his head, sees himself
tale.fits: Revolution’s character first meant an animal’s hide, the coat that is shed and grows back new. The duckling’s change cannot be forced or argued for; the Judgment says it is believed only when its day has come, and that day comes after a whole winter. The first line, bound tight in the hide of a yellow cow, is the long stretch where he can only endure. The Image sets the calendar by the seasons, and spring does what no argument could. The top line’s noble one changes like a leopard, a new coat everyone can see, while the farmyard only ever changes its face.
when: a teenager who feels they belong to no group at school
a friend still in the hard, unglamorous middle of retraining
someone who left a place that never understood them
a colleague whose real talent the team has not noticed yet
tale.open: “You know the story of the ugly duckling? I always forget how much of it happens in winter.”
tale.pause: Slow right down when he bows his head to the water expecting to die, and let the listener get there a beat before you say “a swan.”
tale.close: End on him tucking his head under his wing, not proud at all, and then just stop.
tale.lesson: A true change comes in its own season, after the hard winter, and when it comes it needs no argument.

also.title: Gilgamesh and the Snake
also.source: Mesopotamia · Epic of Gilgamesh, Standard Babylonian version, Tablet XI · c. 1200 BCE, from older Sumerian and Babylonian material
also.gist: Gilgamesh, grieving his friend Enkidu, crossed the waters of death to find Utnapishtim, the one man granted eternal life. He failed the test of staying awake, but as a parting gift learned of a thorny plant at the bottom of the deep. He tied stones to his feet, sank down, tore it up, and named it “The Old Man Grows Young.” He would try it first on an old man of Uruk. On the way home he stopped to bathe in a cool pool. A snake smelled the plant, slid out, carried it off, and shed its skin as it went. Gilgamesh sat down and wept.
also.fits: The shadow of Revolution: the renewal Gilgamesh grabbed for himself goes to the creature that knows how to molt. A new skin cannot be seized before its time; he goes home to the walls of Uruk, the work that will outlast him.

name: The Cauldron
theme: Real worth can enter by the kitchen door, and the person who nourishes others well can end up shaping a whole order.

tale.title: Yi Yin, the Cook Who Became Minister
tale.source: China · Lüshi chunqiu, “Ben wei” (Original Taste), c. 239 BCE, and Sima Qian’s Shiji, “Basic Annals of Yin” · setting c. 16th century BCE
tale.text:
In the oldest days of China, a woman of the Youshen clan was picking mulberry leaves when she heard a baby crying inside a hollow mulberry tree. The story goes that his mother had been warned in a dream: when water rises from the mortar, run east and do not look back. The water rose, and she ran. But she looked back. The flood swallowed her town, and she became that hollow tree, with her child inside it.

The baby was given to the ruler’s cook to raise. So he grew up in the kitchen, among knives and fires and great bronze cauldrons. His name was Yi Yin, and he grew wise.

Word of him reached Tang, a lord gathering strength against the cruel last king of the Xia. Tang asked the Youshen to send him the man. They refused. So Tang asked instead for a bride from the Youshen house. That they granted, and Yi Yin went along in the bride’s household, carrying the cauldron and the chopping board.

Tang received him in the ancestral temple and purified him with torches. Then he asked about ruling, and Yi Yin talked about cooking.

He talked about water, the root of every flavour. About the three kinds of creatures, those of the water, those that eat flesh and those that eat grass, each with its own smell to master. About fire: nine boilings, nine changes, and the fire keeps them in order. Sweet without cloying, sour without harshness, pungent without burning. “What happens inside the cauldron,” he said, “is so fine and subtle that the mouth cannot say it.”

Then he named the finest foods under heaven, fish from far seas and fruit from distant mountains, and told Tang that none of them could be his unless he became the Son of Heaven. And that, he said, could not be forced. The way lies in yourself. When the self is complete, the rest is complete.

Tang listened. He made the cook his chief minister. Together they brought down the tyrant and founded the Shang, and for centuries the Shang kings honoured Yi Yin, the man who had walked into the palace carrying a pot.
beats: Baby found in a hollow mulberry after a flood
Raised by a cook, among bronze cauldrons
Tang wants him; the clan refuses
He arrives as a bride’s servant, carrying the cauldron
Asked about ruling, he talks about flavour and fire
“The way lies in yourself”
Cook becomes chief minister; the Shang begins
tale.fits: The Cauldron is the vessel where raw things are transformed into nourishment and offering, and a dynasty’s cauldrons were the sign it had the right to rule. Yi Yin carries one into history. The first line, the cauldron turned over and a concubine taken for the sake of her son, is his humble entry: a servant in a bride’s retinue who turns out to be the real prize. The second line, food in the cauldron, is his substance, which no one can take from him. And the Image, setting one’s position right to make one’s calling firm, is exactly his advice to Tang.
when: someone embarrassed that they started in a junior or service job
a manager who wants a recipe for running a team well
a friend who cooks for everyone and thinks it doesn’t count
anyone building something new after a big upheaval
tale.open: “There’s an old Chinese story about a cook who talked his way into running a kingdom, and all he talked about was soup.”
tale.pause: Pause after “Then he asked about ruling, and Yi Yin talked about cooking,” and let the listener wonder how that can be an answer.
tale.close: Finish with the image of the man walking into the palace carrying a pot, and leave it there.
tale.lesson: Whoever truly knows how to nourish, and has set themselves right, already knows how to lead.

also.title: Draupadi’s Pot
also.source: India · Mahabharata, Book of the Forest (Vana Parva), with the Durvasa episode as it is popularly told · composed c. 400 BCE to 400 CE
also.gist: In exile in the forest, the Pandavas were given a vessel by the Sun god: each day it fed any number of guests until Draupadi herself had eaten. Their rival Duryodhana sent the fiery sage Durvasa, with thousands of disciples, to arrive after she had eaten. The sages went to bathe, expecting a feast. Draupadi prayed to Krishna. He came, and asked her for food. She showed him the empty pot. He found one grain of rice and a shred of leaf stuck to its side, ate it, and said, “May the whole world be satisfied.” At the river, the sages suddenly felt full, and slipped away.
also.fits: Another side of the Cauldron: what matters is not the size of the meal but that the vessel is sound and offered rightly. The fifth and top lines’ gold and jade bars are like Krishna’s touch, where one true offering feeds a multitude.

name: The Arousing
theme: A sudden fright can send us running in all directions, unless we stop and look at what actually hit us.

tale.title: Henny Penny
tale.source: England · cumulative folk tale, as recorded by Joseph Jacobs in English Fairy Tales (1890); related tales are told across Europe and in the Buddhist Jatakas
tale.text:
One morning Henny Penny was pecking at corn in the farmyard when, whack, something hit her on the head. “Goodness gracious!” she cried. “The sky is falling! I must go and tell the king.”

She hadn’t gone far down the road when she met Cocky Locky. “Where are you off to in such a hurry, Henny Penny?” “The sky is falling, and I’m going to tell the king.” Well, that was news. “I’ll come with you,” said Cocky Locky. So the two of them hurried on.

Before long they met Ducky Daddles. “Where are you two going?” “The sky is falling, and we’re going to tell the king.” “Then I’m coming too,” said Ducky Daddles. So the three of them hurried on.

Next came Goosey Poosey. Same question, same answer, and now there were four of them. And then Turkey Lurkey, puffing along to join them, so that there were five, all in a line, all walking a little faster now, all glancing up at the sky.

And then they met Foxy Woxy.

“Good morning,” said Foxy Woxy, very politely. “Where are you all going?” “The sky is falling, and we’re going to tell the king.” “Ah,” said the fox. “But you don’t know the way to the king’s palace, do you?” They had to admit they didn’t. “Then follow me. I know a short cut.”

So they followed him, Henny Penny, Cocky Locky, Ducky Daddles, Goosey Poosey and Turkey Lurkey, until they came to a narrow, dark hole in the hillside. It was the fox’s den. “Here’s the short way,” said Foxy Woxy. “I’ll go first, and you come in after me, one at a time.”

In went Turkey Lurkey. He did not come out. In went Goosey Poosey. In went Ducky Daddles. Then Cocky Locky went in, and from deep inside came one startled squawk, a warning, and then nothing at all.

Henny Penny heard that squawk. She turned around and ran, all the way home to her own farmyard, and she never did tell the king that the sky was falling.

As for what hit her on the head that morning: it was an acorn.
beats: An acorn hits Henny Penny; she thinks it’s the sky
Off to tell the king
Cocky Locky, Ducky Daddles, Goosey Poosey, Turkey Lurkey join
Foxy Woxy offers a short cut
The dark hole; one at a time they go in
A squawk from the dark; Henny Penny runs home
It was only an acorn
tale.fits: The Arousing is thunder doubled, shock upon shock, and the Judgment accepts the fear but praises the one who does not drop the sacred cup. Henny Penny drops everything. The Image asks the frightened person to examine themselves and set things in order; nobody in this tale ever looks at the acorn. The top line describes trembling and wild glances and warns that setting out now brings misfortune, and the whole parade sets out. Only that squawk from the dark finally does what the thunder should have done, and sends her home.
when: a colleague forwarding every alarming rumour about layoffs
a parent spiralling after one bad school report
a group chat whipping itself into a panic over a headline
a friend about to make a big decision in a fright
tale.open: “This is like Henny Penny, honestly. Do you remember how that one actually ends? It’s darker than you think.”
tale.pause: Slow down at the fox’s den and let each “in went” land on its own, so the listener feels the line shrinking.
tale.close: Say the last line plainly, “It was an acorn,” and then say nothing else.
tale.lesson: When the sky seems to fall, look at what hit you before you follow anyone anywhere.

also.title: The Storm on the Lake
also.source: Gospel of Mark 4:35 to 41 · Greek, c. 70 CE
also.gist: One evening Jesus and his disciples set out across the Sea of Galilee in a fishing boat. A great windstorm came up, and the waves broke into the boat until it was filling. Jesus was in the stern, asleep on a cushion. They woke him: “Teacher, don’t you care that we are going under?” He got up, rebuked the wind, and said to the water, “Quiet. Be still.” The wind dropped and there was a great calm. “Why are you so afraid?” he asked them. And they were filled with awe, saying, “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
also.fits: The other side of the thunder: the sleeper in the stern is the one who does not spill the cup. And the fear does not vanish; it turns into awe, as the Judgment says terror turns to laughter and easy talk.

name: Keeping Still
theme: When everyone is arguing about what is moving out there, the stillness we need is inside.

tale.title: The Wind and the Flag
tale.source: China · Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch (later, Yuan-era edition; the early Dunhuang text lacks this scene), also case 29 of the Gateless Gate (1228) · set c. 676 CE
tale.text:
This is a story about Huineng, who became the Sixth Patriarch of Chan Buddhism in China.

He was a firewood seller from the far south, and he could not read. But one day he heard a man reciting a sutra in the market, and something in him woke up. He walked hundreds of miles to the monastery of the Fifth Patriarch, who set him to work husking rice in the kitchen. Months later, in secret, at night, the old master gave him the robe and the bowl of the lineage, and told him to flee south before the jealous monks could catch him.

So he hid. For years he lived among hunters in the mountains. They set him to watch their nets, and when no one was looking he let the animals go. At meals he ate only the vegetables they cooked alongside the meat. He told no one who he was.

At last he came down to the city of Guangzhou, to a temple where a learned master was lecturing on the Nirvana Sutra. It was a windy day. Outside the hall a long banner was flapping on its pole, and two monks stood watching it.

“The flag is moving,” said one.

“No,” said the other. “The wind is moving.”

“The wind is invisible. What you see moving is the flag.”

“The flag can’t move by itself. It’s the wind.”

Back and forth they went, louder and louder, and neither would give an inch.

Then a plain-looking stranger with long hair stepped up to them. “It is not the wind that moves,” he said, “and not the flag. It is your minds, honourable monks, that are moving.”

Everyone who heard it was startled into silence.

The master of the temple came out, invited the stranger in, and questioned him. Then he asked, “I have heard that the robe of the Fifth Patriarch has come south. Is it you?” Huineng said it was, and showed him the robe and the bowl. And the learned master, who had been teaching for years, shaved the stranger’s head with his own hands and asked to become his student.

Outside, the banner went on flapping in the wind.
beats: Illiterate woodcutter given the robe in secret
Years hiding among hunters, freeing animals from nets
A temple in Guangzhou, a flapping banner
Two monks: the flag moves, no, the wind moves
Stranger: it is your minds that move
The learned master becomes his student
The banner keeps flapping
tale.fits: Keeping Still asks for stillness where the restless self quiets down, and the Image says the wise person does not let their thoughts go beyond their own situation. The two monks have gone out into the wind with their minds. Huineng has spent years keeping still among hunters, and the fifth line, jaws kept still and words in good order, is his single sentence, said once and not argued. The Judgment’s walker in the courtyard who is not pulled by the people there is him standing among the shouting monks.
when: two siblings arguing over whose fault a family row was
someone furious about a comment that keeps replaying in their head
a team stuck debating whether the client or the product is the problem
a friend who cannot stop refreshing the news
tale.open: “That reminds me of a Chinese Zen story about two monks arguing over a flag.”
tale.pause: Let the two monks’ argument speed up and get louder, then pause before the stranger speaks, so his line comes into silence.
tale.close: Say “Outside, the banner went on flapping in the wind,” and let the listener decide what that means.
tale.lesson: The turmoil we argue about outside is usually moving in our own minds.

also.title: Bodhidharma Faces the Wall
also.source: China · Chan legend, in the Transmission of the Lamp (1004) and the Gateless Gate, case 41 (1228) · set 6th century CE
also.gist: Bodhidharma, the monk from the west, came to China and settled at a temple on Mount Song, where he sat facing a cave wall, it is said, for nine years. A seeker named Huike came and stood outside in the snow, begging to be taught, and to prove his sincerity he cut off his own arm. “My mind is not at peace,” he said. “Please pacify it.” Bodhidharma said, “Bring me your mind, and I will pacify it.” Huike was silent a long time. “I have searched for it, and I cannot find it.” “There,” said Bodhidharma. “I have pacified it for you.”
also.fits: This is the Judgment’s still back at its most extreme: nine years facing a wall. Huike’s frantic search shows the third line’s danger, the stiffened back and suffocating heart, which dissolves only when he stops looking.

name: Development
theme: Some things grow only at their own pace, and the harder we pull, the more we kill them.

tale.title: The Man Who Pulled Up the Sprouts
tale.source: China · Mencius, Book 2A (Gongsun Chou I), chapter 2 · 4th century BCE
tale.text:
Mencius, the great follower of Confucius, was once asked by his student Gongsun Chou what he was best at. He said, “I understand words, and I am good at nourishing my flood-like spirit.”

“What is that?” asked the student.

“Hard to say,” said Mencius. It is vast and strong, he explained. Feed it with what is right, do it no harm, and it fills everything between heaven and earth. But it is not something you can grab. It grows from rightness done again and again, day after day. You must work at it, but not fix your eyes on the result. Do not forget it, and do not help it grow. Do not be like the man from Song.

And then he told the story.

There was a farmer in the state of Song. In those days, if you wanted a story about a fool, you made him come from Song. This farmer had planted his field, and the young rice came up green and thin, a hand high. He went out every morning to look at it. Every morning it looked exactly the same.

He fretted. He paced the rows. The neighbours’ fields seemed to be doing fine. His own sprouts just stood there, not growing.

So one morning he decided to help. He went down the rows on his knees, and he took hold of each sprout and pulled it up, just a little, just enough to make it taller. All day long, row after row, until his back ached and his hands were sore.

That evening he came home exhausted, and very pleased with himself. “I’m worn out today,” he told his family. “I’ve been helping the sprouts grow.”

His son ran out to the field to see.

Every sprout had withered.

Mencius said: “There are few people in the world who do not help their sprouts grow. Some think there is no point in tending them, and leave them alone; they are the ones who do not weed. Others help them grow; they are the ones who pull them up. And that is not only useless. It does harm.”
beats: Mencius: nourish your spirit, but don’t help it grow
A farmer from Song, and his thin green sprouts
Every morning he checks; they look the same
He pulls each one up, just a little
Home exhausted: “I’ve been helping the sprouts grow”
His son runs out; every sprout has withered
Some neglect, some pull: both fail
tale.fits: Development is growth that keeps its proper sequence, like a tree on a mountain or the wild goose moving stage by stage, and its Judgment warns that nothing important can be rushed. The farmer wants the plain without the shore. The Image says the wise person changes things gradually by living rightly, which is exactly Mencius’s flood-like spirit, grown from rightness day after day. And the fifth line, three years with no child yet nothing can stop it in the end, is the patience the farmer did not have: the sprouts were growing all along.
when: a parent drilling a young child to read early
a friend checking their new business numbers every hour
someone forcing a new relationship to be serious too soon
a learner who wants to skip the boring basics
tale.open: “There’s a two-thousand-year-old Chinese joke about a farmer that I think about all the time.”
tale.pause: Pause after “His son ran out to the field to see,” so the listener supplies the ending before you say it.
tale.close: You can stop at “Every sprout had withered,” or add Mencius’s last line and then leave it alone.
tale.lesson: Tend what is growing and let it grow at its own pace; forcing it does harm.

also.title: The Tortoise and the Hare
also.source: Greece · Aesop’s Fables (Perry Index 226) · 6th century BCE tradition, written down later
also.gist: The hare laughed at the tortoise for being so slow, and the tortoise, quite calmly, challenged him to a race. They agreed on a course and a finishing post, and off they went. The hare shot ahead, so far that the tortoise was barely in sight behind him. Sure of winning, he lay down by the road and fell asleep. The tortoise did not stop. Step after step, past the sleeping hare, he plodded on, and by the time the hare woke and ran for the finish, the tortoise was already there.
also.fits: The positive face of Development: the tortoise is the goose moving slowly from stage to stage. The hare shows the third line’s danger, the one who goes off and does not come back to finish.

name: The Marrying Maiden
theme: Entering a situation on someone else’s terms, with little say, you can still act with grace and change how it ends.

tale.title: Wang Zhaojun Goes Beyond the Wall
tale.source: China · Han shu (1st century CE) and Hou Han shu (5th century CE), with the painter legend from Miscellanies of the Western Capital · events 33 BCE
tale.text:
More than two thousand years ago, in the palace of the Han emperor Yuan, there lived a young woman named Wang Zhaojun. She came from a village in the gorges of the Yangtze, and she had been chosen for the palace as a girl.

There were so many women in the palace that the emperor could not meet them all. The story goes that he had a court painter make portraits, and chose from the pictures. The other women bribed the painter to make them lovely. Zhaojun would not pay. So he painted her plain, and for years she was never called. She waited, unseen, behind the walls.

Then a great lord came from the north: Huhanye, the chanyu of the Xiongnu, the horsemen of the steppe, who had long raided the Han frontier. Now he wanted peace, and he asked to become the emperor’s son-in-law. A princess was too precious to send. The emperor would give him a lady of the palace instead.

Zhaojun, the history says, asked to go.

At the farewell audience she walked into the hall in her finest clothes, and the whole court fell silent. She was the most beautiful woman there. The emperor stared. He wanted to keep her. But he had given his word to the chanyu, and he could not break it. So she went. In the telling, the painter paid for his lie with his life.

Zhaojun rode north, past the Great Wall, onto the open grassland. Legend says she played the pipa as she rode, so sadly that wild geese forgot to beat their wings and dropped from the sky.

She lived among the Xiongnu as the chanyu’s wife and bore him a son. When he died, she asked to come home. The emperor sent word that she must follow the customs of her new people. So she married the next chanyu, his son by another wife, and bore him two daughters.

For two generations there was peace along the frontier.

Her tomb lies out on the grassland near Hohhot. They call it the Green Tomb, because, they say, the grass there stays green when everything around it has turned to autumn gold.
beats: Palace girl painted plain because she won’t bribe the painter
Years waiting, never called
The Xiongnu chanyu asks for a Han bride; she volunteers
Farewell audience: the emperor sees her, too late
North past the Wall; the pipa, the falling geese
Ordered to stay, she marries the next chanyu
Peace on the frontier; the Green Tomb
tale.fits: The Marrying Maiden is the junior bride who enters a household on terms she cannot set, and the Judgment warns that pushing forward goes badly. Zhaojun does not push; she chooses to go, and she stays when ordered. The fourth line, the maiden who lets the time pass and marries late in her own time, is her years unseen in the palace. The fifth line, where the princess’s sleeves are less fine than the secondary wife’s, is her walking into the hall. And the Image, keeping the far end in view, is the peace her marriage bought.
when: someone joining a partner’s family that doesn’t quite want them
a colleague moved sideways into a role they didn’t choose
a friend moving abroad for a spouse’s career
anyone overlooked for years who refused to flatter the gatekeeper
tale.open: “There’s a Chinese story about a woman everyone overlooked, and the one day they finally saw her it was too late.”
tale.pause: Pause after “Zhaojun, the history says, asked to go,” because that choice is the turn of the whole story.
tale.close: End with the Green Tomb, the grass that stays green when everything else turns gold, and say nothing more.
tale.lesson: From a position with little power, dignity and a long view can still shape how things end.

also.title: Leah and Rachel
also.source: Hebrew Bible · Genesis 29 · written down c. 1st millennium BCE
also.gist: Jacob loved Rachel and worked seven years for her father Laban, and the years seemed like a few days. On the wedding night Laban sent in his elder daughter Leah instead, and in the morning, there was Leah. “It is not our custom to give the younger before the firstborn,” said Laban. So Jacob worked seven more years for Rachel. Leah, the unloved wife, bore sons and named them with longing: surely now my husband will love me. With her fourth son she said only, “This time I will praise the Lord,” and called him Judah.
also.fits: The Marrying Maiden from inside: Leah is placed where she cannot win the love she wants. Her turn at Judah, ceasing to bargain for a place, is the second line’s steadiness of a solitary person.

name: Abundance
theme: At the very top of good fortune, the wisest thing is to shine fully and remember it will not last.

tale.title: This Too Shall Pass
tale.source: Jewish folk tale of King Solomon and Benaiah, with Persian and Sufi parallels about a king’s ring · told widely from the 19th century; legend set c. 10th century BCE
tale.text:
