King Solomon had everything. Gold came to Jerusalem by the shipload. Kings travelled across deserts to hear his wisdom. His palace was the wonder of the world.

He also had a loyal minister named Benaiah, a brave and serious man, and Solomon, the story goes, thought it would do Benaiah good to be humbled a little. So one day he called him in.

“Benaiah, I have heard of a ring with a special power. If a sad man looks at it, he becomes happy. If a happy man looks at it, he becomes sad. I want it by the festival of Sukkot.” That was six months away.

Benaiah bowed and set out. He asked goldsmiths in the great markets. He asked traders from Egypt and Babylon and Sheba. Nobody had heard of such a ring. Spring went by, then summer. The festival came closer, and Benaiah grew grey with worry.

The night before Sukkot, tired and hopeless, he wandered into one of the poorest streets of Jerusalem. There, an old man was laying out cheap trinkets on a cloth. Almost without hope, Benaiah asked him. The old man listened, said nothing, picked up a plain gold band, and with a small tool scratched three Hebrew letters into it. He handed it over.

Benaiah read the letters, and he smiled.

The next day the court was full. Solomon sat on his throne in all his splendour, and the courtiers were already grinning, waiting to see the minister fail. “Well, Benaiah,” said the king. “Have you found my ring?”

“I have, my lord.” And he put it in the king’s hand.

Solomon looked at the three letters, gimel, zayin, yod. Gam zeh ya’avor. “This too shall pass.”

And the smile went out of his face. He looked around at the gold, the courtiers, the great hall, and saw that all of it would pass. And in that same moment he understood the other half: that every sorrow would pass too.

They say he wore that plain ring for the rest of his life.
beats: Solomon at the height of his glory
He sends Benaiah for an impossible ring, by Sukkot
Six months of searching; nobody has heard of it
Last night: an old man in a poor street
Three letters scratched into a plain gold band
“This too shall pass”: the king’s smile fades
He wears the plain ring always
tale.fits: Abundance is the sun at noon: full, bright, and just about to begin its decline. The Judgment says only the king reaches it, and immediately adds, do not grieve. Solomon is that king, and the ring is the noon sun’s knowledge that it will set. The top line warns of the grand, abundant house that shuts its owner away from everyone; the plain ring from the poorest street pulls him back out of it. And the Image’s clarity, lightning lighting up the whole scene at once, is that moment when he sees the hall as it truly is.
when: a friend at the peak of a dream job or big success
someone in the first giddy weeks of a new love
a colleague riding high and getting a little careless
a person in a dark patch who thinks it will never end
tale.open: “Do you know where ‘this too shall pass’ comes from? There’s an old story about King Solomon.”
tale.pause: Pause after “Benaiah read the letters, and he smiled,” and keep the words secret until the king reads them.
tale.close: Say quietly, “They say he wore that plain ring for the rest of his life,” and stop.
tale.lesson: Every height and every low will pass, so shine fully now and hold it lightly.

also.title: The Ring of Polycrates
also.source: Greece · Herodotus, Histories 3.39 to 43 · c. 430 BCE, about events of the 6th century BCE
also.gist: Polycrates, tyrant of Samos, succeeded at everything. His ally, King Amasis of Egypt, wrote to warn him: the gods envy such luck. Throw away the thing you value most, so that your fortune is mixed with some loss. Polycrates chose his emerald signet ring, rowed out to sea, and threw it into the waves. A few days later a fisherman brought him a splendid fish as a gift, and when the cooks cut it open, there was the ring. Hearing this, Amasis broke off the alliance, sure that such a man would come to a terrible end. In time, he did.
also.fits: The shadow of Abundance: instead of shining like the noon sun without grief, Polycrates tries to bargain with the decline, and the sea will not take his offering.

name: The Wanderer
theme: Far from home and without standing, how we take an insult decides whether we ever get home at all.

tale.title: Chong’er and the Clod of Earth
tale.source: China · Zuozhuan, Duke Xi year 23, also in the Guoyu and Shiji · events of the 7th century BCE
tale.text:
In the seventh century before Christ, a prince named Chong’er fled the state of Jin. His father’s favourite wife was plotting to clear the way for her own son, and an assassin was already on his trail. So Chong’er ran, with a handful of loyal companions, and became a man without a country.

He lived among the Di tribes of the north for twelve years. Then he set out again, travelling from one court to another, looking for a ruler who would help him home.

In the state of Wei, the duke would not even receive him properly. So they kept moving. By the time they reached a place called Wulu, out in the countryside, they had nothing left to eat. A farmer was working nearby, and the prince, who had been born in a palace, swallowed his pride and asked him for food.

The farmer looked at the ragged prince and his ragged men. Then he bent down, picked up a clod of earth, and held it out.

Chong’er went red with fury. He reached for his whip.

His uncle Zifan, the wisest of his companions, caught his arm. “It is a gift from Heaven,” he said. Soil, from the hand of a man of the land: what else could it mean, but that one day this land would be his?

The prince stood still. Then he bowed his head all the way to the ground, received the clod of earth with both hands, and put it in his carriage.

He wandered on, for years. In Qi he was given a wife and twenty teams of horses, and he grew so comfortable that his companions had to get him drunk and carry him off in a cart, so that he would not forget why he was travelling. He was snubbed in some courts, welcomed in others, and he learned which was which.

Nineteen years after he fled, he crossed the Yellow River back into Jin and became its ruler, Duke Wen. Within a few years he was the most powerful lord in all of China.

He had carried that clod of earth a long way.
beats: Prince Chong’er flees a palace plot
Twelve years among the Di, then years on the road
Hungry at Wulu, he begs a farmer for food
The farmer hands him a clod of earth
He reaches for his whip; Zifan stops him
“A gift from Heaven”: he bows and keeps it
Nineteen years later: Duke Wen of Jin
tale.fits: The Wanderer has no home ground, no allies and no position, and the Judgment promises only small success, kept by conduct. Chong’er’s whole fate turns on a small moment. The first line warns that the wanderer who frets over petty slights brings disaster on himself, and the whip is that disaster half drawn. The fifth line, one arrow lost to shoot the pheasant and in the end praise and a position, is the pride he gives up when he bows to a clod of earth. Even Qi fits: the Wanderer must not overstay.
when: a friend newly abroad who feels snubbed by the locals
someone humiliated in a temporary or junior job
a person starting over after losing their position
a traveller tempted to make a scene over poor treatment
tale.open: “There’s a story about a Chinese prince in exile who begged a farmer for food and was handed a lump of dirt.”
tale.pause: Pause when Chong’er reaches for his whip, and let the listener feel the insult before Zifan speaks.
tale.close: End on “He had carried that clod of earth a long way,” and let them work out the rest.
tale.lesson: Far from home, how you receive an insult can turn it into a promise.

also.title: Odysseus among the Phaeacians
also.source: Greece · Homer, Odyssey, Books 6 to 8 · c. 8th century BCE
also.gist: Shipwrecked and naked, Odysseus washed up on the island of the Phaeacians and slept under the bushes. Woken by girls playing by the river, he covered himself with a leafy branch and spoke gently to the princess Nausicaa from a distance. She gave him clothes and told him to kneel to her mother, Queen Arete. In the palace he was welcomed, though he would not yet give his name. A young man mocked him; he hurled a discus beyond all the others. When the bard sang of Troy, he hid his face in his cloak and wept. Then he told who he was, and they sent him home.
also.fits: The Wanderer done well: the second line’s traveller who keeps his means close and finds a welcome. His courtesy as a stranger is the conduct the Judgment asks for, and it carries him home.

name: The Gentle
theme: When force has failed and what is needed is patient, attentive work that finds the natural way through.

tale.title: Cook Ding Carves the Ox
tale.source: China · Zhuangzi, chapter 3 (‘The Secret of Caring for Life’) · c. 4th century BCE
tale.text:
Long ago in China, a cook named Ding was carving up an ox for Lord Wenhui.

His hand touched the hide. His shoulder leaned, his foot planted, his knee pressed. And the blade whispered, the meat parted with a soft hiss, and every sound fell in time, like dancers keeping to an old court tune.

The lord was delighted. “Wonderful! How can skill go as far as this?” Ding laid down his knife. “What I care about is the Way, my lord. It goes further than skill. When I began, all I could see was the ox, the whole great mountain of it. After three years I no longer saw the whole ox. Now I meet it with my spirit, not my eyes. I let my senses rest and follow the grain. I slip into the big gaps, I steer along the hollows, I go with how it is made. I never touch a tendon or a ligament, let alone a bone.”

He held up the knife. “A good cook changes his knife once a year, because he cuts. An ordinary cook changes it every month, because he hacks. I have had this one nineteen years. It has done thousands of oxen, and the edge is as keen as the day it came off the whetstone. You see, the joints have spaces, and the blade has no thickness. Put what has no thickness into a space, and there is room, more than room, for it to move.

“Even so, when I come to a knotted place, I see the trouble. I take care. My eyes settle. I slow right down. I move the blade the smallest amount, and then, with a soft thud, it all comes apart, like a clod of earth crumbling to the ground. Then I stand there, knife in hand, and look around me, content. I wipe the blade, and I put it away.”

Lord Wenhui said, “Excellent. From the words of a cook, I have learned how to care for a life.”
beats: Cook Ding carves an ox before Lord Wenhui
Every movement in rhythm, like a court dance
The lord asks: how can skill go so far?
First he saw the whole ox; now only its spaces
Nineteen years, thousands of oxen, the knife still sharp
At the knotted places: slow, careful, the smallest movement
It falls apart like earth; he wipes the knife
tale.fits: The Gentle is wind that gets through by following openings, not by force, and its Judgment promises only ‘small success’ to one with a clear direction. Ding’s knife is that wind: it finds the gaps already there. The hacking cook who wears out a blade every month is the nine in the third place, ‘penetrating again and again’, pushing until it ends in humiliation. And at the knotted place Ding does what the second line asks: he slows down and searches carefully until the hidden structure shows itself.
when: a colleague grinding through a problem by sheer force and exhausted
someone learning a craft who is frustrated by slow progress
a parent locked in a battle of wills with a teenager
a friend about to try the same blunt approach a third time
tale.open: Have you ever watched someone really good at a job make it look like nothing? There’s an old Chinese story about a cook like that.
tale.pause: Pause after ‘nineteen years’ and let the listener picture the knife still gleaming, because that number carries the whole story.
tale.close: End on him wiping the blade and putting it away; if you add anything, wonder aloud, ‘I wonder where the gaps are in this one.’
tale.lesson: Lasting progress comes from finding the grain of a thing and working with it, slowly at the hard parts, rather than forcing through.

also.title: The Tongue and the Teeth
also.source: China · Shuo yuan, compiled by Liu Xiang · 1st century BCE (Laozi and his old teacher Chang Cong)
also.gist: Old Chang Cong lay dying, and his student Laozi came to ask whether he had any teaching left to give. The old man opened his mouth wide. “Is my tongue still there?” “It is.” “And my teeth?” “All gone.” “Do you understand why?” Laozi thought. “The tongue has lasted because it is soft. The teeth are gone because they were hard.” The old man nodded. “Yes. That is all the affairs of the world. I have nothing more to tell you.”
also.fits: It shows the softness at the heart of the Gentle: the yielding thing outlasts the hard one. Its shadow is that softness with no direction becomes the dithering of the first line, which is why Ding’s knife still needs its edge.

name: The Joyous
theme: When someone has withdrawn into gloom and no argument will bring them out, but shared, honest delight might.

tale.title: Amaterasu and the Cave of Laughter
tale.source: Japan · Kojiki (Record of Ancient Matters), book 1 · compiled 712 CE
tale.text:
In the oldest book of Japan, the sun was a goddess, Amaterasu, and her brother Susanoo was a god of storms. Susanoo ran wild through heaven. He broke down the ridges of her rice fields. He fouled her sacred hall. At last he flung a flayed horse through the roof of her weaving hall, and one of her weaving women was struck and died. Amaterasu had had enough. She went into the Rock Cave of Heaven, pulled the stone door shut, and stayed there.

The world went dark. Night after night, and no dawn. Every kind of trouble crept out of the corners. So the gods, eight hundred myriads of them, gathered on the dry bed of the river of heaven to think. Clever Omoikane made a plan. They brought the long-crying birds of the dawn and set them crowing. They forged a mirror and strung curved jewels, and hung them on a sakaki tree before the cave. Strong Tajikarao hid beside the door.

Then the goddess Ame-no-Uzume turned a tub upside down in front of the cave and climbed on it. She stamped until the boards boomed. She danced as if possessed, and in her wildness her clothes came loose until there was almost nothing left. And the gods laughed. Eight hundred myriad gods, laughing all together, until the high plain of heaven shook.

Inside, Amaterasu was puzzled. She opened the door a crack. “I am hidden, and the world is dark. So why is Uzume dancing? Why are you all laughing?” “We are glad,” said Uzume, “because there is a goddess here more glorious than you.”

They held up the mirror. Amaterasu saw a shining face, and leaned out, wondering. Tajikarao took her hand and drew her out, and another god stretched a sacred rope across the cave mouth behind her. “No further back than this.”

And the light came back to the world.
beats: Storm god Susanoo wrecks heaven; a weaving woman dies
Amaterasu shuts herself in the Rock Cave
The world goes dark; all the gods gather
Crowing birds, a mirror, jewels, a strongman by the door
Uzume dances on a tub; the gods roar with laughter
Curious, the sun peeks out and sees her own light
She is drawn out; a rope behind her; light returns
tale.fits: The Joyous is lake upon lake, gladness that spreads by being shared, and its Image is friends gathered to talk and act together. The gods do not argue Amaterasu out of her cave or break the door: they meet, plan together, and laugh together until curiosity opens it from inside. The Judgment says joy succeeds when it stays true, and the nine in the second place calls it ‘sincere joy’. The laughter is real, not a show staged at her, and that is why it works.
when: a friend who has gone quiet after being badly hurt
a household or team that has lost all its lightness
someone trying to reason a sulking person back to cheerfulness
friends planning how to lift someone without pressuring them
tale.open: There’s a Japanese myth about the time the sun hid in a cave, and what finally got her out isn’t what you’d expect.
tale.pause: Pause after ‘the gods laughed’ and let a moment of silence stand in for the sound of heaven shaking.
tale.close: Finish with ‘And the light came back to the world,’ then leave it; at most add, ‘Funny what gets a door open.’
tale.lesson: Shared, honest gladness can draw out what persuasion and force cannot.

also.title: The Happiness of Fish
also.source: China · Zhuangzi, chapter 17 (‘Autumn Floods’) · c. 4th to 3rd century BCE
also.gist: Zhuangzi and his friend, the logician Huizi, were strolling on a bridge over the river Hao. “Look how the minnows dart about, free and easy,” said Zhuangzi. “That is the happiness of fish.” “You are not a fish,” said Huizi. “How do you know what makes fish happy?” “You are not me. How do you know I don’t know?” “I am not you, so I don’t know about you. And you are not a fish, so that settles it.” “Let’s go back to the start,” said Zhuangzi. “You asked how I knew, so you already knew that I knew. I know it from here, on the bridge over the Hao.”
also.fits: Two friends sparring beside the water is the Image of two lakes that refresh each other. It also shows how easily delight can be argued away, and how gladly Zhuangzi refuses to let it go.

name: Dispersion
theme: When people are scattered or in danger, and the only thing that will gather them is a real sacrifice.

tale.title: The Burning of the Rice Fields
tale.source: Japan · Lafcadio Hearn, ‘A Living God’, in Gleanings in Buddha-Fields, 1897; based on Hamaguchi Goryō and the Ansei Nankai tsunami of 1854 at Hiro, Kii Province
tale.text:
On the coast of Japan, on a hill above a fishing village, lived an old man named Hamaguchi. He was the richest farmer there, and the village looked up to him. His whole year’s rice harvest stood in stacks on the level ground beside his house. It was an autumn evening, and down in the village the people were getting ready for the harvest festival. Hamaguchi stood watching the lanterns go up. Then the ground shook. Not hard: a long, slow, rolling shudder, the kind people shrug off.

But Hamaguchi kept looking at the sea. It had turned dark and strange, and it was running backward, away from the land, against the wind. Sand and rocks lay bare that no one had ever seen. People were wandering down to the beach to stare. He had heard of this from his grandfather. He knew what came back after the sea went out like that. And there was no time to go down and tell them.

“Tada!” he called to his little grandson. “Quick, light me a torch!” The boy brought it. And the old man went from stack to stack of his own rice, his whole fortune, and set every one alight. They roared up into the dusk. The boy stared at him, frightened, sure his grandfather had lost his mind.

At the temple on the hill someone saw the flames and rang the great bell. Down below, the villagers looked up and saw the headman’s place on fire. Up the slope they came running, the young men first, then everyone, the old folk, the mothers with babies on their backs. “Let it burn,” said Hamaguchi, and he stopped them at the top. “Is everyone here?”

Then he turned and pointed out to sea. “Look.” A long dark line was coming across the water, rising like a cliff. It struck the shore with a sound like thunder, then again, and again. When the water drew back, the village was gone.

The people stood on the hill among the smoking ashes of his rice. Alive.
beats: A rich old farmer on a hill above a fishing village
Festival evening; a long, slow earthquake
The sea runs backward, away from the land
No time to warn them; he calls for a torch
He burns all his rice; the temple bell rings
The village runs uphill to fight the fire
The great wave takes the empty village below
tale.fits: Dispersion is wind on water breaking up what is frozen and drawing scattered people together, and its Judgment says ‘the king goes to his temple’: the village later honoured Hamaguchi with a shrine. He is the nine in the fifth place, who ‘disperses the royal stores’ in a crisis, and the six in the third, who ‘dissolves his self’, giving up his fortune without a second thought. The top line’s advice, get out and keep far off from harm, is exactly where his fire leads everyone.
when: a manager deciding whether to spend something personal to protect the team
someone who can see trouble coming that everyone else ignores
a family member giving up something precious to bring everyone together
a friend who thinks a polite warning will never be heard
tale.open: Lafcadio Hearn wrote down a story from Japan about an old man who set fire to everything he owned, and was right to.
tale.pause: Pause when the sea runs backward, so the listener can realise what it means before the old man does anything.
tale.close: End with the people standing alive in the ashes, and add only: ‘They built a shrine to him while he was still living.’
tale.lesson: Sometimes the only call loud enough to gather people out of danger is giving up what you hold dearest.

also.title: The Gift of the Magi
also.source: United States · O. Henry, short story ‘The Gift of the Magi’ · 1905
also.gist: Della has one dollar and eighty-seven cents the day before Christmas, and she wants to give her husband Jim something worthy of him. So she sells the thing she is proudest of, her long, rippling hair, and buys a fine platinum chain for his treasured gold watch. That evening Jim comes in and stares at her cropped head. He has sold his watch, the thing he is proudest of, to buy her a set of beautiful combs for the hair she no longer has. They put the presents away for a while, and Della starts the supper.
also.fits: Each dissolves their own pride for the other, as the six in the third place asks. The sacrifices cancel out as things, and gather the two of them together, the kind of gathering the fourth line says ordinary people do not think of.

name: Limitation
theme: When wanting more has no end, and someone cannot say where enough is.

tale.title: The Fisherman and His Wife
tale.source: Germany · Brothers Grimm, Children’s and Household Tales no. 19, from Philipp Otto Runge’s Low German telling · 1812
tale.text:
There was once a fisherman who lived with his wife Ilsebill in a miserable hovel close by the sea. Every day he went out and fished. One day he pulled up a great flounder, and the flounder spoke. “Let me live, fisherman. I’m not a real fish, I’m an enchanted prince. I wouldn’t even taste good.” “No need for so many words,” said the fisherman. “A fish that can talk, I’d let go anyway.” He put it back, and it sank, leaving a long thread of blood in the water.

At home he told his wife. “And you didn’t wish for anything? Go back. Tell it we want a little cottage.” So he went down to the shore. The sea had turned green and yellow. He called out: “Flounder, flounder in the sea, come up quick and hear my plea; my good wife Ilsebill wants what I’d not want for me.” The flounder came. “Well, what does she want?” And when he got home, there was a neat little cottage, with a kitchen and a garden and hens.

For a week or two it was fine. Then she wanted a stone castle. The sea was purple and grey and thick, and he went, and she had it. Then she wanted to be king, and the sea was dark and bubbling and smelled foul, and she was king. Then emperor, with the water black and boiling. Then pope, in a gale, with the sky red at its edges. Each time he went with a heavier heart, and each time she had it.

Then one morning she woke, saw the sun coming up, and could not bear that she had not made it rise. “Go to the flounder. I want to be like God.” He went out into a storm that tore up trees and tossed ships about, with waves as tall as church towers, and he called, and the flounder came.

“Well, what does she want now?” “She wants to be like God.” “Go home,” said the flounder. “She’s sitting in her hovel again.”

And there they sit, the two of them, to this very day.
beats: A fisherman and his wife in a hovel by the sea
He catches a talking flounder and lets it go
She sends him back: a cottage, granted
Castle, king, emperor, pope; the sea darkens each time
She wants to make the sun rise, to be like God
In the storm, the flounder sends him home
She is sitting in her hovel again
tale.fits: Limitation’s Image is a lake that can hold only so much; beyond that it spills. Ilsebill has no measure at all, and the sea shows it, darker and wilder with every wish. She is the six in the third place: ‘those who do not keep limits will have to lament; no one else to blame.’ Her husband, who keeps going though his heart grows heavier, shows the quieter failure: a limit felt but never spoken. The end puts them back in the hovel, the one limit nobody can argue with.
when: a friend whose every promotion only makes them hungrier
someone who keeps going along with demands they know are too much
a couple whose house renovation keeps growing and growing
a person who struggles to say ‘that’s enough’ to themselves
tale.open: Do you know the Grimm story about the fisherman’s wife? It’s the best story I know about wanting more.
tale.pause: Slow down each time the fisherman reaches the shore and describe the colour of the sea, because the sea is telling the real story.
tale.close: Say the flounder’s line, ‘She’s sitting in her hovel again,’ and let it rest; if anything, ask, ‘Where do you think she should have stopped?’
tale.lesson: Without a sense of enough, every gain is lost; a limit kept willingly is what keeps the good things.

also.title: Māui Snares the Sun
also.source: Polynesia · Hawaiian and Māori oral tradition of the demigod Māui
also.gist: Long ago the sun raced across the sky so fast that the days were too short. In the Hawaiian telling, Māui’s mother Hina could never get her bark cloth dry before dark. So Māui made strong ropes and climbed to where the sun rises, the great mountain Haleakalā. As the sun came up he snared its rays, one by one, and held it fast, and would not let go until it promised to travel more slowly. In the Māori telling he goes with his brothers, ropes the sun, and beats it with his grandmother’s magic jawbone. Ever since, the days have been long enough.
also.fits: Here the limit falls on something too fast and too free, and it is agreed rather than simply imposed: a ‘sweet limitation’, as the nine in the fifth place calls it, which gives the day its proper shape.

name: Inner Truth
theme: When someone wants to win trust, or to use it, and finds that hidden intentions are felt before anything is said.

tale.title: The Man Who Loved the Seagulls
tale.source: China · Liezi, chapter 2 (‘The Yellow Emperor’) · text compiled c. 4th century CE from earlier Daoist material
tale.text:
By the sea in old China there lived a man who loved the seagulls. Every morning, at first light, he went down to the shore and out onto the water, and the gulls came to him. Not one or two. Hundreds of them, more than he could count, wheeling down out of the sky to land around him. They walked about at his feet. They bobbed on the waves beside him. They stood close and looked at him sideways with their bright yellow eyes. He wanted nothing from them, and somehow they knew it. He spent all morning among them, and in the evening he came home with salt in his hair and nothing in his hands, happy.

People talked about him. The man the gulls come to. One evening his father said, “I hear the gulls all flock to you and play with you. Catch a few and bring them home for me. I’d like to play with them too.” It was a small thing to ask. Just a few birds, for his own father. The son said he would.

Next morning he went down to the shore as always. He walked the same way, at the same hour, with the same easy step, his hands loose at his sides. Out onto the water, as always. He looked up.

The gulls were there. They wheeled and danced in the air above him, crying, hundreds of them, as many as ever. They circled, and circled, and circled.

Not one came down.

The old book that tells this story adds only a few words after it. The finest speech leaves words behind. The finest doing does nothing. What ordinary cleverness knows is shallow.
beats: A man by the sea who loves the gulls
Every morning hundreds land all around him
He wants nothing from them; they come close
His father asks: catch me a few
Next morning, the same shore, the same easy step
The gulls dance overhead and never come down
tale.fits: Inner Truth’s Judgment speaks of sincerity that reaches even ‘pigs and fishes’, the creatures least moved by words. The gulls are those creatures. Nothing in the man’s face or walk changes on the last morning, but the truth inside him has, and they feel it. The nine in the second place, the crane calling from the shade and its young answering, is the first half of the story: true feeling needs no stage. The ending is the warning hidden inside that line.
when: someone puzzled that people have quietly grown wary of them
a person who loves their clients and is now under sales pressure
a friend tempted to use something told to them in confidence
a parent wondering why their child has stopped confiding
tale.open: There’s a tiny story in an old Daoist book about a man who was friends with the seagulls.
tale.pause: Pause after ‘He looked up,’ and make the listener wait to learn what the gulls will do.
tale.close: End on ‘Not one came down,’ and stop there; leave the old book’s words out if the silence is already doing the work.
tale.lesson: Trust answers to what is really in your heart, and outward behaviour cannot hide a changed intention.

also.title: The Shepherd Boy’s Whistle
also.source: Jewish · Hasidic tale told of the Baal Shem Tov, 18th-century Podolia (oral tradition)
also.gist: On Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the year, a simple shepherd boy came to the synagogue where the Baal Shem Tov was praying. He could not read, and he did not know the prayers. All day he stood and watched, and as the last prayers rose toward the close of the fast he could hold himself in no longer. He pulled out the little whistle he used for his flock and blew it, loud and shrill. People turned on him in outrage. But the Baal Shem Tov raised his hand. Their prayers had been stuck, he said, and that whistle had carried them all up to heaven.
also.fits: The bright side of Inner Truth: a heart with nothing hidden reaches heaven without the proper words, and, like the fifth line’s truth that binds others together, lifts everyone’s prayers with it.

name: Small Exceeding
theme: When pride makes it hard to keep quiet, and one small retort could undo everything.

tale.title: The Tortoise Who Talked Too Much
tale.source: India · Kacchapa Jātaka (Jātaka no. 215), Pali Buddhist canon and commentary · c. 4th century BCE to 5th century CE
tale.text:
In the old Buddhist birth stories of India, there was a king of Benares who talked and talked. Nobody else could get a word in. His wise counsellor wanted to cure him of it, and waited for the right moment.

Now far away, in a pond in the Himalayas, lived a tortoise. Two young wild geese came there to feed, and the three of them became friends. One day the geese said, “Friend, we have a lovely home, a golden cave on Mount Cittakuta. Come and live with us.” “How could I get there? I’m a tortoise.” “We can carry you, if you can keep your mouth shut. Not one word, all the way.” “Easy,” said the tortoise.

So the geese found a stick. The tortoise bit hard on the middle, the geese took the two ends in their beaks, and up they rose into the sky. Over the hills, over the rivers. The whole world lay spread out below like a cloth. They flew over a village, and the children saw them. “Look! Look! Two geese carrying a tortoise on a stick!”

The tortoise heard them laughing. He badly wanted to say, “If my friends choose to carry me, what business is it of yours, you wretched brats?” The geese were flying fast, and by now they were right above the king’s palace in Benares. The tortoise opened his mouth. He let go of the stick. He fell, straight down into the open courtyard of the palace, and split in two.

There was a great commotion. The king came out with his courtiers to find a tortoise lying broken on his stones. “How did this happen?” The counsellor saw his moment. “Your majesty, this is what comes to those who cannot hold their tongue.” And he told the king the whole story.

The king was quiet for a while. From that day on, they say, he spoke less.
beats: A king who never stops talking; a patient counsellor
A tortoise befriends two wild geese
They offer to fly him home on a stick
One rule: not a single word
Children below point and laugh
He opens his mouth to answer them
He falls into the courtyard; the king speaks less
tale.fits: Small Exceeding’s Judgment carries the message of a flying bird: ‘it is not good to climb, it is good to stay low.’ The tortoise is carried higher than any tortoise belongs, and the one small thing asked of him is restraint. The six at the top, which ‘passes far beyond’ and is caught in the net, is his fall. The counsellor shows the Image instead: a little more care than seems needed, waiting quietly for the right small moment to speak.
when: a colleague itching to fire back at a provoking email
a friend who must bite their tongue at a family dinner
someone newly promoted who keeps explaining and defending themselves
a person who talks over everyone in meetings
tale.open: Have you heard the one about the tortoise who learned to fly? It’s from the old Buddhist Jātaka tales.
tale.pause: Pause when the children shout, and let the listener feel how badly the tortoise wants to answer them.
tale.close: Close with ‘From that day on, they say, he spoke less,’ and add nothing.
tale.lesson: When you have been lifted beyond your usual place, small restraint is everything; the need for the last word can bring you down.

also.title: The Talking Skull
also.source: Nigeria · Nupe folk tale, recorded in the early 20th century
also.gist: A hunter in the bush came upon an old skull and asked it, half joking, “What brought you here?” The skull answered, “Talking brought me here.” The hunter ran to tell the king. The king did not believe him, and sent guards back with him under orders: if the skull would not speak, the hunter was to die. All day the hunter begged the skull to say something. It stayed silent. So the guards carried out their orders and went home. When they had gone, the skull asked the hunter’s head, “What brought you here?” And the head answered, “Talking brought me here.”
also.fits: The shadow of Small Exceeding: a man meets something extraordinary and cannot help carrying it straight to the top. He flies too high with his news and, like the bird of the top line, is caught.

name: After Completion
theme: When things have finally come right, and the danger is forgetting how hard it was to get here.

tale.title: “Do Not Forget Ju”
tale.source: China · Lüshi chunqiu (c. 239 BCE) and Liu Xiang’s Xin xu (1st century BCE) · setting: Duke Huan of Qi, 7th century BCE
tale.text:
In the seventh century before our era, the state of Qi in China stood at the height of its power. Duke Huan ruled it. Guan Zhong was his chief minister, still remembered as one of the great statesmen of China. Ning Qi was another trusted officer, and Bao Shuya was the duke’s oldest friend and counsellor.

It had not always been like this. Years before, when Qi fell into chaos, the young prince who would become Duke Huan had to flee for his life to the little state of Ju, a prince with nowhere to call home. Guan Zhong had served his rival brother, and in the race for the throne had even shot an arrow at him, which struck his belt buckle. Afterwards Guan Zhong was sent back from Lu in bonds, a prisoner, until Bao Shuya persuaded the new duke to make him minister instead. And Ning Qi had been a poor carter, feeding his ox under his wagon at night and singing a sad song, when the duke passed by, heard him, and took him into his service.

Now the four of them sat together at a feast. The wine went round. The duke was happy. “Bao Shuya,” he said, “why don’t you rise and drink to my long life?” Bao Shuya stood and raised his cup.

“I wish that my lord will never forget the time he was a fugitive in Ju. I wish that Guan Zhong will never forget the time he was bound in Lu. And I wish that Ning Qi will never forget the time he fed his ox beneath the cart.”

The hall was silent. Then Duke Huan rose from his mat and bowed to his friend, twice. “If I and my officers can all keep from forgetting what you have just said,” he said, “then the altars of Qi will be in no danger.”
beats: Qi at its height: the duke and three great men
Once, the duke was a fugitive in Ju
Guan Zhong a prisoner from Lu; Ning Qi a poor carter
At a feast, the duke asks Bao Shuya for a toast
‘Never forget Ju’, and the other two hard times
Silence; then the duke bows twice
tale.fits: After Completion is water over fire, everything in its place, with the Judgment’s warning: ‘good fortune at the beginning, disorder at the end.’ Its Image asks the wise person to think ahead to trouble and guard against it in advance, and Bao Shuya does exactly that in the middle of a celebration. His toast is the six in the fourth place, ‘be on guard all day long’, said in the kindest way possible, and it keeps the duke from the top line’s fate of getting in over his head.
when: a friend who has just made it and is starting to coast
a couple settled at last after some lean years
a founder whose company has finally stopped struggling
someone asked to give a toast at a promotion or anniversary
tale.open: There’s a famous toast from ancient China that I always think of at celebrations.
tale.pause: Pause after ‘The hall was silent,’ so the listener can wonder whether the duke will be offended.
tale.close: End with the duke’s words about the altars of Qi; if the moment allows, raise your own cup and say only, ‘To Ju.’
tale.lesson: Success stays safe only while you remember the hard times that made it.

also.title: The Sword of Damocles
also.source: Rome · Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 5.61-62 · 45 BCE (about Dionysius I of Syracuse, 4th century BCE)
also.gist: Damocles, a flatterer at the court of Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse, kept telling him how happy he must be, with all his wealth and power. “Would you like to try my life?” asked Dionysius. He set Damocles on a golden couch among rich tapestries, with silver and gold on the tables, perfumes, garlands, the finest food, and handsome servants waiting on him. Damocles thought himself the luckiest man alive. Then he looked up. Over his neck hung a gleaming sword, held by a single horsehair. He stopped eating and stopped admiring, and soon begged to be let go: he no longer wanted to be so happy.
also.fits: The shadow side of After Completion: success at its peak, with the danger hanging right above it. Damocles sees in one glance what the duke needed a friend to remind him of.

name: Before Completion
theme: When the end is almost in reach and the hardest thing is to keep trusting for the last few steps.

tale.title: Orpheus and Eurydice
tale.source: Greece and Rome · Virgil, Georgics 4 (29 BCE) and Ovid, Metamorphoses 10 (c. 8 CE); this telling follows Ovid
tale.text:
Orpheus was the greatest singer who ever lived. When he played his lyre, wild beasts lay down to listen, and trees leaned toward him. He married Eurydice. But just after the wedding, as she walked in a meadow with her friends, a snake bit her heel, and she died.

Orpheus mourned until the upper world had heard all his grief. Then he did what no living man does. He went down through the dark gate at Taenarus, past the crowds of pale shades, all the way to the throne of the king and queen of the dead. And there he sang. He had not come to see the sights of the underworld, he sang. He had come for his wife, whose years were stolen. Let her go, only for a while: in the end every one of us comes back to you. Let her be a loan, not a gift.

And the dead listened. Tantalus stopped reaching for the water. The wheel of Ixion stood still. Sisyphus sat down on his stone. The Furies, for the first time, wept. The king and queen could not refuse.

They called Eurydice. She came, still limping from her wound. There was one condition. Orpheus must lead her up, and must not turn to look at her until they were out of the valley of the dead. If he did, the gift was void.

So they climbed. A steep path, through silence and thick, dark mist. He could not hear her steps. Was she there? Was she tiring? They were close now, very close to the edge of the light. Afraid she was falling behind, and longing to see her, he turned.

She was already slipping back. He reached out and caught only air. She did not blame him: what could she complain of, except that she was loved? She said one last farewell, so faint it barely reached him, and was gone.
beats: Orpheus the singer; Eurydice dies just after the wedding
He goes down alive into the underworld
His song makes even the damned stop and weep
She may follow, if he never looks back
The steep, dark climb; he cannot hear her
Almost at the light, he turns
She slips away with a faint farewell
tale.fits: Before Completion’s Judgment is the little fox that has almost crossed the river and then wets its tail: ‘nothing helps.’ Orpheus has done the impossible part; what remains is a few steps of trust, and that is where it fails. Fire above water, everything not yet in place, is the misty path where he cannot see her. The nine in the second place names what was needed: ‘he brakes his wheels; staying steady brings good fortune.’ He could not stay steady to the edge.
when: a friend in the last month of a long degree or project
someone who keeps testing whether a new relationship is real
a person waiting on final results who cannot stop checking
a colleague tempted to peek early and spoil a launch
tale.open: You know the story of Orpheus? It’s the oldest story I know about the last few steps being the hardest.
tale.pause: Slow right down on the climb, at ‘He could not hear her steps’, so the listener feels the silence that makes him turn.
tale.close: End on her faint farewell and let it sit; or ask quietly, ‘How close do you think they were?’
tale.lesson: The last stretch needs as much trust and steadiness as the first; doubt at the very edge can undo everything.

also.title: One Basket Short of the Mountain
also.source: China · Book of Documents (Shujing), chapter ‘The Hounds of Lü’ (Lü ao) · set in the early Zhou, 11th century BCE; this chapter is of disputed, later date
also.gist: After the Zhou conquered the Shang, the Lü people of the west sent King Wu a tribute gift: a huge hunting hound. The king was delighted. His Grand Protector, the Duke of Shao, warned him. A ruler who delights in strange treasures loses his purpose, he said. Be careful morning and night: if you neglect small conduct, it will stain your great virtue in the end. It is like raising a mountain nine fathoms high, where the whole work can fail for want of a single basket of earth.
also.fits: The proverb form of the little fox’s wet tail: the work is nearly done, and a small slackening at the end, not a great failure, is what leaves it unfinished.
